big-o.name: Big O Notation
big-o.desc: A language for describing how running time and memory grow as the input size n grows, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. It is the first thing an interviewer asks after you propose an algorithm.
big-o.q: Is O(2n) the same as O(n)?
big-o.qsub: Why do we ignore constants and lower-order terms? · How do you count space complexity when recursion is involved? · When is an O(n log n) algorithm actually slower than an O(n²) one in practice?
big-o.what:
Imagine two functions that do the same job. With 10 items, both feel instant. With 1,000,000 items, one still answers instantly while the other takes several minutes. The difference isn't how elegant the code looks. It's how the work grows.

Big O describes that growth: as the input size n increases, how fast does the work increase? It doesn't give you seconds. It gives you the shape of the growth.

That's why a stopwatch is a poor tool here. Your laptop may be fast, the interviewer's may be slow, and the production server is different again. But O(n²) stays O(n²) on every machine.
big-o.analogy: Picture a wedding with 100 guests. If you shake each guest's hand once, that's 100 handshakes: O(n). Now suppose every guest shakes hands with every other guest. That's 4,950 handshakes (100 × 99 / 2). Double the guest list to 200 and you get 19,900, roughly four times as many. That is the pain of O(n²).
big-o.why:
Interviewers ask "what's the complexity?" because that one question shows whether you only wrote the code or actually thought about it. If you can't state the cost of your own solution, you can't improve it either.

It matters in real work too. An O(n²) loop that takes 200 ms on staging (100 rows) can take 30 seconds on prod (50,000 rows). Same code, different data, and you find out only when a customer complains.

How to think:

1. Identify n: the part of the input that can get large, such as array length, string size, or number of tree nodes.
2. Count loops and recursive calls. A loop inside a loop means you multiply (n × n). One loop after another means you add (n + n).
3. In a sum, keep only the biggest term: n² + n + 50 becomes n². At n = 10,000, n² is 100 million while n is only 10 thousand, so the smaller term stops mattering.
4. Drop constant factors: 3n becomes O(n).
5. Count space separately: extra arrays plus recursion depth. This is the step most people forget.
where: Array index, hash lookup · space: constant
Binary search on sorted input · space: constant
A single linear pass · space: usually constant
Merge sort, quick sort, heap operations · space: O(n) for merge sort

qa.q: Is O(2n) the same as O(n)?
qa.a: Yes. Big O ignores constant factors. Both describe linear growth: doubling the input roughly doubles the work. The constant 2 doesn't change how the curve scales, and for large n the gap between 2n and n is tiny compared to the gap between n and n².

qa.q: What is the complexity of a while loop that halves n on each iteration?
qa.a: O(log n). Each step removes half of the remaining input, so it takes about log2(n) steps to reach 1. Binary search is the classic example.

arrays.name: Arrays in JavaScript
arrays.desc: Indexed storage with O(1) access by index. In JS, arrays are special objects that track their own length, and methods like push, pop, splice and slice cover most of what you need.
arrays.q: Why is unshift O(n) but push O(1)?
arrays.qsub: How do you check whether an array is sorted in O(n)? · How do you rotate an array right by k in O(1) space? · What does arr.slice() with no arguments return?
arrays.what:
Think of a shelf of numbered boxes: box 0, box 1, box 2. If you want box 5, you reach straight for it without scanning the shelf. That is arr[5]: O(1), whether the array has 10 elements or 1,000,000.

In JS, an array is conceptually an object whose keys are index numbers, plus a length that updates automatically. Engines like V8 usually store dense arrays in one contiguous block of memory, which is why indexing is so fast.

Almost all of the cost comes from this layout. Work at the end (push/pop) and nothing else moves: O(1). Work at the start or middle (shift/unshift/splice) and every element after that point has to move by one position: O(n).
arrays.analogy: On a train, you walk straight to your seat by its number: O(1). But if a new passenger is inserted at seat 1, everyone behind them has to move down one seat: O(n). That is exactly what unshift does.
arrays.why:
Interviewers look for two things. First, do you know which methods modify the original array (push, splice, sort, reverse) and which return a new array (map, filter, slice)? Mixing these up is one of the most common sources of production bugs. For example, mutating React state in place can prevent a re-render.

Second, do you know the cost? Using shift in a loop to "remove elements from the front" quietly turns your solution into O(n²).

How to think:

1. Treat an array as an object keyed by index, with a hidden length counter that the engine keeps up to date.
2. When you read arr[i], the engine goes straight to that slot, which takes constant time.
3. On push, the engine reads length, writes the value into the next slot, and increments the counter. Nothing shifts.
4. On splice in the middle, the engine moves every later element by one position, which is O(n).
5. map, filter and slice build a brand-new array and leave the original untouched.

qa.q: Why is unshift O(n) but push O(1)?
qa.a: push appends at the end, where the array usually has spare capacity, so it is amortized O(1). unshift inserts at index 0, so every existing element must shift right by one position, which costs O(n).

qa.q: In-place vs creating a new array: when does it matter?
qa.a: In-place avoids O(n) extra space and often lets you solve the problem with two pointers in a single pass. Problems like Rotate Array and Set Matrix Zeroes explicitly ask for an in-place solution to test exactly this.

objects-map-set.name: Objects, Map, and Set
objects-map-set.desc: Hash-based structures with O(1) average lookup, insert and delete. Map keeps insertion order and accepts any key type; Set enforces uniqueness. They are the most-used tools in interviews.
objects-map-set.q: Map vs plain Object: which do you reach for, and why?
objects-map-set.qsub: Why is Set.has faster than indexOf on an array? · How do you build a frequency map of the characters in a string? · What happens when you set a key that already exists in a Map?
objects-map-set.what:
Think of the contact list on your phone: type a name and the number appears instantly. Whether you have 5 contacts or 5,000, the speed feels the same. The phone doesn't scan the whole list. It uses a formula (hashing) to jump straight to where that contact is stored.

Object, Map and Set all work on this principle, so insert, lookup and delete are all O(1) on average.

The differences: Object keys are strings (or symbols). Map accepts any key type and remembers insertion order. Set stores only values and automatically removes duplicates.
objects-map-set.analogy: It works like the index at the back of a book. To find "Recursion", you don't flip through every page. You look it up in the index and go straight to page 142. The hash function is that index.
objects-map-set.why:
This is the most useful tool in interviews. Whenever your solution becomes an O(n²) "for each element, search all the others" loop, the fix is almost always a hash-based structure.

The second test is whether you can choose between Map, Object and Set, and explain why you chose it.

How to think:

1. When you insert a key, a hash function converts it into a number.
2. That number decides which bucket in an internal array the entry goes into.
3. On lookup, the same hash function runs again and takes you directly to the right bucket, with no scan of the full data.
4. If two keys land in the same bucket (a collision), the entries are chained together there. So the worst case is O(n), but the average case is O(1).
5. Map also tracks insertion order, so iteration comes out in the order you added the keys.
where: O(1) average · space: O(1) per entry

qa.q: Map vs plain Object: which do you reach for, and why?
qa.a: Map. It accepts any key type, preserves insertion order, has a built-in size property, and avoids prototype-key collisions (such as a key named 'constructor'). For simple string-keyed counting either works, but Map is the safer default.

qa.q: Two Sum: why does a Map make it O(n)?
qa.a: Store each number with its index as you scan. For each x, check whether target - x is already in the map. That lookup is O(1), so one pass is enough instead of a nested loop.

recursion.name: Recursion
recursion.desc: A function that calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem. It needs two parts: a base case that stops the recursion and a recursive case that makes progress toward it. It is the backbone of trees, backtracking and DP.
recursion.q: What is the space complexity of recursion?
recursion.qsub: What happens if a recursive function has no base case? · How deep can recursion go in JS before a RangeError? · Why is naive Fibonacci exponential while the memoized version is O(n)?
recursion.what:
Imagine cleaning out a wardrobe full of boxes, where some boxes contain more boxes. You don't plan the whole wardrobe at once. You tell yourself: "clean this box, and do the same job again for any box inside it."

Recursion is exactly that: a function calls itself with a smaller input. Two parts are always needed: a base case (where to stop) and a recursive case (how to make the problem smaller).

Here is what many candidates forget in interviews: every call leaves a frame on the call stack. So the space used by recursion is not O(1) but O(depth), even if you never create an array.
recursion.analogy: Think of a Matryoshka doll: each doll contains a smaller one. You keep opening them until you reach the smallest solid doll (the base case). Then you close them one by one on the way back out. That is the unwind, and it is where your answer gets built.
recursion.why:
Trees, graphs, backtracking and DP all sit on top of recursion. If recursion isn't solid, nothing from Phase 4 onward will make sense.

The bug that catches candidates fastest in interviews is a missing or wrong base case, which ends in RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.

How to think:

1. Each call pushes a new frame onto the call stack, holding that call's local variables.
2. Check the base case first. If the input is already in its simplest form, return the value directly.
3. Otherwise, call the function again with a smaller input.
4. This repeats until a base case is reached, and the stack keeps growing. The maximum height of the stack is your space cost.
5. Once the base case returns, values flow back down: each pending call finishes its work and pops off the stack.
where: O(d) space · space: d is the recursion depth
O(n) time · space: O(h), where h is the tree height
O(2^n) time · space: O(n) for the stack

qa.q: What is the space complexity of recursion?
qa.a: O(depth), because of the call stack, not O(1). A function that recurses n levels deep uses O(n) stack space even if it allocates nothing else. That is why deep recursion can overflow the stack while an equivalent iterative loop won't.

qa.q: How do you convert recursion to iteration?
qa.a: Replace the call stack with an explicit stack (LIFO, for DFS-style traversal) or a queue (for BFS-style). The iterative version avoids call-stack growth, so it can't hit a stack overflow, although an explicit stack still uses O(depth) heap memory. That is why iterative tree traversals exist.

5-step.name: The 5-Step Problem Framework
5-step.desc: A repeatable interview loop: understand, work through examples, brute force, optimize, then code and test. Interviewers grade your process as much as your final answer, and this framework keeps you from freezing.
5-step.q: What should you do in the first 60 seconds of a problem?
5-step.qsub: Which clarifying questions do you always ask? · How do you decide that brute force is too slow? · Why should you state the brute force even when you already know the optimal solution?
5-step.what:
Imagine getting a ticket with unclear requirements and starting to code immediately. Halfway through, you realize you're building the wrong thing. Interviews work the same way.

That's why there is a fixed loop: understand → examples → brute force → optimize → code + test. Each step has its own purpose, and each one leads naturally to the next.

Most importantly, the interviewer isn't only scoring your final code. They are watching how you break down a messy problem, because that is what you do every day at work.
5-step.analogy: A good doctor doesn't write a prescription the moment you walk in. They ask questions first (understand), compare your symptoms with known cases (examples), consider the most likely common cause (brute force), order tests to confirm or refine it (optimize), and only then prescribe (code). Would you trust a doctor who prescribed right away?
5-step.why:
The interviewer has 45 minutes and is trying to answer one question: "What would it be like to work with this person?" Typing in silence is their biggest red flag.

The framework also protects you from panic. When an unfamiliar problem shows up and no solution comes to mind, step 1 is still something you can always do, and in those few minutes your mind usually opens up.

How to think:

1. Understand: restate the problem out loud in your own words. Ask about constraints: how large can n be? Can there be negative numbers, duplicates or empty input?
2. Examples: make up a small input and work out the output by hand. Also try an edge case (empty, single element, all values the same).
3. Brute force: propose the simplest solution you can think of, even if it is slow, and state its complexity. This is your safety net, because now you have something on the table.
4. Optimize: ask "which work is being repeated?" That is where a hash map, two pointers or sorting can cut the cost. Name the pattern you're using.
5. Code + test: now write the code. Then trace it line by line on your own example and cover the edge cases.
where: Restate the problem and ask about constraints · space: 2-3 min
Work through 2-3 by hand · space: 2-3 min
State it, then move on to optimizing · space: 5 min
Name the pattern and its complexity · space: 5-10 min
Write it and trace the edge cases · space: remaining time

qa.q: What should you do in the first 60 seconds of a problem?
qa.a: Restate the problem in your own words, confirm the constraints (input size, negatives, empty input, duplicates), and ask a clarifying question. This anchors the problem and signals structured thinking.

qa.q: What if you're stuck after 10 minutes?
qa.a: Go back to examples and work through one more small case by hand. If you're still stuck, say out loud what you know and what is blocking you. Interviewers much prefer a clear "I'm stuck because..." to silent panic.

space-complexity.name: Space Complexity
space-complexity.desc: How much extra memory your algorithm needs beyond the input, as a function of n. It counts new arrays, hash maps and the recursion call stack. Interviewers ask about it as often as time complexity.
space-complexity.q: What's the space complexity of a recursive tree traversal?
space-complexity.qsub: What does 'in-place' strictly mean? · Does slice() count as extra space? · What's the stack space of an iterative vs a recursive binary search?
space-complexity.what:
Think of your function as being given a room to work in. Space complexity asks: how much new stuff did you bring into that room?

The input itself isn't counted, because it was already there. Only the space your solution creates is counted: new arrays, hash maps and, the one most often missed, the recursion call stack.

So a function that creates no arrays but recurses n levels deep uses O(n) space, not O(1). Every pending call on the stack takes up space of its own.
space-complexity.analogy: Imagine working at a desk. The documents handed to you are the input, and they don't count. The extra notepads you fill in while working are your extra space. And every half-finished task you set aside in a pile to come back to later also takes up desk space. That pile is the call stack.
space-complexity.why:
While rushing to improve time, people often increase space without noticing. They add a hash map or make a copy, and then still claim the solution is O(1) space. Interviewers catch that.

Many problems also say "solve in O(1) extra space". That line tells you a two-pointer or in-place swap solution is expected, not a hash map.

How to think:

1. Look for the new arrays, objects or maps created inside the function that were not part of the input.
2. See how the size of each one grows with n. That is its order.
3. Is the function recursive? Then find the maximum number of calls that can be pending on the stack at the same time. That is the depth. (Count simultaneous calls, not total calls.)
4. Combine both and keep the largest term.
5. Variables that don't grow with n are O(1), even if there are ten of them.
where: O(n) extra · space: avoid unless asked

qa.q: What's the space complexity of a recursive tree traversal?
qa.a: O(h), where h is the tree height, because the call stack holds one frame per level. For a balanced tree that is O(log n). For a degenerate (linked-list-shaped) tree it is O(n).

qa.q: When would you trade time for space, or the reverse?
qa.a: Caching (memoization) spends O(n) extra space to get O(1) lookups per subproblem instead of recomputing it. If the problem forbids extra space, you accept a slower algorithm. The problem statement usually dictates the trade-off.

fibonacci.name: Fibonacci & Recursion Trees
fibonacci.desc: The canonical recursion lesson: without memoization, fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) explodes into an exponential tree that recomputes the same subproblems. Memoizing collapses it to O(n). The same tree shape underlies Climbing Stairs and House Robber.
fibonacci.q: Why is naive fib O(2^n) when it only recurses n levels deep?
fibonacci.qsub: How many nodes does fib(5) have, naive vs memoized? · Why does the iterative version need only two variables? · Which problems share the same recurrence tree as fib?
fibonacci.what:
Expand fib(5): it is fib(4) + fib(3). Expand fib(4): it is fib(3) + fib(2). Notice that fib(3) is computed twice, and each time the whole calculation is done from scratch.

The number of calls roughly doubles at every level. fib(5) makes 15 calls, while fib(30) makes about 2.7 million, all of them recomputing answers we already had. That growth is why we describe it as O(2ⁿ).

The cure takes one idea: once you compute a result, write it down. That is memoization, the gateway to Dynamic Programming.
fibonacci.analogy: Imagine a teacher asks a class, "What was yesterday's homework?" Each student asks two friends, who each ask two more, and soon the whole room is buzzing with the same question. If one student writes the answer on the board, everyone else just reads it. The board is the memo.
fibonacci.why:
This topic isn't really about Fibonacci. It's about recognizing overlapping subproblems, the skill that unlocks all of Phase 7 (DP).

In an interview, stopping after an exponential solution earns only half the credit. The real test is saying: "The same subproblem repeats here, so memoization brings it down to O(n)."

How to think:

1. fib(n) calls itself twice: fib(n-1) and fib(n-2).
2. Each of those makes two more calls, so the tree roughly doubles at every level.
3. Small values such as fib(2) and fib(3) show up again and again in different branches.
4. Each repeated call does all its work again, because the answer isn't stored anywhere.
5. With memoization, every repeated branch becomes an O(1) lookup, and the tree collapses to n distinct subproblems.
6. Remember: the depth was always n. Time comes from branching, and space comes from depth.

qa.q: Why is naive fib O(2^n) when it only recurses n levels deep?
qa.a: Depth is O(n), but each call spawns two more, so the tree has on the order of 2^n nodes (the tight bound is about 1.618^n, which is still exponential) and the same work is repeated in many branches. Depth determines SPACE; branching determines TIME.

qa.q: What does memoization actually do here?
qa.a: It caches the answer for each n the first time it is computed. Every duplicate branch becomes an O(1) lookup, so roughly 2^n calls shrink to n distinct subproblems: O(n) time and O(n) space.

arrays-2.name: Arrays & Strings
arrays-2.desc: Index-based storage with O(1) access by index. It is the default container for most problems, and mastering it means knowing which JS methods mutate the array, which return a copy, and what each costs.
arrays-2.q: What's the time cost of arr.shift()?
arrays-2.qsub: How do you find the second-largest element in one pass? · When is arr.sort() O(n log n) but still fine to use? · How do you merge two sorted arrays in place, working from the end?
arrays-2.what:
In Phase 0 we saw how arrays work. Now the practical question: which methods change the original array, and which return a new one?

This is more than trivia. If you call state.push(item), the array changes but its reference (address) stays the same. React compares references and doesn't look inside, so it concludes nothing changed and skips the re-render.

There is no error and no warning. The UI just goes stale. That is why interviewers ask about it, and why it bites in production.
arrays-2.analogy: Imagine a security guard who checks only the label on a folder, never the pages inside. If you swap pages inside the same folder (mutate), the guard notices nothing. If you hand over a new folder (copy), the change is obvious at once. React is that guard: it checks the label, not the contents.
arrays-2.why:
One sentence is enough for an interviewer to tell whether you have only used React or truly understand it. push/splice/sort/reverse mutate; map/filter/slice/spread return a new array.

The DSA side has its own version of this: in-place solutions. "O(1) extra space" means you may not create a new array. You have to solve it with two pointers.

How to think:

1. Ask whether the method directly changes the array's length or order. If yes, it is mutating.
2. If it returns a new array and leaves the original alone, it is non-mutating.
3. For React state, copy first: [...arr] or arr.slice().
4. Make your changes on the copy, then pass that copy to setState. A new reference goes in, so a re-render happens.
5. In DSA you want the opposite: when O(1) space is required, modify the original with two pointers.

qa.q: What's the time cost of arr.shift()?
qa.a: O(n), because every remaining element has to move down by one index. For a queue-like structure, use a head-pointer index or a proper Deque implementation instead.

qa.q: Why do interviewers love in-place algorithms?
qa.a: They show you can work within O(1) extra space. Problems like Rotate Array and Set Matrix Zeroes explicitly require it, and in-place techniques such as two pointers and cycle sort show up in harder problems too.

strings.name: Strings & Characters
strings.desc: Immutable sequences of characters. In JS, string methods return NEW strings, so building a string in a loop can cost O(n²) if done naively. Character codes and palindrome checks are the core patterns.
strings.q: Why is string concatenation in a loop slow?
strings.qsub: How do you check for a valid palindrome while ignoring non-alphanumeric characters? · What does charCodeAt return for an emoji vs an ASCII character? · How do you reverse the words in a sentence in place?
strings.what:
A string is like a printed book. To change one word, you can't edit the page. You have to print a new one. In JS, strings are immutable.

So s += c looks like a tiny operation, but conceptually it copies the whole old string, adds one character, and produces a new string.

Do that n times in a loop and the amount copied grows each time: 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n = O(n²). The fix is simple: push pieces into an array, then call join('') once at the end.
strings.analogy: Think of a photocopier. To add one line to a page, you photocopy the entire old page again with the new line on it. To build a ten-line document that way, you end up copying 55 lines in total (1 + 2 + ... + 10). Array + join means writing all the lines separately and stapling them together once at the end.
strings.why:
This is the classic "small change, big impact" signal. The interviewer wants to see whether you recognize the hidden cost of +=.

Most other string questions, such as anagrams, palindromes and sliding window, rest on the same fact: a string can't be modified, only read. So the work is done with a frequency map or the two-pointer technique.

How to think:

1. s += c creates a new string. The old string is never touched.
2. Building the new one means copying every character of the old one, which costs time proportional to its current length.
3. The string gets longer each iteration, so each copy costs more than the last.
4. Add them up: 1+2+3+…+n = n(n+1)/2 → O(n²).
5. Push into an array instead. Arrays are mutable, so nothing is recopied and each push is O(1).
6. At the end, a single join('') walks everything once, so the total is O(n).
where: Building a string with += in a loop
O(n) · space: O(k) for k distinct characters

qa.q: Why is string concatenation in a loop slow?
qa.a: Strings are immutable. Each += conceptually allocates a new string and copies the whole previous content, so n concatenations cost 1+2+...+n = O(n²). Modern engines such as V8 often soften this with internal optimizations, but you shouldn't rely on that. Collect the pieces in an array and join() once for a guaranteed O(n).

qa.q: Anagram detection: what's the optimal approach?
qa.a: Either sort both strings and compare them (O(n log n)), or build two frequency maps and compare them (O(n)). The frequency-map approach is the optimal one; sort-and-compare is shorter to write and fine when n is small.

hashmaps.name: Hash Map
hashmaps.desc: Key-value storage with O(1) average insert, lookup and delete, thanks to hashing the key. It is the number-one interview tool: it turns "scan the array for something" from O(n) per check into O(1).
hashmaps.q: HashMap vs Array: when does each win?
hashmaps.qsub: How do you count the frequency of every character? · Why is 'value -> index' a Map in Two Sum but a plain array in other problems? · How do you group anagrams with a map?
hashmaps.what:
Take Two Sum: find two numbers in an array that add up to a target. The straightforward way is to take each number and search the rest of the array for its partner. That is a nested loop, O(n²).

Now flip the question. For each number x, ask: "I need target - x. Have I already seen it?" If you record the numbers you've seen in a map, that question is answered in O(1).

That's the whole solution: one pass, O(n). A hash map does exactly this job: it turns "searching" into "remembering".
hashmaps.analogy: Imagine a wedding with 500 guests and you need to find your friend. Walking from table to table is O(n). But at the entrance there's a register listing every guest's name and table number. Give a name, get a table. The register is the hash map.
hashmaps.why:
This is the interview tool with the highest return. A single pattern, "have I seen this before?", unlocks dozens of problems.

Interviewers watch for this specifically: after you describe the brute-force O(n²) approach, do you arrive at the hash-map solution on your own, or do you need a hint? It tests pattern recognition, not memorization.

How to think:

1. Traverse the array once, left to right.
2. For each element, first ask: is the value I need (a complement or a previous count) already in the map?
3. If yes, you have the answer. Return immediately.
4. If not, insert the current element into the map (value → index, or value → count).
5. Move to the next element. The array is traversed only once: O(n) time, O(n) space.
6. Order matters: check first, then insert. Doing it the other way round lets an element match itself.
where: O(1) average · space: O(1) per entry

qa.q: HashMap vs Array: when does each win?
qa.a: An array wins when the keys are dense integers 0..n-1 (counting by index, cycle sort). A HashMap wins for arbitrary keys such as strings, objects or sparse integers, and gives O(1) average access.

qa.q: What's the worst case for a hash map, and why don't we usually worry about it?
qa.a: With a bad hash function or adversarial inputs, many keys land in the same bucket and operations degrade to O(n). In interviews we assume a good hash function and quote O(1) average, but mentioning the caveat shows depth.

linked-lists.name: Singly Linked List
linked-lists.desc: Nodes that each hold a value and a next pointer, chained in a line. There is no O(1) index access, so traversal is O(n). Its strengths are O(1) insertion and deletion at a known node, and pointer tricks such as fast & slow pointers and dummy nodes.
linked-lists.q: Why use a dummy head node?
linked-lists.qsub: What's the cost of finding the k-th node? · Why can't you do arr[i]-style access on a linked list? · When reversing, why must you save next before rewiring cur.next?
linked-lists.what:
Think of a treasure hunt where each clue tells you where the next one is hidden. You have to start at the first clue, because you can't jump straight to the 50th.

A linked list is exactly that. Every node holds a value and a next, the reference to the following node. There is no index, so a jump like arr[50] isn't possible. To reach the 50th node, follow next 50 times: O(n).

In exchange you get a strength: if you already hold a reference to a node, inserting after it or removing it just means changing two pointers: O(1). The same operation on an array needs O(n) shifting.
linked-lists.analogy: In a treasure hunt you can't open a middle clue directly. You have to move forward one clue at a time. But once you're holding a clue, slipping a new clue in after it is easy: you only change two addresses, and the rest of the hunt stays as it was.
linked-lists.why:
Interviewers use this to test the array vs linked list trade-off: arrays win at random access, while linked lists win at insert and delete when you already have the node.

It is also a test of pointer manipulation. In reverse, cycle detection and merge, changing pointers in the wrong order breaks the whole list. The interviewer checks whether you remember to save next.

How to think:

1. head points to the first node. There is no other entry point into the list.
2. To reach any node, start at head and follow next one hop at a time.
3. Insert: set the new node's next first, then point the previous node's next at the new node. Doing it the other way loses the rest of the list.
4. Delete: point the previous node's next directly at the node after the one you're removing, so the middle node drops out of the list.
5. Reverse: use three pointers, prev, cur and next. At each step, save next first, then set cur.next = prev.
where: Insert / delete at a known node

qa.q: Why use a dummy head node?
qa.a: It removes the special case for the head, so you never write 'if this is the first node'. Operations like inserting before the head or building a result list all start from a dummy node and return dummy.next. That means less branching and fewer bugs.

qa.q: How do fast & slow pointers detect a cycle?
qa.a: Two pointers move at speed 1 and speed 2. If there is a cycle, the fast pointer eventually laps the slow one and they meet. This takes O(n) time and O(1) space. The same idea finds the middle node: when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle.

stacks.name: Stack
stacks.desc: LIFO (last-in, first-out). Push, pop and peek are all O(1). It is used wherever the most recent item matters: bracket matching, undo, function calls, monotonic-stack patterns and parsing.
stacks.q: What's the difference between a Stack and a Queue?
stacks.qsub: What does the stack's depth represent in bracket matching? · How do you evaluate Reverse Polish Notation with a stack? · When should you use a stack instead of recursion for DFS?
stacks.what:
Think of a pile of plates. The last plate placed on top is the first one lifted off, and you can't pull one out of the middle. This is LIFO: Last In, First Out.

Push and pop both happen at the same end, so nothing has to slide around. Both are O(1).

This isn't just an analogy. It's exactly how JavaScript's call stack works: the function called last returns first. If you understand recursion, you understand the stack, and vice versa.
stacks.analogy: Picture the stack of clean plates in a cafeteria: you always take the top one. Or the browser's back button: the page you opened last is the first one you return from. Whenever you need "the most recent thing", think stack.
stacks.why:
A stack is a signal. When a problem involves nesting (brackets, tags, expressions) or needs the "previous one", the answer is almost always a stack.

It is also the Phase 1 topic that takes you furthest: monotonic stacks, iterative DFS, expression parsing and undo are all built on this single structure.

How to think:

1. A new element always goes on the top: push.
2. Removal also always happens at the top: pop. It never reaches the elements below.
3. peek only looks at the top without removing it. In JS that is arr[arr.length-1].
4. Both operations work at the same end, so no shifting is needed: O(1).
5. Bracket matching: when an opening bracket arrives, push it. When a closing bracket arrives, pop and check that it's the matching pair. At the end the stack should be empty. If anything is left, some bracket was never closed.

qa.q: What's the difference between a Stack and a Queue?
qa.a: A stack is LIFO: the newest element is removed first (like a stack of plates). A queue is FIFO: the oldest element is removed first (like a ticket line). That one property decides which fits the problem.

qa.q: How would you implement a queue using two stacks?
qa.a: Use one stack for pushes (the inbox). On pop, if the outbox is empty, move everything from the inbox to the outbox, which reverses the order, then pop from the outbox. Each operation is amortized O(1).

queue.name: Queue
queue.desc: FIFO (first-in, first-out). Enqueue and dequeue are O(1). It is the engine behind BFS: level-order tree traversal and shortest paths in unweighted graphs. In JS a plain array works, but shift() is O(n), so use a head index or a real queue.
queue.q: Why does BFS give the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
queue.qsub: How does BFS avoid infinite loops on graphs? · In level-order traversal, why do you snapshot the queue size? · What changes if the edges are weighted? (→ Dijkstra)
queue.what:
Think of a line at a ticket counter. Whoever arrived first is served first, and nobody can cut in from the middle. This is FIFO: First In, First Out.

It's the opposite of a stack. A stack does both operations at the same end, while a queue has two separate ends: the back for insertion (enqueue) and the front for removal (dequeue). Both are O(1).

A queue is more than a data structure. It is the engine of BFS. All nodes of one level are processed before the next level starts, and the queue is what guarantees that. That guarantee is what gives you the shortest path on an unweighted graph.
queue.analogy: The ticket line is first come, first served. Now think of BFS as dropping a stone into a pond: the ripples spread outward in circles, one ring at a time. First you reach every point at distance 1, then distance 2, and so on. So the first time you reach a spot, you've reached it by the shortest route.
queue.why:
You can't understand BFS without understanding a queue, and the queue pays off fully once you reach Phase 4 (trees) and Phase 5 (graphs). Level-order traversal, shortest path, Rotting Oranges and Word Ladder all start here.

There is also a JavaScript-specific trap that interviewers watch for: arr.shift() is O(n). Using it inside a BFS loop can quietly turn the algorithm into O(n²). The answer stays correct, but large inputs hit the time limit (TLE).

How to think:

1. A new element always joins at the rear (back): enqueue.
2. Removal always happens at the front: dequeue.
3. Because the two ends are separate, nothing gets in the way, and both operations are O(1).
4. In BFS: dequeue a node, then enqueue all its unvisited neighbors at the back.
5. Need level order? Before starting each level, capture size = queue.length and process exactly that many nodes. Otherwise the next level gets mixed in with the current one.
6. On a graph, a visited set is essential. Without it, a cycle keeps refilling the queue and it never empties.
where: O(1) with a head index · space: O(1)
O(V + E) · space: O(V) worst case

qa.q: Why does BFS give the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
qa.a: It explores level by level: every node at distance d is processed before any node at distance d+1. So the first time a node is reached, it is reached by a shortest route. DFS has no such guarantee.

qa.q: Why is arr.shift() bad for a queue?
qa.a: shift() reindexes every remaining element, so each dequeue costs O(n) and n operations cost O(n²). A head-pointer index (or a linked list) makes dequeue O(1).

hashset.name: Hash Set
hashset.desc: An unordered collection of unique values with O(1) add, remove and membership check. Whenever a problem says 'distinct', 'unique' or 'have I seen this', a Set is the right tool, and it is cleaner than a Map of booleans.
hashset.q: Set vs Map: when do you use each?
hashset.qsub: How do you find the intersection of two arrays in O(n)? · When does a Set become worse than sorting? · How do Sets dedupe objects (identity vs equality)?
hashset.what:
A Set is basically a Map that stores only values, with no key-value pairs. It answers one question: "Is this item in here or not?" in O(1) time.

With an array you'd ask the same question using includes(), which checks every element: O(n). Put that inside a loop and you've quietly built an O(n²) solution.

As a bonus, duplicates vanish automatically. [...new Set(arr)] is one line, O(n), and it keeps the order of first appearance.
hashset.analogy: Picture a bouncer outside a club with a guest list. You say your name and he finds your entry directly, without reading the whole list. And a name can't appear twice on the list: writing it again changes nothing.
hashset.why:
Interviewers look for one thing: when a problem mentions "distinct", "unique", "have I seen this before" or "visited", a Set should come to mind immediately.

This tests pattern recognition, not syntax. Use a Map when you need to remember something extra along with the value, such as an index or a count. When you only need "is it there or not", a Set is the clear choice.

How to think:

1. When a value is added, a hash function converts it to a number.
2. That number picks a slot in an internal array.
3. The value is stored in that slot. If two values hash to the same slot (a collision), they are kept together in a small list there.
4. On has(x), the same hash is computed and you go straight to the slot. The whole set is never scanned.
5. On add, the same check runs first, so duplicates are rejected automatically.
6. That is why add, has and delete are all O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case.
where: O(1) average · space: O(1) per entry

qa.q: Set vs Map: when do you use each?
qa.a: Use a Set when you only need membership (do I have this? is it distinct?). Use a Map when each key carries associated data, such as a count or an index. A Set is essentially a Map without the values.

qa.q: Contains Duplicate: Set or sort?
qa.a: With a Set, make one pass: if set.has(x) return true, otherwise add x. That is O(n) time and O(n) space. Sorting is O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space if done in place. For small arrays both are fine, but the Set solution is the one usually expected.

doubly-linked-lists.name: Doubly Linked List
doubly-linked-lists.desc: Like a singly linked list, plus a prev pointer on every node. The prev pointer enables O(1) deletion of a node you already hold, with no need to find its predecessor. This is what makes an LRU Cache possible.
doubly-linked-lists.q: Why can a doubly linked list delete a known node in O(1) when a singly linked list can't?
doubly-linked-lists.qsub: Why do LRU implementations use sentinel head and tail nodes? · When is a doubly linked list worse than a singly linked one? · What breaks if you forget to fix both the prev and next links?
doubly-linked-lists.what:
A singly linked list has a limitation. Say you hold a reference to the node you want to delete. To remove it, you must change the previous node's next, but you can't walk backwards. You have to start again from the head: O(n).

A doubly linked list fixes this with one extra field: every node also has a prev. Now the previous node is right there, so deletion means changing just two pointers: O(1).

This is what makes an LRU Cache possible. The hash map gives you the node instantly, and thanks to prev, moving it to the front of the list is also O(1).
doubly-linked-lists.analogy: Imagine a chain of people where each person holds hands with both the person in front and the person behind. If someone in the middle wants to leave, their two neighbors simply grab each other's hands. Nobody has to count along the chain from the start.
doubly-linked-lists.why:
This topic exists mainly for one design question, but that question is asked very often: the LRU Cache. Its whole trick is this: find the node with a Map in O(1), then move it to the head with the doubly linked list in O(1).

Interviewers also check whether you understand the cost: an extra pointer per node uses more memory, and every operation requires discipline in fixing links on both sides.

How to think:

1. Each node stores three things: the value, next and prev.
2. On insertion, four pointers are set: both pointers of the new node, plus one pointer on each of its two neighbors.
3. On deletion, two are updated: node.prev.next = node.next and node.next.prev = node.prev. No traversal is needed.
4. Keep a sentinel (dummy) head and tail. Then no real node's prev or next is ever null, and all the if (node === head) checks disappear.
5. Moving a node to the front takes two steps, not one: first unlink it, then insert it. Get the order wrong and the list breaks.
where: O(n) for the search · space: O(1)

qa.q: Why can a doubly linked list delete a known node in O(1) when a singly linked list can't?
qa.a: Deletion requires the predecessor, whose next pointer must be rewired. A doubly linked list reaches it directly through node.prev. A singly linked list has to traverse from the head to find it, which is O(n).

qa.q: How does an LRU Cache combine a Map and a doubly linked list?
qa.a: The Map gives O(1) lookup by key. The list tracks recency, with the most recently used node at the head and the least recently used at the tail. On get or put, move the node to the head. On eviction, remove the tail. Every operation is O(1).

circular-linked-lists.name: Circular Linked List
circular-linked-lists.desc: A linked list whose tail points back to the head, forming a loop. It is common in round-robin scheduling and Josephus-style problems, and it is the mental model for cycle detection.
circular-linked-lists.q: How does Floyd's algorithm find the entry point of a cycle?
circular-linked-lists.qsub: Why does fast move two steps at a time, and what can go wrong with three? · What happens if the cycle is the whole list? · How do you iterate a circular list safely without an infinite loop?
circular-linked-lists.what:
In a normal list, the last node ends with null. In a circular list, the last node points back to the head. That is the only difference, and it changes the behavior completely.

The list now has no end. Traversal wraps around on its own, and "the item after the last one" comes for free, so you don't need % length.

The flip side matters more: if a list accidentally forms such a loop, a plain while (cur) never terminates. To catch this, we use Floyd's slow-fast pointer technique.
circular-linked-lists.analogy: Think of kids sitting in a circle passing a parcel: when the last child finishes, the turn passes back to the first. There is no "last person". To catch a cycle, imagine two runners on a circular track, one running at normal speed and the other twice as fast. On a loop, the fast runner eventually laps the slow one and catches up. On a straight road, they would never meet again.
circular-linked-lists.why:
Interviewers look for two things. First, that you know a stopping condition is required, because forgetting it gives an infinite loop, a very common mistake.

Second, and more important, why Floyd's algorithm works. Reciting the code isn't enough. The answer is that inside the cycle, the gap between the two pointers shrinks by exactly 1 on every step, so they are guaranteed to meet. If the fast pointer moved three steps, the gap would shrink by 2 and could jump over zero forever.

How to think:

1. Set the last node's next to head instead of null. That creates the ring.
2. To traverse, use do { ... } while (cur !== head): one full lap, then stop. while (cur) would never stop here.
3. To detect a cycle, move slow one step and fast two steps at a time.
4. If there is no cycle, fast reaches null first, so you can stop: no cycle.
5. If there is a cycle, both pointers end up inside it and the gap shrinks by 1 each step, so they meet.
6. Need the start of the cycle? After they meet, reset slow to head, then move both one step at a time. The node where they meet again is the cycle's entry point.

qa.q: How does Floyd's algorithm find the entry point of a cycle?
qa.a: After slow and fast meet inside the cycle, reset slow to head. Then advance both pointers one step at a time. The math shows they meet exactly at the start of the cycle. Total cost is O(n) time and O(1) space.

qa.q: What's the difference between a circular list and a list with a cycle?
qa.a: A true circular list deliberately points the tail at the head, so traversal is well defined. A 'cycle' is usually an unintended bug. The detection algorithm is the same, but a circular list is a design choice, not a defect.

monotonic-stack.name: Monotonic Stack
monotonic-stack.desc: A stack that always stays sorted (increasing or decreasing) by value: before pushing, you pop any elements that would break the order. Each element is pushed and popped at most once, so it runs in O(n) and solves 'next greater / next smaller' problems elegantly.
monotonic-stack.q: Why is a monotonic stack O(n) even though there's a nested while?
monotonic-stack.qsub: How do you get the previous greater element instead of the next one? · What changes for next smaller? · How does Largest Rectangle in Histogram use a monotonic stack?
monotonic-stack.what:
Say that for each element you need the first larger element to its right. The straightforward approach is to scan forward from every element: O(n²).

Now turn it around. When a new larger element arrives, it becomes the answer for many earlier elements at once: all those still waiting for a larger value.

So keep those "waiting" elements in a stack, always in decreasing order. When a new element arrives, every waiting element smaller than it has found its answer, so pop them. Each element is pushed once and popped once, so the total work is O(n).
monotonic-stack.analogy: Imagine people waiting in a line, each wanting to know who is the first taller person to their right. When a tall person walks up, every shorter person still waiting gets their answer all at once and leaves the waiting line.
monotonic-stack.why:
This is the most "algorithmic" topic in Phase 1. The interviewer is looking for one thing: can you reason in amortized terms?

The code has a while inside a for, so at first glance it looks like O(n²). But each element is pushed at most once and popped at most once over the whole run, so the total work is about 2n, which is O(n). Explaining that is the real answer.

How to think:

1. Store indices in the stack, not values. You need the index to compute distances.
2. For each new element, while the top of the stack violates the invariant, pop it.
3. For every element you pop, the current element is its answer. Record the answer at pop time, not at push time.
4. Then push the current index.
5. At the end, any indices left in the stack have no answer (use the default, 0 or -1).
6. To remember the direction: for next greater, keep the stack decreasing. For next smaller, keep it increasing.

qa.q: Why is a monotonic stack O(n) even though there's a nested while?
qa.a: Each element is pushed exactly once and popped at most once across the whole run. The inner while loop therefore executes at most n pops in total, not n per iteration, so the algorithm is O(n) amortized.

qa.q: Should the stack store values or indices?
qa.a: Indices. Values alone lose the distance information (Daily Temperatures needs i - idx) and can't distinguish duplicate values cleanly. Store indices and read the value from the array.

deque.name: Deque (Double-Ended Queue)
deque.desc: A queue that supports O(1) push and pop at BOTH ends. It is the workhorse for sliding-window maximum/minimum problems, where candidates are added at the back and expire at the front.
deque.q: Why is Sliding Window Maximum O(n) and not O(nk)?
deque.qsub: What invariant does the deque maintain for window maximum? · How would you get the minimum instead? · Does it matter whether you pop with <= or with < when comparing nums[dq[last]] to nums[i]?
deque.what:
A deque is a queue that is open at both ends. You can insert and remove at the front as well as at the back, and every operation is O(1).

Why do we need it? Think of Sliding Window Maximum. As the window slides forward, you must drop the oldest index from the front (it has left the window), and drop smaller values from the back (they can never be the maximum once a larger element has arrived after them).

Two ends, two different reasons. A plain queue isn't enough, so you use a deque. Its contents are kept in decreasing order, which means the front is always the maximum of the current window.
deque.analogy: Imagine a line of candidates competing to be the tallest in the room. People at the front leave when their time is up. When a taller person joins at the back, any shorter people already standing at the back are pointless candidates: they are shorter and will leave sooner, so they can never be the tallest again. The tallest person is always at the front of the line.
deque.why:
Interviewers ask about Sliding Window Maximum because the naive solution is O(n·k) while the deque solution is O(n). Explaining that difference is the test.

There is also a JavaScript-specific trap: dq.shift() is O(n). Even with the right algorithm, you can fall back to O(n·k). Pointing out that "you need a real deque or a head index" earns extra points.

How to think:

1. Keep indices in the deque, not values. The index tells you when an element leaves the window.
2. When a new element i arrives, pop from the back every element whose value is less than or equal to nums[i]. They can never be the maximum again.
3. Then push i at the back.
4. Check the front: if its index has left the window (<= i - k), remove it.
5. Once the window is full (i >= k-1), nums[front] is the maximum of the current window.
6. Each index enters once and leaves once, so the total work is O(n), just like a monotonic stack.

qa.q: Why is Sliding Window Maximum O(n) and not O(nk)?
qa.a: Each index enters the deque once and leaves it once, so the inner while loop pops at most n times in total across the whole run. The window maximum is always at the front, which is O(1) to read. No element is ever rescanned.

qa.q: Why use a deque instead of a max-heap here?
qa.a: A heap returns the max in O(1) and can insert in O(log k), but it can't directly remove the element that just left the window (you need lazy deletion, and the heap can grow). The deque keeps candidates in decreasing order, evicts expired indices from the front in O(1), and reads the max from the front in O(1).

matrix-2d.name: 2D Matrix Traversal
matrix-2d.desc: Arrays of arrays used as grids. Core patterns: row/column iteration, diagonal walks, spiral order, and in-place transforms (rotate, transpose, zero-out). These are heavy favorites at big tech companies like Google and Meta.
matrix-2d.q: How do you rotate a matrix 90° in place with O(1) space?
matrix-2d.qsub: How do you zero out rows and columns with O(1) extra space? · What are the edge cases for a spiral on a single row or column? · How do you check neighbors without index errors?
matrix-2d.what:
A 2D matrix is essentially an array of arrays. Any cell can be accessed with matrix[r][c] in O(1). That part is easy.

The difficulty is in the traversal pattern. Row by row is straightforward. But spiral? Diagonal? A 90° rotation without an extra array? In these, all the work is index arithmetic.

Two tricks cover a large share of matrix problems: rotate = transpose + reverse each row, and spiral = four boundaries that shrink after each loop.
matrix-2d.analogy: Think of a chessboard. Naming a single square is easy (row, column). But "spiral from the outer ring inward" means remembering the four edges and moving all four inward by one step after each lap.
matrix-2d.why:
Rotate Image, Spiral Matrix and Set Matrix Zeroes are favorites at Google and Meta. They test index discipline more than algorithmic cleverness. Miss a bounds check in one place and the code crashes.

This is also the foundation for Phase 5 (graphs). On a grid, BFS/DFS treats each cell as a node with four neighbors, and the same dirs array you learn here will come in handy a hundred times later.

How to think:

1. Let m = matrix.length (rows) and n = matrix[0].length (cols). Don't assume the matrix is square. Assuming it is square is the classic first mistake. (In-place rotation problems do guarantee an n × n matrix.)
2. Rotate 90° clockwise: first transpose, swapping [i][j] with [j][i] only when j > i. Otherwise you swap every pair twice and end up where you started. Then reverse each row. Done.
3. Spiral: keep four variables, top, bottom, left, right. One lap goes right → down → left → up. After finishing each side, move that boundary one step inward.
4. In a spiral, a final single row or column can be visited twice. So before the left and up steps, re-check top <= bottom and left <= right.
5. Neighbors: use a dirs array like [[1,0],[-1,0],[0,1],[0,-1]]. For each neighbor, do the bounds check first, then read the cell.

qa.q: How do you rotate a matrix 90° in place with O(1) space?
qa.a: For an n × n matrix, use two mechanical steps: transpose (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]), then reverse each row. That gives a 90° clockwise rotation. For counter-clockwise, reverse each row first and then transpose. No new matrix is needed.

qa.q: Spiral traversal: what's the cleanest loop structure?
qa.a: Track four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right). Walk right, down, left, up, shrinking a boundary after each side, and stop when the boundaries cross. It is four simple loops inside one while loop.

static-dynamic-arrays.name: Static vs Dynamic Arrays
static-dynamic-arrays.desc: How arrays actually live in memory. A static array has a fixed capacity allocated once. A dynamic array (ArrayList in Java, vector in C++, and conceptually every JS array) grows by allocating a bigger block and copying. Understanding the doubling strategy explains why append is O(1) amortized.
static-dynamic-arrays.q: Why is push on a dynamic array O(1) even though resizes copy everything?
static-dynamic-arrays.qsub: How do you insert at index 0 of an array, and what does it cost? · Why would you ever prefer a static array over a dynamic one? · How many times is an element copied over n appends?
static-dynamic-arrays.what:
In C, an array is static: you choose the size when you create it, and it never changes. If it fills up, you're out of room.

In JavaScript, an array is dynamic. When space runs out, the engine quietly allocates a larger block (typically about double), copies the old elements over, and then adds the new one. You never notice.

So why do we call push O(1) when it occasionally does an O(n) copy? Because resizes happen only at exponentially spaced sizes. The total copy work for n pushes is roughly 2n, about two steps of extra work per push. This is called amortized O(1).
static-dynamic-arrays.analogy: Your wardrobe is full, so you buy one that is twice as big and move all your clothes over. That day takes the whole afternoon. After that, putting clothes away takes seconds for a long time. The next move will be even bigger, but it comes much later. Averaged over all the days, the moving hardly shows.
static-dynamic-arrays.why:
This is a vocabulary question. Saying "push is O(1)" is only half the answer. The full answer is "O(1) amortized, with a worst case of O(n) when a resize happens."

It is also another form of the amortized thinking introduced in Phase 0. Hash-map resizing and stack growth rely on the same idea. Once you get it, it works everywhere.

How to think:

1. An array tracks two numbers: size (how many elements are present) and capacity (how many fit). They are separate.
2. On push, first check whether size < capacity. If yes, place the element directly: O(1).
3. If not, allocate a new block of capacity × 2 and copy all the old elements. That costs O(n).
4. Resizes happen when the size reaches 1, 2, 4, 8, 16…, so the gap between resizes doubles each time.
5. Total copies for n pushes: 1+2+4+…+n ≈ 2n. Spread over the pushes, that is about 2 extra steps each, so O(1) amortized.
6. We double instead of adding 1 because adding 1 would trigger a resize on every push, and the total work would become O(n²).
where: O(n) · space: O(n) for the new block

qa.q: Why is push on a dynamic array O(1) even though resizes copy everything?
qa.a: Amortization. The sum of all copy costs over n pushes is less than 2n, because each resize copies only the current elements and resizes become exponentially rarer. The total work is O(n), so the average cost per push is O(1).

qa.q: What is the space overhead of a dynamic array?
qa.a: Capacity is always at least the size, and can be up to about twice the size. That is O(n) slack in the worst case, which is the price paid for amortized O(1) append.

hash-impl.name: Hash Table Implementation
hash-impl.desc: A hash table maps keys to values using an array of buckets and a hash function. Collisions are handled by chaining (a list per bucket) or open addressing (probe for the next free slot). The quality of the hash decides whether lookups stay O(1) or degrade to O(n).
hash-impl.q: How do you handle two keys hashing to the same bucket?
hash-impl.qsub: What makes a good hash function for a HashMap? · Compare chaining vs open addressing. · Why is a JS object lookup not always O(1)? · When does a hash table degrade to O(n)?
hash-impl.what:
So far you've used Map and Set. Now let's look inside, because an interviewer may also ask you to "build a HashMap" yourself.

Inside, there is just an array of buckets. When a key arrives, the hash function turns it into a number, % buckets.length gives the bucket index, and the value is stored there.

Everything comes down to two issues. First, a collision: two keys land in the same bucket, so what do you do? Second, the load factor: when the buckets get too full, you double their number. If the hash function is bad, all keys end up in one bucket and O(1) degrades to O(n).
hash-impl.analogy: Think of a mailroom with one pigeonhole per apartment number. The number tells you exactly which pigeonhole a letter goes into, so you never read every letter. Two letters for the same apartment? Both go into that pigeonhole (chaining), and you only have to sift through that small pile. And when the pigeonholes fill up, you move to a mailroom with twice as many.
hash-impl.why:
There are two reasons. First, "Design a HashMap" is a standard interview question (LeetCode 706).

Second, and more important: until now you have been saying O(1) average. The interviewer asks "why average, why not always?" The answer is collisions and load factor. Explaining this separates junior from senior candidates.

How to think:

1. Create an array, say with 16 buckets.
2. Hash: Convert the key into a number. For a string, combine the character codes, then take % buckets.length to get the bucket index.
3. Collision (chaining): Keep a small list in each bucket. Add new entries to it, and on lookup search only that small list.
4. Collision (open addressing): If the bucket is taken, probe for the next empty slot. This uses less memory, but deletion becomes tricky.
5. Load factor: entries ÷ buckets. When it crosses about 0.75, double the buckets and re-insert every key (rehash), because the % result changes.
6. A good hash spreads keys evenly across buckets. A bad hash puts everything in one bucket, which means O(n).
where: O(1) average, O(n) worst case · space: O(1)
O(1) average, O(n) worst case · space: O(1)
O(1) average, O(n) worst case · space: O(1)

qa.q: How do you handle two keys hashing to the same bucket?
qa.a: With separate chaining, each bucket holds a linked list (or a tree). With open addressing, you probe linearly (or quadratically) to the next empty slot. Chaining is simpler and is what most textbook maps use.

qa.q: Why does the load factor matter?
qa.a: It is the ratio of entries to buckets. Above roughly 0.75, the average chain length grows and lookups slow down, so the table resizes and rehashes. That costs O(n) but happens rarely, so insertion stays O(1) amortized.

linear-search.name: Linear Search
linear-search.desc: Scan the elements one by one until you hit the target: O(n) time, O(1) space. It's simple, always correct, and the baseline every other search improves on. In interviews the skill is recognizing when a plain scan is all you need, such as on small or unsorted data.
linear-search.q: When is linear search the right answer?
linear-search.qsub: What does an array need for binary search to work? · Why is one full pass the lower bound for searching unsorted data? · How would you find the second-largest element in a single pass?
linear-search.what:
Check each element in turn until you find the target. That's the whole algorithm. It's the simplest one in Phase 2, which is exactly why people overlook what it teaches.

Here's the lesson: if the array is unsorted, no algorithm can beat O(n). The target might be in the very last slot, and nothing tells you that in advance, so you have to look at every element.

That isn't a flaw in the algorithm. It's a lower bound, and every faster algorithm later in the course is measured against it.
linear-search.analogy: Your clothes are piled in a drawer with no order, so you dig through them one at a time to find a particular shirt. If you had sorted everything first, you could grab any shirt almost instantly. But sorting the whole drawer to find a single shirt is wasted effort. If you dress from that drawer every day, sorting pays off.
linear-search.why:
The interviewer isn't checking whether you can write a for loop. They want to see your judgment: do you know when the simple approach is enough?

There's also a common trap: running binary search on an unsorted array. It won't crash, it will just return wrong answers silently. Asking "Is the array sorted?" before you start earns you points.

How to think:

1. Start at index 0 and walk to the end.
2. Compare each element with the target. On a match, return right away with return i.
3. If the loop ends with no match, return -1. Forgetting this "not found" case is the most common mistake.
4. One pass can also give you the min, max, count, or second-largest. Track everything in a single loop instead of writing several.
5. Decision: searching once means a linear scan. Searching many times means sorting or building a hash map once, so each later lookup is cheap.

qa.q: When is linear search the right answer?
qa.a: When the data is unsorted and you only search once, or when the task needs a full pass anyway (min/max, counting). O(n) is optimal there because every element must be inspected. The interview skill is knowing that binary search doesn't apply without sorted input.

qa.q: Can you find the max of an unsorted array in better than O(n)?
qa.a: No. The max could be at any position, so every element has to be inspected at least once. That's a lower bound on the problem itself, not a weakness of the algorithm.

binary-search.name: Binary Search
binary-search.desc: Repeatedly halve a sorted search space: check the middle and discard the half that can't contain the answer. O(log n) time, O(1) space. Common variants are basic search, lower/upper bound, and search on an answer space ("minimize the maximum").
binary-search.q: What does 'binary search on the answer' mean?
binary-search.qsub: How do you find the first and last position of a target? · How do you search a rotated sorted array? · Why must the feasibility function be monotonic for answer-space search?
binary-search.what:
Sorted data gives you a big advantage: by checking the middle element you can discard half the data at once. If the middle is smaller than the target, everything to its left is irrelevant.

Each step halves the range: n → n/2 → n/4 → … → 1. Even 1,000,000 elements take only about 20 steps. That's O(log n).

The bigger idea is that binary search isn't limited to arrays. It works anywhere there's a monotonic property, meaning once a condition becomes true it stays true. Applying it that way is called "binary search on the answer", and it's what interviews love to test.
binary-search.analogy: Looking up a word in a paper dictionary: open to the middle, see whether your word comes before or after that page, and ignore the other half. Nobody reads a dictionary from page one. It only works because the words are sorted. If they were shuffled, the middle page would tell you nothing.
binary-search.why:
Almost everyone can write the basic version. Interviews ask for variants, and that's where people get stuck: first occurrence, last occurrence, insertion position, rotated arrays.

The top level is binary search on the answer. There may be no sorted array at all. For example: "What is the minimum speed that finishes the work in h hours?" Here you binary-search over the range of possible answers, [lo, hi]. Spotting that is the real test.

How to think:

1. Set lo = 0 and hi = n - 1, then compute the middle with mid = lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1).
2. If arr[mid] equals the target, you're done.
3. If it's smaller, the target must be on the right, so lo = mid + 1.
4. If it's larger, the target is on the left, so hi = mid - 1.
5. When lo > hi the target isn't present, so return -1.
6. Answer search: use the range of possible answers [lo, hi] instead of an array. Write a feasible(x) function that checks in O(n) whether x works. It must be monotonic: once it returns true, it stays true for every larger value. Then binary search on it.
where: O(log R) × O(n) check · space: O(1)

qa.q: What does 'binary search on the answer' mean?
qa.a: Instead of searching an array, you search the range of possible answer values. For 'minimum eating speed to finish all the bananas in h hours', speeds run from 1 to the largest pile. Binary search that range, and for each candidate speed simulate the eating in O(n). It works because feasibility is monotonic: if a speed works, every higher speed works too.

qa.q: When does while (l <= r) fail?
qa.a: The pattern l <= r with l = mid + 1 and r = mid - 1 suits exact-match search. If you instead keep the candidate with r = mid (typical for lower-bound problems), l <= r can loop forever. For first/last occurrence the cleaner pattern is while (l < r) with r = mid, which converges to a single index.

merge-sort.name: Merge Sort
merge-sort.desc: Divide and conquer: split the array in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves in O(n). Guaranteed O(n log n) and stable, at the cost of O(n) extra space. The merge step is a reusable interview pattern.
merge-sort.q: Why is merge sort always O(n log n) while quick sort isn't?
merge-sort.qsub: What makes merge sort stable? · How does the merge step count inversions? · Why does merge sort need O(n) extra space?
merge-sort.what:
Merging two lists that are already sorted is easy: compare the front elements, take the smaller one, repeat. One pass, O(n).

Merge sort builds on that. Split the array in half again and again until each piece has one element (a single element is already sorted). Then merge the pieces pairwise on the way back up.

The split always happens at the exact middle, so the depth is always log n. Unlike quick sort, it never degrades. You get a guaranteed O(n log n), and the price is O(n) extra space.
merge-sort.analogy: You have two stacks of exam papers, each already sorted by score, and you want one combined stack. Compare the top paper of each stack, move the lower score to the new pile, and repeat. You never have to search through a stack, because both are already in order.
merge-sort.why:
When someone says "show me a sort", merge sort is the safest pick: even the worst case is O(n log n), and it's stable.

But the real value is the merge step. It's useful on its own for merging two sorted lists, counting inversions, sorting a linked list, and external sorting (when the data doesn't fit in RAM). Knowing the merge matters more than memorizing merge sort.

How to think:

1. If the array has length 0 or 1, it's already sorted, so return it. That's the base case.
2. Split it into two halves at the middle.
3. Sort both halves recursively. Trust the recursion; don't trace it by hand.
4. Merge: put one pointer at the start of each half, take the smaller element, and advance that pointer.
5. When one half runs out, append the rest of the other half as is. It's already sorted.
6. For stability, take from the left half when values are equal (use <=, not <). That's what makes the sort stable instead of unstable.
where: O(n log n) · space: O(n) extra
O(n log n) · space: O(log n) stack

qa.q: Why is merge sort always O(n log n) while quick sort isn't?
qa.a: Merge sort always splits exactly in half, so the recursion depth is always log n and each level does O(n) work. Quick sort's pivot can split badly: on already-sorted input with a naive pivot it degrades to O(n²). Merge sort trades that guaranteed time for O(n) extra space.

qa.q: Why is merge sort good for linked lists?
qa.a: Linked lists have no O(1) random access, so array tricks like indexing and quick sort's partitioning are awkward. Merge sort only walks the list and rewires pointers, giving O(n log n) time with just O(log n) recursion stack.

partition-algos.name: Quick Sort
partition-algos.desc: Pick a pivot, partition the array so smaller elements go left and larger go right, then recurse on both sides. O(n log n) on average and in-place (only O(log n) stack), but O(n²) in the worst case, for example a sorted input with a bad pivot choice.
partition-algos.q: Quick sort vs merge sort: which do you choose and when?
partition-algos.qsub: Why is quick sort not stable? · What does the partition step leave behind that Quick Select reuses? · How much stack space does the recursion cost in the worst case?
partition-algos.what:
Pick one element as the pivot. Rearrange the array so that everything smaller than the pivot is on the left and everything larger is on the right.

With the standard (Lomuto) partition, the pivot ends up in its final sorted position, so you never touch it again. Then repeat the same process on the left and right parts separately.

It's the mirror image of merge sort: merge sort does its work while joining, quick sort does it while splitting. That's why quick sort needs no extra array and works in place. The catch is that a bad pivot choice leads to O(n²).
partition-algos.analogy: Line up a class by height. Choose one student as the reference: shorter students stand to the left, taller ones to the right. That student is now in the correct spot and can be ignored. Then repeat for each group. But if you always pick the shortest student as the reference, each round fixes only one person, and you need n rounds.
partition-algos.why:
Interviewers test two things. The first is pivot selection. If you always take the first element as the pivot on an already-sorted array, every partition is completely lopsided and you get O(n²). Use a middle or random pivot. That's the answer they want to hear.

The second matters more: the partition step is an algorithm in its own right. Quick Select and Dutch National Flag, the next two topics, are built on exactly this step. You can forget quick sort, but don't forget partition.

How to think:

1. Choose a pivot, either the middle or a random element. Don't always use the first or last.
2. Use two pointers: i from the left and j from the right.
3. Move i forward until you find an element greater than or equal to the pivot. Move j backward until you find one that is smaller.
4. If both have stopped and i <= j, swap them and move each pointer one step.
5. Once i > j, the array is split into two parts. Recurse on both.
6. Balanced partitions give depth log n and O(n log n) total. If one side is empty every time, the depth is n and the total is O(n²).
where: O(n log n) · space: O(log n) stack

qa.q: Quick sort vs merge sort: which do you choose and when?
qa.a: Quick sort when you want in-place sorting with low memory and fast average O(n log n), which suits arrays. Merge sort when you need a guaranteed O(n log n), stability, or you're sorting linked lists. If worst-case guarantees matter, pick merge sort; if memory is tight, pick quick sort.

qa.q: How do you avoid quick sort's O(n²) worst case?
qa.a: Choose a good pivot: a random element, the middle element, or the median of three. A fixed first or last pivot on already-sorted input triggers the worst case. Randomizing keeps the partitions balanced in expectation. You can also recurse into the smaller side first to keep the stack at O(log n).

kadanes.name: Kadane's Algorithm
kadanes.desc: Find the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in one pass. At each element, decide whether to EXTEND the current subarray or START a new one. O(n) time, O(1) space. It underlies Maximum Subarray and its circular variant.
kadanes.q: What is the ONE decision Kadane's makes per element?
kadanes.qsub: How do you extend Kadane's to return the subarray itself? · How does the circular variant handle all-negative arrays? · Why does best start at -Infinity?
kadanes.what:
Say you have a month of daily profit and loss figures, and you want the continuous stretch of days with the highest total.

Brute force tries every stretch, which is O(n²). Kadane solves it with one question per day: do I extend the previous stretch, or start a new one here?

The rule is simple: if the running total so far is negative, carrying it forward can only lower your future total, so drop it and start fresh. That's it: one pass, O(n), one running variable.
kadanes.analogy: Think of a running balance in your expense notebook. Last week left you at −5,000, and today you earn 2,000. Continuing the old balance gives −3,000. Opening a fresh page gives +2,000. Don't carry forward a balance that only drags you down.
kadanes.why:
This is the smallest version of DP: instead of a full table, you keep just one number. You'll use that mindset repeatedly in Phase 7.

There's also a classic trap: initializing best = 0. If every number is negative ([-3, -1, -7]), you'd return 0, but an empty subarray isn't allowed. The correct answer is -1.

How to think:

1. Keep two variables: cur (the sum of the current stretch) and best (the best sum seen so far).
2. For each element x, make one decision: cur = max(x, cur + x).
3. If x wins, start a new stretch here because the old one was dragging you down. If cur + x wins, extend the old stretch.
4. Then update best = max(best, cur). Keep this separate: cur may drop later, but best remembers the peak.
5. Initialize best to -Infinity, not 0.
6. Need the indices? When x wins, set start = i. When best improves, store [start, i].

qa.q: What is the ONE decision Kadane's makes per element?
qa.a: Whether to extend the current subarray (cur + x) or start a new one at x. If the running sum is negative, extending only hurts, so we restart at x. Alongside that, we track the best sum seen so far.

qa.q: Why does Kadane's work when brute force is O(n²)?
qa.a: It relies on optimal substructure: the best subarray ending at index i is either nums[i] alone or nums[i] plus the best subarray ending at i-1. That single recurrence collapses all O(n²) candidate subarrays into n states, each computed in O(1).

boyer-moore.name: Boyer-Moore Voting
boyer-moore.desc: Find the majority element (one that appears more than n/2 times) in O(n) time and O(1) space. Keep a candidate and a counter: a matching element increments the counter, a different one decrements it, and when the counter hits zero the current element becomes the new candidate. A favorite at Meta.
boyer-moore.qsub: Why can't a non-majority element win the voting? · How do you extend it to n/3? · Why is this better than a frequency map here?
boyer-moore.what:
One element in the array appears more than half the time, and you must find it in O(n) time and O(1) space. A hash map is off the table because it uses O(n) space.

The trick is hidden in the constraint. "More than half" means that even if every majority vote is cancelled by a different vote, some majority votes are still left over, while every other element gets wiped out completely.

So keep a candidate and a count. A match gives +1, a mismatch gives −1, and when the count hits 0 the next element becomes the candidate. Whatever survives at the end is the majority.
boyer-moore.analogy: Picture a tug-of-war. Each person pulls toward one side, and two people pulling opposite ways cancel each other out. If one team has more than half of all the people, then after every cancellation someone from that team is still standing, and the rope points their way.
boyer-moore.why:
With a frequency map you can solve this in 30 seconds: O(n) time, but O(n) space. Then the interviewer asks the real question: "Can you do it in O(1) space?"

This tests whether you can turn the constraint into a tool. "> n/2" isn't just a condition, it's the heart of the algorithm, and noticing that is the real answer.

How to think:

1. Start with candidate = null and count = 0.
2. For each element x: if count === 0, set candidate = x. (The old candidate has been fully cancelled out.)
3. If x === candidate, do count++. Otherwise do count--.
4. That's all. At the end, candidate is the majority.
5. Why it works: every count-- cancels one majority vote against one non-majority vote. The non-majority elements have fewer than half the votes in total, so they can never cancel out the majority completely.
6. If a majority isn't guaranteed, run a second pass to count the candidate and confirm it.

qa.q: Why does Boyer-Moore work?
qa.a: Pair each occurrence of the majority element with a different element and cancel the pairs. Since the majority outnumbers all other elements combined, something from the majority survives every cancellation. The counter is just bookkeeping for that pairing.

qa.q: Does it need a verification pass?
