qa.a: Not if the problem guarantees that a majority exists. If it doesn't, the surviving candidate may be wrong, so count its occurrences and confirm it exceeds n/2. Verifying is a safe habit even when a guarantee is given.

quick-select.name: Quick Select
quick-select.desc: Find the k-th smallest or largest element without fully sorting: run the partition step and recurse only into the side that contains the target index. O(n) average, O(1) extra space when written iteratively, O(n²) worst case.
quick-select.q: Why is Quick Select O(n) on average instead of O(n log n)?
quick-select.qsub: What is the target index for k-th smallest vs k-th largest? · How does the partition guarantee the left side is all smaller? · Why doesn't the worst case show up on random data?
quick-select.what:
Suppose you need the k-th largest element. The simplest way is to sort the whole array and pick that index, which costs O(n log n). But that ranks the entire list when you only need one position.

Quick Select reuses the partition step from Quick Sort. After partitioning, the pivot sits in its final position, say p. Now exactly one of three things is true:

p === k → found. p < k → the answer is on the right. p > k → it's on the left. You go into only one side and discard the other completely. The total work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n, so O(n) on average.
quick-select.analogy: A race has finished and you only want to know who came 5th. Ranking everyone is wasteful. Pick one runner as a reference and split the field into those who finished ahead of them and those behind. Now their rank is fixed. If they came 8th, the 5th-place runner must be in the group ahead, so you search only there and ignore the rest.
quick-select.why:
Interviewers ask for the "k-th largest" because there are three valid answers, each best in a different situation:

Sort + index is O(n log n) and the simplest. A min-heap of size k is O(n log k) and best for streaming data. Quick Select is O(n) on average, but it mutates the input and has an O(n²) worst case. Mention all three and say when to use which. That's the complete answer.

How to think:

1. For the k-th largest, convert to an index: target = n - k. (For the k-th smallest, target = k - 1.) Getting this conversion wrong is the most common mistake.
2. Run partition from lo to hi, using the same Lomuto scheme as in quick sort.
3. Partition returns the pivot's final position p.
4. If p === target, then nums[target] is the answer. Stop.
5. If p < target, set lo = p + 1. Otherwise set hi = p - 1. You keep only one side.
6. To avoid the worst case, pick the pivot randomly. Otherwise a sorted input gives O(n²).

qa.q: Why is Quick Select O(n) on average instead of O(n log n)?
qa.a: Because it recurses into only ONE side, not both. The work is n + n/2 + n/4 + ..., which converges to 2n. The worst case is O(n²) when every pivot is extreme, the same risk as quick sort.

qa.q: Quick Select vs a heap for the k-th largest: which, and when?
qa.a: A heap costs O(n log k), works on streams, and gives you the whole top-k. Quick Select is O(n) on average for just the single k-th value, but it mutates the array. If you need the sorted top-k or are processing a stream, use a heap. If you only need the k-th value from an in-memory array, use Quick Select.

dutch-national-flag.name: Dutch National Flag
dutch-national-flag.desc: Sort an array containing three distinct values (such as 0s, 1s and 2s) in one pass with O(1) space, using three pointers. This three-way partition technique is the standard solution to Sort Colors.
dutch-national-flag.q: Why don't you advance mid after swapping with hi?
dutch-national-flag.qsub: What is the exact invariant at the start and end of each iteration? · How would this generalize to k colors? · Why is it called the 'Dutch national flag'?
dutch-national-flag.what:
The array holds only three distinct values: 0, 1 and 2. You must sort it in a single pass and without extra space.

Three pointers carve the array into zones. Everything left of lo is already 0, and everything right of hi is already 2. The mid pointer scans the middle, and everything between lo and mid is 1.

Here's the mistake nearly everyone makes: after swapping with hi, you must not advance mid. The element that just arrived from the right hasn't been examined yet.
dutch-national-flag.analogy: Imagine sorting laundry into three zones: whites on the left, colors in the middle, darks on the right. You pick items from the unsorted middle. A white goes to the left pile and you move on. A color stays where it is and you move on. A dark goes to the right pile, but whatever you pulled in from the right is something you haven't seen yet. Don't move on; look at it first.
dutch-national-flag.why:
This is the three-way version of Quick Sort's partition, and it helps when the array has many duplicates. A normal two-way partition performs poorly on duplicates, while a three-way partition groups all equal elements together.

Interviews often add a twist. Counting sort (two passes: count, then write) is also O(n), so the interviewer will say "do it in a single pass". That's when you need DNF.

How to think:

1. Set lo = 0, mid = 0 and hi = n - 1.
2. Remember the invariant: [0, lo) is all 0, [lo, mid) is all 1, (hi, n) is all 2, and [mid, hi] is not yet examined.
3. If nums[mid] === 0, swap it with lo, then do both lo++ and mid++. (The element that came from lo was a 1, which you've already examined.)
4. If nums[mid] === 1, it's already in the right place. Just do mid++.
5. If nums[mid] === 2, swap it with hi, do hi--, and leave mid unchanged. The new element hasn't been examined yet.
6. Stop when mid > hi. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.

qa.q: Why don't you advance mid after swapping with hi?
qa.a: The value swapped in from hi is unexamined. It could be a 0 that belongs at lo, so the loop re-checks it at the same mid index. Swaps with lo do advance mid, because the value that comes back is one you've already seen (a 1).

qa.q: When is three-way partitioning better than counting and rewriting?
qa.a: Counting the 0s, 1s and 2s and rewriting is also O(n), but it needs a second pass. Dutch National Flag is a single in-place pass, which matters when the problem forbids extra counts or arrays, and it also works on objects, where you can't just rewrite values. It's the same two-pointer idea extended to three zones.

insertion-sort.name: Insertion Sort
insertion-sort.desc: Build the sorted array one element at a time: take each element and insert it into the already-sorted prefix, shifting larger elements to the right. O(n²) in the worst case but O(n) on nearly sorted input. It is stable, in-place, and often the fastest choice for tiny arrays.
insertion-sort.q: When is insertion sort actually the right choice?
insertion-sort.qsub: What happens on an already-sorted array, and how many shifts occur? · Why does the best case run in O(n)? · How does shifting differ from swapping?
insertion-sort.what:
Think of sorting playing cards in your hand. You pick up a new card, and the cards you already hold are sorted. You slide the new card into its correct spot, nudging larger cards to the right. You never rebuild the whole hand.

That's insertion sort. Treat the array's prefix as always sorted, and insert each new element into that prefix at the right place.

Its key property is that it's adaptive. When the data is already nearly sorted, few or no shifts are needed, so it runs in O(n). Merge sort and quick sort still do their full O(n log n) work in that case.
insertion-sort.analogy: A hand of cards again: each new card goes straight to its spot, and you shift only the larger cards over a bit. If the cards already arrive in order, each new card simply goes on the end and there is no work at all.
insertion-sort.why:
The interviewer won't ask you to implement an O(n²) sort for its own sake. They want to see that the right algorithm depends on the shape of the input.

It also shows up in real libraries. Timsort (Python, Java, V8) uses insertion sort on small runs and then merges them, and introsort (C++) switches to insertion sort on small partitions. For small n, the constant overhead of O(n log n) algorithms costs more than a simple O(n²) pass.

How to think:

1. Start with i = 1. Treat [0, i) as already sorted (a one-element prefix always is).
2. Save cur = arr[i] in a variable, because its slot will be overwritten.
3. Walk backward with j = i - 1. While arr[j] > cur, shift that element one position right: arr[j+1] = arr[j].
4. When the loop stops, the gap that remains is where cur belongs: arr[j+1] = cur.
5. Note that this is shifting, not swapping. A shift is one write and a swap is three, so shifting is faster.
6. Use >, not >=. Stopping on equal elements keeps the sort stable.

qa.q: When is insertion sort actually the right choice?
qa.a: On nearly sorted data, where each element moves only a short distance, so the whole sort is close to O(n). Also on tiny arrays (roughly n < 15), where its low overhead beats the recursion and allocation costs of merge or quick sort.

qa.q: Why is it stable?
qa.a: The inner loop only shifts elements that are strictly greater than cur (arr[j] > cur). Equal elements are never moved past each other, so their original relative order is preserved.

bucket-sort.name: Bucket Sort
bucket-sort.desc: Distribute elements into k ordered buckets by value range, sort each bucket (often with insertion sort), then concatenate the buckets in order. O(n + k) on average when values are spread uniformly, but it degrades to O(n²) when they all land in one bucket.
bucket-sort.q: Why is the average case O(n + k)?
bucket-sort.qsub: How do you pick the bucket index formula? · What is the space overhead if k = n? · Why does a uniform distribution matter so much?
bucket-sort.what:
A well-known fact: any sort that works by comparing elements needs at least O(n log n) time. This is a proven lower bound.

Bucket sort gets around it because it doesn't compare elements at all. It uses the values' range: by looking at one value, it can tell directly which bucket it belongs in.

There are three steps: scatter (drop each value into its range bucket), sort (each bucket is small, so insertion sort is enough), and gather (join the buckets in order). The one condition is that the data must be evenly spread. If everything lands in one bucket, you're back to O(n²).
bucket-sort.analogy: Think of a post office. Letters are first dropped into separate bags by ZIP code range, with no comparing involved: read the code, toss the letter in the right bag. Then each bag is sorted on its own. The order of the bags does most of the sorting, so at the end you just line the bags up.
bucket-sort.why:
This topic answers a conceptual question: "Can a sort beat O(n log n)?" Not with comparisons. But if you know something about the values' range or distribution, yes.

The same idea underlies counting sort and radix sort. The most common interview form is "top K by frequency". There the frequency (0 to n) becomes the bucket index, and the whole job takes O(n).

How to think:

1. Find min and max, and decide how many buckets (k) to use. A common choice is k = n.
2. Scatter: compute each value's bucket index as ((x - min) / (max - min)) × k, then take the floor.
3. The largest value gives an index equal to k, which is out of range. Clamp it with Math.min(k - 1, idx).
4. Sort: sort each bucket separately. Buckets are small, so insertion sort works well.
5. Gather: concatenate buckets 0 through k-1 in order, for O(n + k) total. The array is now sorted.
6. With a uniform distribution you get about one element per bucket, so O(n) overall. If everything lands in one bucket, it becomes one big O(n²) insertion sort and the speed-up is lost.

qa.q: Why is the average case O(n + k)?
qa.a: Scattering and gathering each touch every element once, which is O(n). With a uniform distribution each bucket holds about n/k elements, and insertion-sorting one costs O((n/k)²). Across k buckets that's O(k·(n/k)²) = O(n²/k), which is O(n) when k is about n. Adding the O(k) to create the buckets gives O(n + k).

qa.q: When does it degrade to O(n²)?
qa.a: When the distribution is not uniform, for example when all values pile into one bucket. That bucket then holds n elements and insertion sort on it is O(n²). Bucket sort is only fast when the values are known to be well spread.

search-range.name: Binary Search on a Range
search-range.desc: The lower-bound/upper-bound form of binary search: find the FIRST index where a predicate becomes true (or the first element >= target). It unlocks first/last occurrence, insertion position and counting occurrences, which plain 'find the target' binary search can't handle.
search-range.q: Why hi = mid instead of hi = mid - 1 here?
search-range.qsub: Why does hi start at arr.length (not length-1)? · What does lowerBound return when the target is absent? · How do you adapt this for a peak or rotated array?
search-range.what:
Normal binary search looks for a value. This version looks for a boundary: the first position where a condition flips from false to true.

The whole idea in one line: instead of actual values, picture the array as F F F F T T T T. You want the first T.

This is more powerful because it handles duplicates (first or last occurrence) and because the "condition" can be anything, for example "Can speed x finish the work in h hours?" That's binary search on the answer.
search-range.analogy: Picture mobile signal in a tall building: none on the lower floors, strong on the higher ones, and once it appears it stays on every floor above. You want the first floor with signal. You don't need to stop at every floor. Jump to a middle floor, check it, and rule out half the building.
search-range.why:
This is the foundation of the "binary search on the answer" family, which comes up often in FAANG interviews.

The problem may not give you a sorted array at all. It might ask: "What is the minimum speed that finishes the work in h hours?" You have to notice that the range of answers has a monotonic yes/no condition. That recognition is the real answer, and the code afterwards is only about 8 lines.

How to think:

1. Set lo = 0 and hi = n, not n - 1, because the answer might be "insert at the end".
2. Loop with while (lo < hi), not <=. This template converges on the answer instead of exiting on a match.
3. Compute mid = lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1) and check the condition at mid.
4. If the condition is false (for example arr[mid] < target), the answer is later, so lo = mid + 1.
5. If the condition is true, mid itself could be the answer, so hi = mid. Not hi = mid - 1, which could throw the answer away.
6. The loop ends when lo === hi. That's the boundary, so return lo.

qa.q: Why hi = mid instead of hi = mid - 1 here?
qa.a: We are converging on a boundary, not pinning down a match. When arr[mid] >= target, mid could itself be the first such index, so discarding it with mid - 1 could skip the answer. Keeping mid lets the range shrink to exactly the boundary.

qa.q: How does this find the first AND last occurrence?
qa.a: lowerBound gives the first index with value >= target. For the last occurrence, find the first index with value > target and step back one. The gap between the two bounds is exactly the count of the target.

string-matching.name: String Matching (KMP / Rabin-Karp)
string-matching.desc: Finding a pattern inside a text. Naive scanning is O(n*m). KMP precomputes a prefix table so the text pointer never backtracks (O(n+m)), and Rabin-Karp uses a rolling hash to compare each window in O(1). Know both: KMP for worst-case guarantees, Rabin-Karp for multiple patterns.
string-matching.q: Why is KMP O(n+m) when naive is O(n*m)?
string-matching.qsub: What does the lps array store, conceptually? · Why does Rabin-Karp use modulo arithmetic? · What is the worst case for Rabin-Karp and when does it hit it? · How would you find all occurrences of a pattern in a text?
string-matching.what:
You need to find a pattern in a long text. The straightforward way is to try matching at every position. On a mismatch, move one step forward in the text and start over. That costs O(n×m).

That's wasteful, because after a mismatch you re-compare characters you already know matched.

KMP avoids this. It first preprocesses the pattern itself into an lps table, which says how far to shift the pattern on a mismatch. The text pointer never moves backward, so the total is O(n + m).

Rabin-Karp takes a different route: keep a rolling hash of each window. If the hash differs, skip the window in O(1). If it matches, compare the actual characters.
string-matching.analogy:
KMP: if you stumble on a line in the middle of a song, you don't restart from the first verse. You know how much of the lyrics you already got right, so you pick up from there.
Rabin-Karp: give every page of a book a short fingerprint. If the fingerprint doesn't match what you're looking for, don't bother opening the page. Only when it matches do you read the page.
string-matching.why:
This topic shows two fundamentally different ways to speed up the same problem: preprocessing the pattern (KMP) and hashing (Rabin-Karp).

In practice, if strStr comes up, just saying indexOf isn't enough. Explaining the KMP idea, that the text pointer never backtracks, can earn points even without full code. Rabin-Karp is better when you search many patterns at once or look for duplicate substrings.

How to think:

1. The lps table: for each position i, store the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. For "ABAB", lps[3] = 2 because "AB" appears at both ends.
2. To build the table, match the pattern against itself with the same loop: advance i, and on a mismatch set j to lps[j-1].
3. Scan: run i over the text and j over the pattern.
4. If the characters match, advance both. On a mismatch, set j = lps[j-1] and don't move i.
5. When j === m, the pattern is found at index i - m + 1.
6. Rabin-Karp: compute the hash of the first window. As the window slides, subtract the outgoing character and add the incoming one in O(1). When hashes match, still compare the characters, because two different strings can share a hash.

qa.q: Why is KMP O(n+m) when naive is O(n*m)?
qa.a: The lps table tells KMP exactly how far to shift the pattern on a mismatch, so the text pointer never moves backward. The naive approach restarts from the next text position after every mismatch, re-reading characters up to O(n*m) times in total.

qa.q: When is Rabin-Karp the better choice?
qa.a: When searching for many patterns at once (such as detecting duplicate code or scanning a corpus), because you can slide one rolling hash over the text and look each window up against all the pattern hashes in O(1). Its weakness is hash collisions, which you handle by re-checking the characters on a hash match.

two-pointers.name: Two Pointers
two-pointers.desc: Two indices scan the array from opposite ends (or at different speeds) to replace an O(n²) nested loop with a single O(n) pass. When the ends move toward each other, they exploit the sorted order of the data.
two-pointers.q: When can two pointers replace a nested loop?
two-pointers.qsub: How do you avoid duplicate triples in 3Sum? · When do you use fast/slow pointers instead of left/right? · Does two pointers require the array to be sorted?
two-pointers.what:
You have a sorted array and need two numbers that add up to a target. The first idea is to pair every number with every other number, a nested loop that costs O(n²).

But the array is sorted, and that is information you're not using yet.

Put one pointer at the start and one at the end. If the sum is too large, move the right pointer inward, which drops the larger number. If the sum is too small, move the left pointer forward. Each step shrinks the search space by one, so the whole array is processed in a single pass: O(n) time with no extra space.
two-pointers.analogy: Two shoppers start at opposite ends of a shelf of items sorted by price, trying to pick two items that cost exactly your budget together. If the pair is too expensive, the shopper at the pricey end steps inward. If it's too cheap, the shopper at the cheap end steps inward. They close in on the answer without ever checking every pair.
two-pointers.why:
Interviewers ask about this pattern to see whether you think beyond brute force: can you spot extra information (sorted order, a monotonic property) and use it to eliminate an entire loop? Without that, your solution stays at O(n^2) while the interviewer expects O(n).

How to think:

1. Put one pointer at the start of the array and the other at the end.
2. Add the values at both pointers and compare the sum to the target.
3. If the sum is greater than the target, move the right pointer one step left, since you need to drop the larger number.
4. If the sum is less than the target, move the left pointer one step right, since you need a bigger value in place of the smaller one.
5. If the sum equals the target, you've found the answer.
6. Repeat until the pointers meet. Each step shrinks the search space by one, so the total work is proportional to the array's length.

qa.q: When can two pointers replace a nested loop?
qa.a: When the data has structure (sorted order or a monotonic property) that lets you commit to moving one pointer without checking all remaining pairs. In Two Sum, if the sum is too small, every pair that uses the current left element is also too small, so you move the left pointer and never rescan it.

qa.q: Why move the shorter side in Container With Most Water?
qa.a: The area is limited by the shorter line. Moving the taller line inward can never increase the area, because the height is still capped by the shorter line while the width shrinks. Moving the shorter line is the only move that could improve the result, so it's the only one worth trying.

sliding-window.name: Sliding Window
sliding-window.desc: Maintain a contiguous window with two pointers that slide across the array. For each element, either extend the window or shrink it to restore the invariant. This turns O(n²) substring scans into O(n).
sliding-window.q: What is the ONE question to ask before using a sliding window?
sliding-window.qsub: Why is each element visited at most twice? · How do you prove the O(n) bound? · What changes for a fixed-size window?
sliding-window.what:
Say you need the longest (or shortest) contiguous segment of a string or array that satisfies some condition. The naive approach tries every start and end, which is O(n²).

But when you move from one start to the next, you don't need to redo the entire work. Just ask what is new and what has left.

That's the sliding window: a moving range that you expand (the right edge moves forward) and shrink (the left edge moves forward) until the condition holds again. Each edge crosses the array only once, so the total is O(n).
sliding-window.analogy: Think of a chat app that shows only the last 5 messages. When a new message arrives, you don't reread the whole history. You drop the oldest message and add the new one, so the window always holds exactly 5.
sliding-window.why:
This pattern tests whether you can avoid redundant recomputation. Fixed-size windows (such as "subarray of size k") and variable-size windows (such as "smallest subarray with sum at least target") show the interviewer that you can go from O(n^2) to O(n) without losing correctness.

How to think:

1. Put both the left and right pointers at the start of the array. The window starts empty.
2. Move the right pointer forward, add the new element to the window, and update the window's state (sum, count, or set).
3. Check whether the window is still valid or the condition has been violated.
4. If it's violated (the window grew too large in the fixed-size case, or the invariant broke in the variable-size case), move the left pointer forward and remove that element from the window until the condition is restored.
5. For every valid window, update the answer (length, sum, or count).
6. The right pointer crosses the array once and the left pointer only ever moves forward, never back, so the total movement is O(n).

qa.q: What is the ONE question to ask before using a sliding window?
qa.a: What invariant must the window satisfy? For 'longest substring without repeating characters' it's 'no duplicates in the window'. For 'minimum window containing all required characters' it's 'contains every needed character'. Everything else, the shrink logic and the answer updates, follows mechanically from that invariant.

qa.q: When does sliding window NOT apply?
qa.a: When the answer isn't a contiguous window. Subsequences (order-preserving but skippable) usually need DP, and arrays with negative numbers can break the monotonic shrink rule, since adding an element no longer reliably moves the sum in one direction. If extending the window doesn't move the condition in a predictable direction, the window can't slide.

binary-search-2.name: Binary Search (minimize/maximize)
binary-search-2.desc: The same halving idea applied to the space of answers instead of an array: when feasibility is monotonic, binary-search the answer value. It's behind Koko Eating Bananas, Split Array Largest Sum, and Capacity to Ship Packages.
binary-search-2.q: How do you recognize this pattern?
binary-search-2.qsub: What if the answer range is huge (10^9)? · How do you pick lo for a 'maximize the minimum' variant? · Why does the check have to be monotonic?
binary-search-2.what:
"What is the minimum eating speed that finishes all the bananas before the guard returns?" There's no sorted array here, but the answer lies in a range, say from 1 to 1,000,000.

Trying every value is slow. But notice this: speeds below a certain point fail, and from that point on every speed works. That's monotonic: F F F F T T T T.

So binary-search over the value of the answer, not over array indices. For each guess, run a feasible(x) check (usually O(n)) and discard half of the range based on the result. The total is O(log R × n).
binary-search-2.analogy: Imagine haggling over a used TV that you know costs somewhere between 0 and 10,000. You ask "Will you take 5,000?" If yes, you try 2,500. If no, you try 7,500. Each answer halves the price range until you find the lowest price the seller accepts. There's no array here, only a search along a number line.
binary-search-2.why:
This is a big mental shift that interviewers test on purpose: can you see that binary search applies not only to sorted arrays but to any monotonic feasibility function? Without it, candidates fall back on linear search or brute force and time out, while this pattern gives O(log(range) * check_cost).

How to think:

1. Decide the smallest and largest possible values of the answer. That is your search range, not an array.
2. Take the middle value (mid) and run a feasibility check: can the problem be solved with this value?
3. If mid is feasible and you want the minimum, record it and move to the lower half to try smaller values.
4. If mid isn't feasible, move to the upper half to try larger values.
5. For a maximize problem the logic is reversed: if mid is feasible, try larger values; if not, try smaller ones.
6. When the range narrows to a single value, that is your optimal answer.

qa.q: How do you recognize this pattern?
qa.a: The answer is a single number with a natural range (say 1 to max), and checking 'does answer x work?' is easy, but you'd otherwise have to test every value. The deciding feature is that feasibility is MONOTONIC: once a value works, everything beyond it works too.

qa.q: Why while (lo < hi) instead of while (lo <= hi)?
qa.a: In answer-space search we converge on a single boundary value rather than look for an exact hit, and a valid answer always exists in the range. The lo < hi form with hi = mid keeps the current candidate in range and converges cleanly, without extra bookkeeping or off-by-one risk. With lo <= hi you'd use mid - 1 and have to record the best answer separately.

prefix-sum.name: Prefix Sum
prefix-sum.desc: Precompute prefix[i] = the sum of the first i elements. Then any subarray sum over [l, r) is prefix[r] - prefix[l], in O(1). Extending it with prefix-sum counts in a hash map solves 'subarray sum equals k'.
prefix-sum.qsub: How does a 2D prefix sum answer rectangle queries? · What does seeding the map with {0: 1} do? · How would you find the longest subarray with sum k?
prefix-sum.what:
"What is the sum from index 3 to 7?" And then the same kind of question keeps coming for other ranges. Looping each time costs O(n) per query, which adds up fast over thousands of queries.

Compute prefix[i] once: the running total from the start up to i. Now the sum of any range is a difference: prefix[r] − prefix[l]. One O(n) preprocessing pass, then every query is O(1).

The real power comes next. Store prefix sums in a hash map, and you can count how many subarrays sum to exactly k in a single pass, because you can check in O(1) whether sum − k has been seen before.
prefix-sum.analogy: Think of a bank statement that shows your running total of spending up to each day, not just that day's spending. To find what you spent from day 5 to day 10, subtract the running total at the end of day 4 from the total at the end of day 10. You never re-add anything.
prefix-sum.why:
This pattern tests whether you can make repeated range queries fast by precomputing. Without it, problems like range sum or subarray-sum-equals-k stay at O(n^2). Adding a hash map to the prefix sums (prefix sum to count) tests another level: can you turn cumulative state into a lookup-friendly structure?

How to think:

1. Build a new array whose first element equals the first element of the original.
2. At each later index, add the previous prefix value to the current original value. That gives the running total up to that position.
3. To get the sum of any range from i to j, subtract prefix[i-1] from prefix[j]. (When i is 0, there is nothing to subtract; a leading zero in the prefix array removes this special case.)
4. To count subarrays whose sum equals k, create a hash map that stores how often each prefix sum has occurred, and seed it with prefix sum 0 seen once.
5. Walk the array once, compute the current prefix sum, and look up how many times current_prefix - k has already appeared in the map. Add that count to the answer.
6. After each step, add the current prefix sum to the map.

qa.q: Why does prefix[0] = 0 help?
qa.a: It makes range queries uniform: the sum over [l, r) is prefix[r] - prefix[l] with no special case for l = 0. Many off-by-one bugs disappear once you keep that zero sentinel at the front.

qa.q: How does the hash-map trick count subarrays that sum to k?
qa.a: A subarray [i, j] sums to k exactly when prefix[j] - prefix[i-1] = k, that is, prefix[i-1] = prefix[j] - k. As you scan, every earlier prefix sum equal to (current - k) marks the start of one valid subarray, and the map gives you that count in a single O(1) lookup per step.

intervals.name: Intervals
intervals.desc: Problems about ranges [start, end]: merging, inserting, counting overlaps. The near-universal trick is to SORT by start time, then compare each interval's start against the running end. The overlap test is next.start <= current.end.
intervals.q: What's the first move for almost every interval problem?
intervals.qsub: What's the difference between 'merge' and 'insert' strategies? · How does the greedy proof work for arrows and balloons? · When do you sort by start vs by end?
intervals.what:
You have a list of meetings, each with a start and an end. You need to find the overlaps or merge them into a clean schedule.

Comparing every interval with every other one costs O(n²). But if you first sort everything by start time, the problem changes completely.

In sorted order, if an interval doesn't overlap the one right after it, it can't overlap any later one either. So checking just the neighbor is enough. After one pass, the only real cost is the sort: O(n log n). Merging, inserting and counting all rely on this single trick.
intervals.analogy: Think of a meeting-room booking sheet. If you sort the bookings by start time, you only need to check that each booking doesn't start before the previous one ends. You never have to cross-check the whole list again and again.
intervals.why:
The interviewer wants to see that you know overlap detection can be done in O(n log n) (thanks to sorting) instead of O(n^2), and that sorting simplifies the structure of the problem. Without it, handling the edge cases (partial overlap, containment, touching intervals) in merge and insert problems gets very messy.

How to think:

1. Sort all intervals by their start value.
2. Create a result list and put the first interval in it.
3. Go through the remaining intervals one by one, comparing each with the last interval in the result.
4. If the current interval's start is less than or equal to the last interval's end, they overlap. Merge them by keeping the larger end.
5. If they don't overlap, append the current interval to the result as a new entry.
6. When all intervals are processed, the result list holds the final merged, non-overlapping intervals.
where: O(n log n) · space: O(n) output

qa.q: What's the first move for almost every interval problem?
qa.a: Sort: by start time for merging, by end time for 'maximum non-overlapping intervals'. Intervals come with no inherent order, so sorting gives them the structure that makes a single linear sweep meaningful.

qa.q: Why does sorting by end maximize the number of non-overlapping intervals?
qa.a: It's a greedy choice: picking the interval that ends earliest leaves the most room for the rest. This is the classic interval-scheduling argument. If an optimal solution picks a different first interval, swapping in the earliest-ending one never makes it worse.

weekly-mock.name: Weekly Timed Mock (start here)
weekly-mock.desc: From this phase onward, do one 45-minute timed mock every week: 2 problems, no hints, talking out loud. Solving in your room and solving under a clock are different skills. Start training the second one now, not in week 23.
weekly-mock.q: Which problems go into a weekly mock?
weekly-mock.qsub: Did I state the brute force and its complexity within the first 5 minutes? · Did I go silent for more than 30 seconds? · Did I test with an example before saying "done"?
weekly-mock.what: Once a week, set a 45-minute timer, pick two problems, and solve them out loud as if an interviewer were sitting in front of you. Record your screen and audio on your phone.
weekly-mock.why:
A Google-style round tests performance more than knowledge: in about 20 to 25 minutes you solve a Medium problem while thinking aloud and catching edge cases yourself. That habit doesn't develop in four weeks, so start in Phase 3 (week 7). By Phase 9 you will have done around 15 mocks.

How to think:

0-5 min: restate the problem and clarify constraints and examples.
5-10 min: state the brute-force solution and its complexity, then propose a better approach.
10-30 min: write the code while continuing to talk.
30-40 min: dry-run it, consider edge cases, and discuss complexity.
Afterwards, watch the recording. Note where you went silent or got stuck, and fix that habit next week.
where: 10-15 min after · space: log in P9 → Timed Mock template

qa.q: Which problems go into a weekly mock?
qa.a: One from your current phase and one from an older phase you haven't touched in 2+ weeks. Whenever possible, pick problems you have NOT solved before (use the LeetCode list for the same pattern). The old-phase problem doubles as spaced repetition.

qa.q: What if I fail the mock?
qa.a: That's the point: a failed mock in week 8 is cheap, a failed onsite is not. Write down WHERE you got stuck (understanding, approach, code, or bugs) and re-solve that exact problem three days later without looking at the solution.

binary-tree.name: Binary Tree Structure
binary-tree.desc: A hierarchical structure where each node has at most two children (left and right). It is recursive by nature: every subtree is itself a binary tree, which is why recursion is the natural tool.
binary-tree.q: Why is recursion a natural fit for trees?
binary-tree.qsub: What is a leaf node? What are full, complete and perfect trees? · Why does height() return 0 for null? · How would you build a tree from an array representation?
binary-tree.what:
Each node has at most two children: left and right. That is the whole definition.

The key idea is that every subtree is itself a complete binary tree. Pick any node and its left subtree is a valid tree on its own, so the structure repeats at every level.

That is why tree problems yield to recursion. You never need to reason about the whole tree. You only decide three things: what to do with this node, what answer comes back from the left, and what answer comes back from the right. Recursion handles the rest.
binary-tree.analogy: Think of a company org chart. A manager asks their two direct reports, "What's the status of everyone under you?" Each of them does the same with their own reports, so the manager never has to inspect hundreds of people. They only need two answers.
binary-tree.why:
This lesson is the foundation for all of Phase 4. Once you can break any problem into "what to do with this node, plus the answers from its two children", DFS, BFS, height and diameter all become straightforward.

There is also a trap: a binary tree is not a BST. In a plain binary tree the values have no order. Assuming a tree is sorted is the most common mistake, so ask the interviewer first.

How to think:

1. A node has three parts: a value, a left reference and a right reference.
2. A missing child is null, and that is your base case.
3. root is the top node, the one with no parent. If you lose it, you lose the whole tree.
4. Most recursive tree functions share one shape: if (!node) return <empty answer>, get the left answer, get the right answer, then combine them with this node.
5. The empty answer depends on the problem: 0 for a count, 0 for a sum, false for an existence check, [] for a list.
6. Space is O(h) because the call stack holds one frame per level. Balanced: O(log n). Skewed: O(n).

qa.q: Why is recursion a natural fit for trees?
qa.a: A binary tree is defined recursively: a node plus two (possibly empty) binary trees. A recursive function mirrors that definition: handle the empty case, trust the recursive call for each child, then combine the results. Without recursion you have to manage a stack or queue yourself.

qa.q: What is the space complexity of tree recursion?
qa.a: O(h), where h is the height, because the call stack holds one frame per level. A balanced tree gives O(log n) and a degenerate tree (every node has one child) gives O(n). An iterative traversal with an explicit stack has the same worst case, but it avoids the risk of a native stack overflow.

dfs.name: DFS (Preorder / Inorder / Postorder)
dfs.desc: Depth-first search goes all the way down one subtree before visiting the other. The three orders differ only in WHEN you process the node: before its children (pre), between them (in), or after them (post).
dfs.qsub: How do you write DFS iteratively? · What is the difference between a path and a subtree in DFS? · Why do preorder and inorder together uniquely reconstruct a binary tree?
dfs.what:
DFS means going all the way down one subtree before moving to the other. The route through the tree is always the same. The three "orders" are not different traversals.

The only difference is when you touch the node: before visiting its children (preorder), after the left subtree but before the right (inorder), or after both (postorder).

This timing is not a minor detail, because the problem decides it. Does the answer depend on the children, as with height or diameter? Use postorder. Need sorted output from a BST? Use inorder. Want to copy or serialize a tree? Use preorder.
dfs.analogy:
Imagine a cupboard full of boxes, with more boxes inside those. You open one box and explore its first inner box completely before coming back to open the next.
The three orders depend on when you write your note: as you open the box, in the middle, or as you close it. The route never changes.
dfs.why:
Interviewers aren't checking whether you can write three short functions. They want to see whether you can pick the right order.

The most useful rule: use postorder when a node's answer is built from its children's answers. Height, diameter, "is it balanced" and "sum of this subtree" are all postorder problems. And inorder is the BST's secret weapon: you get sorted output for free.

How to think:

1. if (!node) return is always the first line.
2. Preorder: process the node, then go fully into the left subtree, then the right.
3. Inorder: go fully into the left subtree, process the node, then go into the right.
4. Postorder: left, then right, and only then process the node. By now you already have both children's answers.
5. For path problems, carry an array down the recursion and pop() on the way back. That is backtracking.
6. Time is always O(n) because each node is visited once. Space is O(h) for the stack.

qa.q: When do you use postorder?
qa.a: Use it when a node's answer depends on its children's answers, such as height, diameter, max path sum or balance checks. You have to compute the children first, which is exactly what postorder does. Preorder is for cases where you can decide something at the node before descending.

qa.q: What is inorder traversal of a BST useful for?
qa.a: It visits the nodes in sorted order. That makes it the basis for Kth Smallest in a BST and for validating a BST (check that the sequence is strictly increasing).

bfs.name: BFS (Level Order)
bfs.desc: Breadth-first search visits a tree level by level using a queue: it processes every node at depth d before any node at depth d+1. Snapshotting the queue size cleanly separates the levels.
bfs.q: Why do you snapshot the queue size?
bfs.qsub: How do you find a tree's minimum depth with BFS and an early exit? · What is the queue's worst-case width? · How would you use BFS to check whether a tree is a perfect binary tree?
bfs.what:
Think of exploring a building floor by floor: every room on the ground floor, then the first floor, then the second. You don't jump from one room straight to the top.

Recursion can't do this, because it naturally goes deep along one path. You need a queue instead, which is first in, first out.

The one trick in BFS is to measure the queue size before you start a level. That many nodes belong to the current level, and anything enqueued afterwards belongs to the next level. This single line cleanly separates the levels.
bfs.analogy: Drop a stone into a pond. The ripples spread in concentric rings: first everything one step away, then everything two steps away. Whatever you reach first is the closest, and that one fact is the whole reason BFS finds shortest paths.
bfs.why:
There are two reasons to know this. First, some problems ask for a level-wise answer, such as the average per level, the right side view or a zigzag order. DFS can do these, but it gets clumsy.

Second, and more important, is shortest path. For minimum depth, DFS may wander deep into one subtree while the answer sits in a shallow branch. BFS reaches every node at its smallest distance first, guaranteed.

How to think:

1. Create a queue and enqueue root, after checking for !root.
2. Loop while the queue is not empty.
3. At the start of each iteration, set size = queue.length. This is the number of nodes in the current level.
4. Repeat exactly size times: dequeue a node from the front, process it, and enqueue its left and right children if they exist.
5. After that many nodes, the level is finished, and the next iteration handles the next level.
6. In JS, avoid shift() because it is O(n). Keep a head index and increment it instead.

qa.q: Why do you snapshot the queue size?
qa.a: Without it, the inner loop would keep draining the children you just enqueued and merge the levels together. The snapshot fixes how many nodes belong to the current level before any nodes from the next level are added.

qa.q: BFS vs DFS on a tree: when do you choose BFS?
qa.a: Choose BFS when the answer is level-based or when you need the shortest path (fewest edges). Choose DFS when recursion keeps path or sum computations simple. On wide trees BFS typically uses more memory (queue width) than DFS (stack depth).

bst.name: Binary Search Tree
bst.desc: A binary tree with an ordering invariant: everything in the left subtree < node < everything in the right subtree. Each step of a search halves the remaining space, giving O(log n) on balanced trees. Inorder traversal yields sorted order.
bst.q: How do you validate a BST without comparing against a global min/max?
bst.qsub: What makes a BST unbalanced, and what is the worst-case height? · How do you insert without breaking the invariant? · How would you find the lowest common ancestor in a BST using values?
bst.what:
In a plain binary tree the values have no order. A BST adds one rule: every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node, and every value in the right subtree is larger.

With just this rule, each comparison discards half the tree. It is binary search on a tree instead of an array, and it costs O(h).

You also get a free bonus: inorder traversal yields sorted values, because inorder visits everything smaller, then the node, then everything larger. That is why many BST questions (kth smallest, validate, range sum) are solved with inorder.

One caveat: O(log n) holds only when the tree is balanced. If you insert sorted data, the tree degenerates into a linked list and operations cost O(n).
bst.analogy: Imagine a decision guide where every page says "smaller names go left, larger names go right". To find a name you don't read everything. Each page makes one decision: left or right. But if names arrive already in alphabetical order, they all pile up on one side, and the guide turns back into a long list.
bst.why:
Validating a BST is a classic interview trap. Many people compare a node only with its parent, which is wrong. A node must respect the limits set by all of its ancestors, so you have to pass (lo, hi) bounds down the recursion.

Another test is whether you claim O(log n) without mentioning balance. On a skewed BST everything is O(n), so stating this caveat earns extra credit.

How to think:

1. Search: start at the root. If the target is smaller, go left. If larger, go right. If equal, you found it.
2. Insert: follow the same path until you reach null, and put the new node there.
3. Validate: give each node a (lo, hi) range. Going left sets hi = node.val, and going right sets lo = node.val. Comparing only with the parent is wrong.
4. Kth smallest: run an inorder traversal and count. The k-th node visited is the answer.
5. Delete has three cases. No children: remove the node. One child: replace the node with that child. Two children: swap in the inorder successor (the smallest node in the right subtree), then delete that successor.
6. Everything is O(h): log n when balanced, n when skewed.

qa.q: How do you validate a BST without comparing against a global min/max?
qa.a: Pass the allowed range (lo, hi) down the recursion: going left, hi becomes node.val, and going right, lo becomes node.val. This catches the classic trap where a node satisfies its parent but violates an ancestor, for example a 5 in the right subtree of a 10, even if its own parent is 15.

qa.q: Why does inorder traversal give sorted order?
qa.a: By the BST invariant, everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node and everything in the right subtree is larger. Visiting left, then node, then right therefore emits the values in ascending order, and applying that argument recursively covers every subtree.

construct-tree.name: Construct Tree from Traversals
construct-tree.desc: Two traversals can uniquely rebuild a binary tree. With preorder + inorder, the first preorder value is the root, and finding it in inorder splits the left and right subtrees. Recursion plus an index map does the rest.
construct-tree.q: Why do preorder + inorder uniquely determine a tree?
construct-tree.qsub: How does the version with postorder differ? · What does the index map save you? · Why does the recursion need to track the current root's position?
construct-tree.what:
You are given only two lists, preorder and inorder, and must rebuild the entire tree. At first this seems impossible, because a traversal doesn't show the structure.

But one fact is certain: the first value in preorder is always the root. Now find that value in inorder. Everything to its left is the whole left subtree, and everything to its right is the whole right subtree.

Then repeat the same step on each side. The next preorder value is the new root, and inorder splits around it into two parts.

One optimization matters: searching for the root in inorder every time costs O(n), which makes the whole algorithm O(n²). Build a hash map (value → index) first, and each lookup becomes O(1), so the total drops to O(n).
construct-tree.analogy: Imagine two descriptions of the same family. One tells you who to start with (the first preorder value is the root). The other lists everyone in left-to-right order. Find the starting person in the second list: everyone before them is the "left branch", and everyone after them is the "right branch".
construct-tree.why:
This problem tests three skills at once: recursion, hash maps and index tracking. A naive solution keeps slicing arrays with slice, which makes it O(n²). Passing indices instead is the right answer.

A conceptual follow-up often comes up: why aren't preorder + postorder enough? Because they don't reveal whether a lone child is a left or a right child. Inorder is the traversal that separates left from right.

How to think:

1. Build a hash map for inorder: value → index. This gives O(1) lookups.
2. Keep a pointer into preorder that only moves forward: pre = 0.
3. Give the recursion a range of inorder: build(lo, hi). If lo > hi, return null.
4. Create a node from preorder[pre++] and look up its index in the inorder map. Call it i.
5. Build the left side first: build(lo, i-1). Then build the right: build(i+1, hi). The order matters, because in preorder the entire left subtree comes before the right.
6. With inorder + postorder, the root is the last value, the pointer moves backward, and you must build the right side first.

qa.q: Why do preorder + inorder uniquely determine a tree?
qa.a: The first preorder element is the root. Inorder then tells you exactly which nodes are in the left and right subtrees: everything before the root and everything after it. Recursing on those split ranges rebuilds the whole tree, with one root taken per preorder element and one split per inorder lookup.

qa.q: Why can't you reconstruct a tree from preorder + postorder alone?
qa.a: Both orders put the root at an end of the sequence and neither separates left from right. When a node has only one child, you can't tell whether it is the left or right child, so the tree is determined only up to such choices. The exception is a full binary tree, where every node has zero or two children, and there the pair is enough.

tree-measurements.name: Height, Depth, Diameter
tree-measurements.desc: The measurement family: height (node to its deepest leaf), depth (root to a node) and diameter (the longest path between any two nodes). Height uses postorder, and diameter is left height + right height computed along the way.
tree-measurements.q: What is the difference between depth and height?
tree-measurements.qsub: Does the diameter always pass through the root? · How do you count nodes instead of edges? · How would you return the actual diameter path, not just its length?
tree-measurements.what:
These are three similar-looking questions with different answers:

Height is how far the farthest leaf is below a node. Depth is how far a node is below the root, so it measures in the opposite direction. Diameter is the longest path between any two nodes in the whole tree.

Height needs postorder, because you must know both children's heights before you know your own. Depth uses preorder, because it is passed down from the top.

The real trick with diameter is that the longest path does not necessarily pass through the root. It can lie entirely inside a subtree. So the function returns the height while tracking the diameter separately, and both are computed in one pass.
tree-measurements.analogy: Think of a family tree. Height is how many generations the farthest descendant is below you. Depth is how many generations you are below the oldest ancestor. Diameter is the longest chain of relationships between any two relatives, and it can run between two cousins through their shared grandparent, without touching the oldest ancestor at all.
tree-measurements.why:
Diameter is a classic interview trap. The naive solution recomputes the height at every node, which is O(n²). The interviewer wants you to compute height and track the diameter in a single traversal.

This pattern pays off later: the function returns one thing while tracking another separately. Max Path Sum, Longest Univalue Path and the balanced check all have this shape.

How to think:

1. Height: null gives 0. Otherwise it is 1 + max(left, right). This is postorder.
2. Depth: carry a counter down from the root, using depth + 1. This is preorder.
3. Diameter: the longest path that goes through a given node is leftHeight + rightHeight.
4. Update an external best with that value at every node.
5. But return 1 + max(left, right), because a path extended through the parent can use only one side of this node. It cannot fork at the node and continue upward.
6. Learn this "return one thing, track another" pattern well. It appears repeatedly throughout Phase 4.

qa.q: What is the difference between depth and height?
qa.a: Depth of a node is the number of edges from the root down to it, so the root has depth 0. Height of a node is the number of edges from it down to its deepest leaf. A leaf has height 0 or 1 depending on the convention, so agree on one before coding. Depth is computed top-down and height is computed bottom-up.

qa.q: Why does the diameter function return the height but track the diameter separately?
qa.a: The diameter through a node is its left height + right height. But when the parent extends a path through this node, only the node's own height (1 + max child height) matters, since the path can use just one side. So the function returns the height and records the diameter in a shared best variable as a side effect.

dfs-iterative.name: Iterative DFS
dfs-iterative.desc: The explicit-stack version of depth-first traversal. It is useful when recursion depth might overflow, or when the interviewer asks you to avoid recursion. A stack (LIFO) mimics the call stack exactly.
dfs-iterative.q: How does iterative inorder keep the left-first order?
dfs-iterative.qsub: How do you do iterative postorder? · Does iterative traversal save space? · When is recursion still the better answer?
dfs-iterative.what:
Recursive DFS also uses a stack; it is just implicit. The JS engine keeps a frame for each function call on the call stack, and that is what remembers your path through the tree.

The problem is that this stack is limited. In JS, somewhere around 10,000 frames (the exact limit depends on the engine) you get RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. A skewed or very deep tree can hit that limit.

Iterative DFS does the same work with your own stack, an ordinary array. It lives on the heap, which is far larger. The traversal is identical, but you control the stack.

Note: both versions use O(h) space. Iterative DFS doesn't use less memory; it just stores it somewhere else. Mention this in an interview.
dfs-iterative.analogy:
Picture a waiter who memorizes every order and runs to the kitchen on each one. That is recursion: it works, but his memory is limited.
Now give him a notepad where pending orders are written down, so he can always take the top one next. The job is the same, but the notepad can be as long as needed.
dfs-iterative.why:
"Can you do it iteratively?" is the most common follow-up question. It isn't only about syntax. The interviewer wants to see that you understand recursion is essentially a stack.

Preorder has one small detail that shows full understanding: push the right child first, then the left. The stack is LIFO, so the last item pushed comes out first. Get that one line wrong and the order flips.

How to think:

1. Preorder: push the root onto the stack. Then loop: pop, process, and push right, then left. Left is pushed last, so it pops first.
2. Inorder: work in two phases. While cur exists, push it and move down to the left. Then pop, process, and set cur = cur.right.
3. Don't forget cur = cur.right in inorder, or the same node repeats forever.
4. Postorder (easy way): run a reversed preorder, node, then right, then left, and reverse the final result.
5. Postorder (real way): keep a flag with each node. On the first visit, push it back with the flag set. On the second visit, process it.
6. The loop condition is while (stack.length). Inorder needs while (cur || stack.length), and both parts are required.

qa.q: How does iterative inorder keep the left-first order?
qa.a: Push every node along the left spine first, so the stack holds them from root down to the leftmost node. Pop the deepest one, visit it, then move to its right child and push that node's left spine in turn. This reproduces the left, root, right rhythm of recursion exactly.

qa.q: Why is iterative preorder just a stack?
qa.a: Preorder visits a node BEFORE its children, so you can push the children onto a stack and immediately pop the next node to visit. Pushing right before left makes the left child pop first, with no extra bookkeeping.

balanced-bst.name: Balanced BSTs (AVL / Red-Black)
balanced-bst.desc: A plain BST can degenerate into a linked list, making every operation O(n). Balanced trees rebalance on insert and delete to keep the height at O(log n). AVL enforces a height difference of at most 1 using rotations. Red-Black uses color rules that keep the longest path within twice the shortest.
balanced-bst.q: Why not just use a plain BST and call it O(log n)?
balanced-bst.qsub: What invariant does an AVL tree maintain? · How many rotations does an AVL insert need at most? · Why does a balanced BST beat a sorted array for inserts? · Name two real-world data structures built on balanced trees.
balanced-bst.what:
Take a plain BST and insert 1, 2, 3, 4 in that order. Each new number becomes the right child of the previous one, and your "tree" is really a straight linked list.

Now search, insert and delete all cost O(n) instead of O(log n), and the whole advantage of a BST is gone. This is not a rare case either, since inserting sorted data is very common.

A balanced BST fixes this after every insert or delete. It checks whether the tree has tilted to one side and, if so, rotates a few nodes to bring the height back to O(log n).

AVL is strict: the height difference at every node must be ≤ 1. Red-Black is looser: its color rules keep the longest path from exceeding twice the shortest.
balanced-bst.analogy: Picture a bookshelf where new books keep getting stacked on the left end while the right end stays empty. Eventually the shelf tips over. A careful librarian checks the tilt after each new book and, when needed, moves some books to the other side. It costs a little extra work, but the shelf never falls.
balanced-bst.why:
This topic is for discussion, not implementation. You will rarely be asked to write out every AVL rotation in an interview.

What interviewers test is whether you know that saying "BST is O(log n)" is an incomplete answer. The correct statement is: "a balanced BST gives O(log n), while a plain BST is O(n) in the worst case."

It also ties into system design. Java's TreeMap, C++'s std::map and database indexes (B-trees, a close relative) all rely on this guarantee.

How to think:

1. Balance factor = left height − right height. In an AVL tree it must always be -1, 0 or 1.
2. Insert as in a normal BST. Then, on the way back up, check the balance factor at each node.
3. If a factor becomes 2 or -2, rotate.
4. There are four cases: LL (one right rotation), RR (one left rotation), and LR and RL (two rotations, which people often forget).
5. A rotation does not break the BST property. It changes the shape but not the order, so the inorder traversal stays the same.
6. Red-Black takes a different route, with node colors and color rules. It does fewer rotations, so inserts and deletes are faster, but the tree can be a bit taller, so searches are slightly slower.

qa.q: Why not just use a plain BST and call it O(log n)?
qa.a: Inserting sorted data into an unbalanced BST produces a linear chain, so every operation becomes O(n). A balanced tree enforces the height bound structurally, whatever the insertion order.

qa.q: AVL vs Red-Black: which do you pick and why?
qa.a: Pick AVL for read-heavy workloads, because its tighter height bound gives faster lookups. Pick Red-Black for write-heavy workloads, because it does fewer rotations on insert and delete. The trade-off is search speed against rebalancing cost.

graph-repr.name: Graph Representation
graph-repr.desc: How you store edges decides how fast every operation is. Adjacency list: node to list of neighbors, O(V+E) space, the default. Adjacency matrix: V×V booleans, O(V²) space, O(1) edge lookup. Edge list: an array of [u, v, weight], compact and easy to sort.
graph-repr.q: Adjacency list vs matrix: how do you choose?
graph-repr.qsub: How do you store a directed acyclic graph? · When would an edge list beat an adjacency list? · What is the space of each representation for n=1000, e=10000?
graph-repr.what:
The first step in most graph problems is to turn the input into a structure that instantly answers "who are this node's neighbors?".

An adjacency list stores, for each node, a list of its actual neighbors. Space is O(V + E). It is the default choice for the vast majority of problems.

An adjacency matrix is a V × V grid where each cell says whether an edge exists. It takes O(V²) space even for an empty graph, but edge lookup is O(1).

An edge list is simply an array of [u, v, weight]. It suits Kruskal's algorithm, which needs the edges sorted.
graph-repr.analogy: A list is like your phone contacts: only people you actually know are saved. A matrix is like a giant table with a cell for every possible pair of people, filled in even when the two have never met. In a sparse graph, nearly all of that table stays empty.
graph-repr.why:
Interviewers notice this within the first two minutes. Picking the wrong representation can silently turn your O(V + E) solution into O(V²).

The most common bug is forgetting the reverse edge in an undirected graph. The code runs and doesn't crash, but half the graph is missing and the answer is wrong.

How to think:

1. The input is often an edge list, such as [[0,1],[1,2],[0,3]].
2. Create an array of arrays with Array.from({length: n}, () => []). Don't write Array(n).fill([]), because every row would then reference the same array.
3. For each edge [u, v], do g[u].push(v). If the graph is undirected, also do g[v].push(u), so both directions are stored.
4. For weighted edges, store each neighbor as a pair: g[u].push([v, w]).
5. If nodes are numbered from 1, either create an array of size n + 1 or subtract 1 everywhere. This off-by-one error is a frequent pitfall.
6. Use a matrix only when the graph is dense (E ≈ V²) or when you need frequent edge checks.

qa.q: Adjacency list vs matrix: how do you choose?
qa.a: Use a list when the graph is sparse, which covers most real graphs: it takes O(V+E) space and iterating over neighbors is cheap. Use a matrix for dense graphs, or when you need O(1) checks of whether an edge exists between u and v, at the cost of O(V²) space.

qa.q: What are the most common bugs in the first two minutes of a graph problem?
qa.a: Forgetting the second push for undirected graphs (adding u to v but never v to u), and mixing 1-indexed input with 0-indexed arrays. Checking these two up front saves you from entire wrong solutions.

bfs-graphs.name: BFS on Graphs
bfs-graphs.desc: Queue-based, level-by-level exploration. On unweighted graphs it finds the SHORTEST path in number of edges. A visited set (or distance array) is mandatory, because unlike trees, graphs can have cycles.
bfs-graphs.q: Why must you mark nodes visited when ENQUEUEING, not when popping?
bfs-graphs.qsub: When is BFS the right choice over DFS? · What is the queue's worst-case memory? · How do you reconstruct the actual path, not just its length?
bfs-graphs.what:
BFS on a graph works like BFS on a tree: a queue, one level at a time. The new danger is that graphs can have cycles, whereas in a tree you can never walk back to where you came from.

So the visited set is no longer optional, it is required. Without it the queue never becomes empty.

The real gift of BFS is the shortest path on an unweighted graph. It expands one ring at a time, so the first time you reach a node you have used the fewest edges, guaranteed. DFS cannot promise this.

Many people get one detail wrong: mark a node as visited when you add it to the queue, not when you remove it. Otherwise the same node can enter the queue many times.
bfs-graphs.analogy:
Think of dropping a stone in a pond. The ripples spread one ring at a time, first everything one step away, then everything two steps away. So whatever the ripple touches first is the closest.
If you don't remember where the ripple has already been, it will keep circling forever.
bfs-graphs.why:
A single question can test the whole topic: "Do you mark visited on enqueue or on dequeue?"

If you mark on dequeue, a node can enter the queue many times and be expanded each time. On layered graphs the work can blow up from O(V + E) to exponential, so you get a time limit exceeded even if the answer is right.

Another thing interviewers test: did you use DFS for a shortest path? That is wrong, because DFS gives no guarantee that the first path it finds is the shortest.

How to think:

1. Create a queue, insert the source, and at the same time add it to visited.
2. If you need level-wise processing, measure size at the start of the loop, the same trick as for trees.
3. Dequeue a node from the front and look at its neighbors.
4. For each unvisited neighbor, mark it visited first, then enqueue it. This order is essential.
5. If you need distances, either keep a level counter or write dist[v] = dist[u] + 1.
6. Multi-source: enqueue all the sources at the start so they expand together. Rotting Oranges and 01 Matrix rely on this.

qa.q: Why must you mark nodes visited when ENQUEUEING, not when popping?
qa.a: If you mark on pop, the same node can be enqueued by several parents before it is popped. Duplicates flood the queue, waste work, and can even overwrite distance values. Marking at enqueue guarantees each node enters the queue exactly once.

qa.q: What is multi-source BFS and when do you use it?
qa.a: Seed the queue with ALL starting nodes at distance 0. In Rotting Oranges that means every rotten cell, and in 01 Matrix it means every zero. The wavefront then expands uniformly from every source, and the first time a cell is reached is its true minimum distance.

dfs-graphs.name: DFS on Graphs
dfs-graphs.desc: Recursive (or stack-based) exploration that dives deep before backtracking. It is a good fit for connectivity (components, islands), cycle detection and path existence. A visited set prevents infinite loops on cycles.
dfs-graphs.q: How does DFS detect cycles in a directed graph?
dfs-graphs.qsub: Why can DFS use less memory than BFS on wide graphs? · How do you count the size of each connected component? · What is the difference between visited and on-stack in cycle detection?
dfs-graphs.what:
In a maze, you pick a path and follow it all the way in. When you hit a dead end, you turn back and try another route. That is DFS.

On a graph, DFS differs from the tree version in one way: the visited set is required, otherwise the recursion never stops when it meets a cycle.

The real point comes next. In a directed graph, a plain "visited" flag is not enough to find cycles. Meeting a node again can mean two different things: its processing is already finished (which is fine), or it is still on your call stack (a cycle!).

So you need three colors: 0 means not visited yet, 1 means currently on the stack, and 2 means finished. Reaching a node with color 1 means there is a cycle.
dfs-graphs.analogy:
While walking through a maze, leave two kinds of marks. Chalk says "I'm currently on this path". A sticker says "I've fully explored this path and found nothing new".
If you run into a chalk mark, you have looped back onto your own path, which is a cycle. If you reach a sticker, just skip it.
dfs-graphs.why:
This is one of the most frequently tested ideas in Phase 5: directed cycle detection needs three states, not two.

People try a boolean visited and end up reporting a "cycle" in a DAG, because a node can be reached by two different paths without forming a cycle.

In undirected graphs the story is different. Two states are enough, but you must skip the parent, otherwise every edge looks like a "cycle".

How to think:

1. Create a state array with one entry per node, all 0 at first.
2. When DFS enters a node, set state[u] = 1 (on the stack).
3. For each neighbor v: if state[v] === 1, you have found a cycle, so return. If state[v] === 2, skip it. If it is 0, recurse into it.
4. After all neighbors are processed, set state[u] = 2 (finished) and return.
5. Undirected: a boolean visited works, but pass parent down the recursion and skip the neighbor when v === parent.
6. A graph can have multiple components, so start a DFS from every node that is not yet visited.

qa.q: How does DFS detect cycles in a directed graph?
qa.a: Use three colors: unvisited, on-stack and done. If DFS reaches a node that is still on-stack, it has found a back edge, which means a cycle. The on-stack state matters because reaching a finished node is NOT a cycle; it is just a shared subtree.

qa.q: BFS vs DFS on a graph: how do you decide?
qa.a: Use BFS for shortest paths and anything level-based. Use DFS for connectivity, components and cycles, or when recursion gives cleaner code. On memory, BFS uses queue width, up to O(V), and DFS uses stack depth, also O(V) in the worst case, so they are comparable on dense graphs.

union-find.name: Union-Find (Disjoint Set)
union-find.desc: A data structure for dynamic connectivity: "are u and v in the same set?" and "join the sets of u and v". With path compression and union by rank, both operations run in nearly O(1) amortized time (inverse Ackermann). It is a good fit for connected components and cycle checks in undirected graphs.
union-find.q: How does path compression make find nearly O(1)?
union-find.qsub: Why use union by rank and not just path compression? · How does union-find detect a cycle in an undirected graph? · How does its memory footprint compare to an adjacency list?
union-find.what:
The same question keeps coming up: "are u and v in the same group?" And now and then, two groups merge.

Running BFS or DFS each time costs O(V + E), and this question can be asked thousands of times.

The Union-Find idea is simple: each group has a leader (root). find(x) returns the leader of x. If two nodes have the same leader, they are in the same group. union(u, v) joins the two leaders.

A naive version can degrade to O(n) per operation because a long chain forms. Two small optimizations (path compression and union by rank) make it practically O(1).
union-find.analogy:
Every club has a president. To ask "are these two people in the same club?", ask each person who their president is. If it is the same person, the answer is yes.
To merge two clubs, make one president report to the other.
Path compression means that each time you look up the president, everyone you passed on the way gets the president's number directly, so next time nobody has to go through the chain.
union-find.why:
Interviewers usually ask two things. First, why do you need both optimizations? Each one alone gives roughly O(log n) amortized time. Only together do they get you close to constant time.

Second, and more useful, is cycle detection in an undirected graph. Before adding an edge, ask whether its two endpoints are already in the same group. If they are, this edge would create a cycle. Kruskal's whole MST algorithm hinges on this single check.

How to think:

1. Start with parent[i] = i, so every node is its own leader.
2. find(x): while parent[x] !== x, move up.
3. Path compression: while moving up, link every node on the path directly to the root. It is one line: parent[x] = find(parent[x]).
4. union(u, v): find both roots. If they are the same, do nothing, and treat it as a cycle signal.
5. Union by rank: attach the shorter tree under the taller one, so trees don't keep growing tall.
6. To count components, start a counter at n and decrement it on each successful union.

qa.q: How does path compression make find nearly O(1)?
qa.a: After find(x), we rewire x and every node on its path to point directly at the root. The tree flattens over time, so later finds take a single hop. Combined with union by rank (attach the shorter tree under the taller), the amortized cost per operation is the inverse Ackermann function, which is effectively constant.

qa.q: Union-Find vs BFS/DFS for connected components?
qa.a: Union-Find shines when connections arrive incrementally, or when you need many "are they connected?" queries without re-traversing the graph. BFS/DFS is simpler when you only need a one-time component count on a static graph. Both are in the O(V+E) class, but Union-Find adds near-O(1) point queries.

grid-problems.name: Grid Problems
grid-problems.desc: A 2D grid IS a graph: each cell is a node and adjacent cells are edges. Add a visited marker and BFS/DFS to solve islands, rotting oranges, flood fill and surrounded regions without building an explicit graph.
grid-problems.q: Why is sinking a cell in place a valid visited marker?
grid-problems.qsub: How do you find the largest island's area? · How does Surrounded Regions flip only the cells that are not connected to the boundary? · How would you run a multi-source BFS from all boundary cells?
grid-problems.what:
A grid looks like a matrix, but it is really a graph. Each cell is a node, and the cells above, below, left and right are its neighbors.

Once you see that, problems like "Number of Islands", "Rotting Oranges" and "Flood Fill" are ordinary BFS or DFS.

One advantage is that you don't need to build an adjacency list. Neighbors are generated on the fly from a small dirs array: [[1,0],[-1,0],[0,1],[0,-1]].

There is also a neat trick: you don't need a separate visited set. Just modify the cell itself (turn land into water). That costs O(1) extra space and keeps the code short.
grid-problems.analogy:
Think of a building's floor plan. Each room is a node, and doors exist only between adjacent rooms. There is no direct path to diagonal rooms unless the problem says so.
Once you have visited a room, put a mark on it, so you don't need a separate checklist.
grid-problems.why:
Interviewers want to see whether you recognize a grid as a graph. Someone who starts building a separate adjacency list hasn't yet grasped that a grid is an implicit graph.

There is also a bug that shows up every time: a missing bounds check. Reading grid[nr][nc] before verifying that nr and nc are inside the grid causes a crash on undefined. Check the bounds first, then the cell.

How to think:

1. Set m = grid.length and n = grid[0].length, assuming the grid is rectangular.
2. Use dirs = [[1,0],[-1,0],[0,1],[0,-1]] for four directions. Use eight if diagonals count, and confirm this from the problem statement.
3. Loop over every cell. When you find unvisited land, start a DFS or BFS there and increment a counter with +1.
4. Inside that DFS or BFS, immediately mark the cell (or turn it into '0'), then try the four neighbors.
5. For each neighbor, check the bounds first, then visited, then the value, in that order.
6. Choose DFS if you need an area or shape. Choose BFS if you need distances or step counts, or if the grid is large enough that recursion could overflow.
where: O(m × n) · space: O(m × n) worst

qa.q: Why is sinking a cell in place a valid visited marker?
qa.a: Setting grid[r][c] = '0' marks the cell as visited without O(m×n) extra memory. It is safe as long as '0' already means "not a cell of interest", so the mutation can't confuse later logic. It is a classic memory saving that interviewers appreciate, but mention that it mutates the input.

qa.q: BFS or DFS for islands?
qa.a: Both run in O(m×n). DFS is shorter to write with recursion. BFS avoids recursion-depth limits on huge grids and is the natural fit when the problem asks for distance spreading, as in Rotting Oranges. Know both and justify your choice by grid size.

dijkstra.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
dijkstra.desc: Shortest path in a graph with NON-NEGATIVE weights. It is BFS with a priority queue: repeatedly extract the closest unvisited node and relax its edges. O((V + E) log V) with a min-heap.
dijkstra.q: Why does Dijkstra fail on negative edge weights?
dijkstra.qsub: How is Dijkstra like BFS? · When do you use a visited set in Dijkstra, and when not? · What changes if you want the path itself?
dijkstra.what:
BFS finds the shortest path, but only when every edge has the same weight. That isn't true on a real map, where some roads are long but fast and others are short but congested.

Dijkstra is the same idea as BFS, but it uses a min-heap instead of a plain queue. Each time, it picks the node with the cheapest path found so far.

For every edge leaving that node, it asks: "Does going through this node make some other node cheaper to reach?" If so, it updates that node's distance and pushes it into the heap. This step is called relaxation.

There is one condition: no weight may be negative. Dijkstra assumes that once a node is picked as the cheapest, no later path can beat it. A negative edge breaks that assumption.
dijkstra.analogy:
Imagine planning a trip across a country with a different ticket price on every route. You always go next to the city you can reach with the lowest total cost so far, check every connection from there, and update your price list whenever a cheaper route appears.
Now suppose one route pays you money (a negative price). The reasoning that a city is final once you pick it no longer holds.
dijkstra.why:
This is the default answer for weighted shortest-path questions, and interviewers follow up immediately with "why does it fail on negative weights?" Explaining it clearly shows you understand the core idea.

Another point is stale entries. The same node can sit in the heap several times with older, larger distances. When you pop an entry, compare it with dist[]. If the popped distance is larger, it is outdated, so skip it. Missing this check makes the code slower, and it can do redundant work on the same node.

How to think:

1. Create a dist array filled with Infinity, then set dist[src] = 0.
2. Push [0, src] into the min-heap, with the distance first so the heap sorts by it.
3. Extract the node u with the smallest distance from the heap.
4. Stale check: if d > dist[u], this is an old entry, so continue.
