5. Relax: for each neighbor v, if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v] and push [dist[v], v] into the heap.
6. When the heap is empty, you are done. dist now holds the cheapest path to every node. Time is O((V + E) log V).
where: O((V + E) log V) · space: O(V + E)

qa.q: Why does Dijkstra fail on negative edge weights?
qa.a: It greedily finalizes the closest node, assuming no later path can improve it. A negative edge breaks that assumption, because a distance that was already locked in could shrink afterwards. Bellman-Ford handles negative edges by relaxing all edges V-1 times.

qa.q: Why skip stale heap entries?
qa.a: A node can be pushed onto the heap several times as better distances are found. When an old copy with a larger distance is popped, relaxing from it is wasted work. Skipping whenever d > dist[u] keeps the result correct and efficient, and it lets you use lazy deletion instead of tracking which entries are in the heap.

topological-sort.name: Topological Sort
topological-sort.desc: Order the nodes of a DIRECTED ACYCLIC GRAPH so that for every edge u→v, u comes before v. Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degrees) is the go-to: repeatedly peel off nodes with zero in-degree. If not every node gets processed, the graph has a cycle.
topological-sort.q: Why can a zero-in-degree node always start a valid order?
topological-sort.qsub: What is the DFS-based alternative to Kahn's algorithm? · How do you produce the lexicographically smallest valid order? · Why is topological sort only defined on DAGs?
topological-sort.what:
Imagine a set of courses where some have prerequisites. You need an order in which no course comes before its prerequisite.

Kahn's algorithm is straightforward: first take any course that has no remaining dependencies, meaning in-degree = 0.

After you process it, the in-degree of every course that depends on it drops by 1. Any course whose in-degree reaches 0 is now "unblocked", so add it to the queue. This chain continues until nothing is left.

As a bonus, if not all nodes appear in the final order, the graph contains a cycle. Inside a cycle every node waits on another, so none of them ever reaches an in-degree of 0.
topological-sort.analogy:
Think of tasks in an office. First you pick any task that has no pending dependency. When it is finished, some of the tasks that were waiting on it become unblocked.
If you can't find any task that can start, then two or more tasks are waiting on each other, which is a deadlock. That is exactly a cycle.
topological-sort.why:
Topological sort answers two questions at once: ordering and cycle detection. Course Schedule I only asks "is it possible?", while Course Schedule II asks for the full order, and the code is almost identical.

A common mistake is reversing the edge direction. The pair [a, b] means "do b before a", so read the statement carefully. If you flip the direction, the order comes out reversed, but the code doesn't crash.

How to think:

1. Build the graph and an indeg array. For each edge u → v, do g[u].push(v) and indeg[v]++.
2. Add every node with indeg === 0 to the queue. Add all of them, not just one.
3. Dequeue a node u and append it to order.
4. For each neighbor v, do indeg[v]--. If it reaches 0, enqueue it.
5. When the queue is empty, check order.length === n. If yes, the order is valid. If no, there is a cycle.
6. For the lexicographically smallest order, use a min-heap instead of a queue.

qa.q: Why can a zero-in-degree node always start a valid order?
qa.a: A node with no incoming edges has no prerequisites, so it can be scheduled immediately without violating any dependency. Removing it only DECREASES the in-degrees of other nodes, which is exactly "one prerequisite satisfied". Repeat until everything is scheduled.

qa.q: How does topological sort detect cycles?
qa.a: In a DAG, there is always at least one zero-in-degree node to pick. If the algorithm gets stuck with nodes remaining, those nodes all lie on or behind a cycle, and none of them can ever drop to zero in-degree. So order.length < V means the graph has a cycle.

mst.name: Minimum Spanning Tree (Prim / Kruskal)
mst.desc: An MST connects every vertex with the minimum total edge weight. Kruskal sorts all edges and greedily adds them using union-find (O(E log E)). Prim grows one tree from a start vertex, always taking the cheapest edge leaving the tree (O(E log V) with a heap).
mst.q: When should you use Kruskal over Prim?
mst.qsub: State the cut property in one sentence. · Why does Kruskal need the graph to be undirected? · How would you build the MST of a complete graph from (x,y) points? · What if the graph is not connected? What does Kruskal return?
mst.what:
Say you are laying electric cable to every house in a new neighborhood. Cable is expensive, so you want to connect all the houses with the minimum total length and leave none out.

The answer is always a tree: connecting n nodes needs exactly n - 1 edges. Any extra edge would form a cycle, and an edge on a cycle is redundant.

Kruskal: sort all edges by weight. Go from the cheapest and keep taking edges, but skip any edge that would create a cycle. Union-Find does the cycle check.

Prim: start from one node. Each time, pick the cheapest edge that goes from the tree to a vertex outside it. The tree grows one vertex at a time. A min-heap drives it.
mst.analogy:
Kruskal is like a planner who lists every possible road by price and always buys the cheapest one next, but never builds a road between two places that are already connected.
Prim is like a tree growing from a single seed: it always extends toward the nearest (cheapest) spot around it.
mst.why:
MST and Dijkstra are the two algorithms people confuse most. Both are greedy, both use a heap, and both are about "minimum".

But their goals are completely different. MST minimizes the total cost of connecting everyone. Dijkstra finds the shortest path from one node to every other node. In an MST, the path between two nodes is not necessarily the shortest one.

One practical point: if the graph is not connected, no spanning tree exists (you only get a spanning forest). So at the end, check whether n - 1 edges were used.

How to think:

1. Kruskal: sort all edges [u, v, w] by w.
2. Create a DSU. For each edge, try union(u, v). If it returns true, take the edge. If it returns false, the edge would form a cycle, so skip it.
3. Once you have n - 1 edges, the MST is complete, so stop.
4. Prim: start from any node and push all its edges into the heap.
5. Pop the cheapest edge. If its other endpoint is already in the tree, skip it. Otherwise take it, and push all edges of the new node into the heap.
6. Which to choose: if you have an edge list or the graph is sparse, use Kruskal. If you have an adjacency list or the graph is dense, use Prim.

qa.q: When should you use Kruskal over Prim?
qa.a: Use Kruskal when the edge list is already available (so sorting is easy) or the graph is sparse. Use Prim when you have an adjacency list or a dense graph, since it needs no global sort, only a heap of edges leaving the current tree.

qa.q: How do you detect a cycle in Kruskal?
qa.a: With union-find. If the two endpoints of an edge are already in the same component, adding the edge would create a cycle, so skip it. A union-find with path compression makes each check nearly O(1).

bellman-ford.name: Bellman-Ford (negative weights)
bellman-ford.desc: Single-source shortest paths that, unlike Dijkstra, also handle negative edge weights. Relax every edge V-1 times: each pass extends the correct distances by one more edge. If a V-th pass still improves anything, a negative cycle exists.
bellman-ford.q: Why does Bellman-Ford need exactly V-1 passes?
bellman-ford.qsub: When is Dijkstra wrong but Bellman-Ford right? · What does "relax an edge" mean? · Why is Bellman-Ford slower than Dijkstra? · How would you enforce a maximum of K edges (hops)?
bellman-ford.what:
Dijkstra assumes that once a node is extracted as the cheapest, its distance is final. A negative edge breaks this, because a later path can make it cheaper.

Bellman-Ford makes no such assumption. It repeatedly relaxes all edges, exactly V - 1 times.

Why V - 1? A shortest simple path can have at most V - 1 edges, since more would mean repeating a node, which forms a cycle. Each round extends the correct distances by one more edge.

As a bonus, run a V-th round. If something still improves, the graph contains a negative cycle, where looping keeps lowering the distance forever and a shortest path is undefined.
bellman-ford.analogy:
Think of news spreading through a city. In the first round it reaches only the source's direct neighbors. In the second round it reaches their neighbors, and so on. After V-1 rounds even the farthest node has the news.
If another round still changes something, then there is a cycle of updates that keeps feeding itself.
bellman-ford.why:
The interviewer's first question is usually "Why not Dijkstra?" The answer is negative weights. This is not just theory, since negative weights show up in currency arbitrage and some routing protocols.

But the most common interview variant is Cheapest Flights Within K Stops. There are no negative weights there, but there is a limit of "at most k stops". Dijkstra can't handle that directly, while Bellman-Ford with k+1 rounds implements the constraint exactly.

How to think:

1. Create a dist array of Infinity and set dist[src] = 0.
2. Loop V - 1 times.
3. In each round, go over all edges. If dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v].
4. If nothing changes in a round, nothing will change later either, so stop early.
5. Negative cycle: run a V-th round. If anything still decreases, a negative cycle exists.
6. K-hop version: run k+1 rounds instead of V-1, and in each round read from a copy of dist. Otherwise one round could propagate a change across two edges.

qa.q: Why does Bellman-Ford need exactly V-1 passes?
qa.a: A shortest simple path in a graph with V vertices uses at most V-1 edges. Each pass extends the correct distances by one more edge, so after V-1 passes every shortest path from the source has been computed.

qa.q: How do you detect a negative cycle?
qa.a: Run one extra pass. If any edge can still relax a distance, a negative cycle reachable from the source exists, and shortest paths are undefined because they can keep decreasing forever.

floyd-warshall.name: Floyd-Warshall (all pairs)
floyd-warshall.desc: Computes shortest paths between every pair of vertices using dynamic programming. For each intermediate vertex k, check whether routing through k improves any (i, j) distance. It is simple, O(V^3), best for dense graphs, and works with negative edges (as long as there are no negative cycles).
floyd-warshall.q: Why must k be the outermost loop?
floyd-warshall.qsub: What does dist[i][j] mean after processing intermediate k? · How do you reconstruct the actual path after computing the distances? · Can Floyd-Warshall handle negative weights? · How do you detect a negative cycle with it?
floyd-warshall.what:
So far, every algorithm started from one source. Here the question is different: you need the shortest distance from every city to every other city, all at once.

You could run Dijkstra from each node. Floyd-Warshall is another option, and its idea is so simple that the whole algorithm is just 4 lines.

Treat each node k in turn as a possible stopover, and for every pair (i, j) ask: is going through k cheaper than the best route so far? If yes, update the table.

This is dynamic programming. After round k, each entry means "the cheapest path from i to j using only nodes 0..k as intermediates". That is why the k loop must be the outermost: it represents a DP layer.
floyd-warshall.analogy:
Think of an airline fare chart. Consider each city as a hub, one at a time, and scan the whole chart: "Is flying via Dubai cheaper than the best fare I have for this pair?" After each hub, the chart gets a little better.
Once every hub has been considered, the chart is fully correct.
floyd-warshall.why:
Two things get tested. First, k must be the outermost loop. Changing the loop order silently gives wrong answers, and the bug is hard to spot.

Second, when is it better than Dijkstra? When V is small (up to a few hundred) and you need the answer for all pairs. As V grows, O(V³) becomes infeasible: at V = 1000 it already takes about a billion steps.

How to think:

1. Create a V × V matrix and fill it with Infinity.
2. Set dist[i][i] = 0, since staying at a node costs nothing. Don't forget this step.
3. For each edge [u, v, w], set dist[u][v] = w. If there are multiple edges between the same pair, take the min.
4. Write three nested loops with k outermost, then i, then j.
5. Inside, use just one line: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]).
6. Negative cycle: after the algorithm, check whether any dist[i][i] < 0. If so, you can leave i and come back with a net gain, which means a negative cycle.

qa.q: Why must k be the outermost loop?
qa.a: After pass k-1, dist[i][j] holds the best path using only intermediates 0..k-1, for every pair. Pass k then adds k as an allowed intermediate by combining two such already-final values. If i or j were the outer loop, you would combine entries that hadn't yet been updated for earlier intermediates, and could miss better paths.

qa.q: When is Floyd-Warshall a better answer than running Dijkstra from each node?
qa.a: For dense graphs with small V. Running Dijkstra V times costs O(V E log V), which is worse than O(V^3) when E is close to V^2. Floyd-Warshall is also far simpler to write, and it handles negative edges.

euler-path.name: Euler Path / Hierholzer
euler-path.desc: An Eulerian path uses every edge exactly once (an Eulerian circuit if it starts and ends at the same vertex). Hierholzer's algorithm builds it by following unused edges and splicing cycles back in. Classic problem: Reconstruct Itinerary (use every flight exactly once).
euler-path.q: What is the difference between an Eulerian path and a Hamiltonian path?
euler-path.qsub: State the degree condition for an Eulerian circuit. · Why does Reconstruct Itinerary require sorted adjacency lists? · How do you choose the starting vertex? · What makes Eulerian paths easy but Hamiltonian paths hard?
euler-path.what:
So far, every traversal aimed to visit each node once. Here the goal is different: use each edge exactly once, and revisiting nodes is fine.

This is called an Euler path. If it ends where it started, it is an Euler circuit. The classic example is a postman who must walk every street exactly once.

Nicely, you can tell whether it is possible before running the algorithm, just by counting degrees. In a connected undirected graph: all degrees even means a circuit exists, exactly 2 odd degrees means a path exists, and anything else is impossible.

Hierholzer constructs the path with a slightly unusual method: keep moving forward along unused edges. When you get stuck, add that node to a list and backtrack. At the end, reverse the list to get the answer.
euler-path.analogy:
Imagine a courier who must drive down every street in a city exactly once. Passing through a square again is fine, but repeating a street is not.
He drives as far as he can. When there is no new street ahead, he notes that spot and backs up, checking whether any streets were skipped along the way.
euler-path.why:
The first test is the difference between Euler and Hamilton. Euler means each edge once, and it can be solved in O(E). Hamilton means each node once, and it is NP-hard, so no fast algorithm is known. A one-word difference puts you in a completely different world.

The second is Reconstruct Itinerary. People write a naive DFS with backtracking and get a time limit exceeded. Hierholzer solves it in O(E) because it never re-explores an edge; it just builds the result in reverse.

How to think:

1. First count the degrees (for a directed graph, compare in-degree and out-degree). If all are even, start anywhere (circuit). If exactly 2 are odd, start at one of the odd nodes (path). Otherwise it is impossible.
2. Take a stack and push the start node onto it.
3. If the node on top of the stack has an unused edge, take one, remove that edge, and push the other endpoint onto the stack.
4. If it has no unused edge left, append that top node to the result and pop it from the stack.
5. Repeat until the stack is empty.
6. Reverse the result. That is the Euler path.
7. For the lexicographically smallest path (as in Reconstruct Itinerary), sort each node's adjacency list beforehand.

qa.q: What is the difference between an Eulerian path and a Hamiltonian path?
qa.a: An Eulerian path visits every EDGE once. You can check whether one exists from the degrees in O(V + E) and then build it in O(E). A Hamiltonian path visits every VERTEX once, and even deciding whether one exists is NP-complete. Interviewers test that you know which is which.

qa.q: Why does Hierholzer build the answer in reverse?
qa.a: A node is added to the result only when it has no unused edges left. The first node to get stuck is therefore the true end of the path, and any side cycles that were skipped get spliced in as the algorithm backtracks. Reversing the recorded order gives one valid path that uses every edge.

trie-structure.name: Trie Structure
trie-structure.desc: A tree where each node maps characters to child nodes and carries a flag marking the end of a word. Inserting or looking up a word of length m costs O(m), no matter how many words are stored, because shared prefixes are never re-scanned.
trie-structure.q: Why is a Trie faster than a Set for prefix queries?
trie-structure.qsub: How do you delete a word from a Trie? · How much more memory can a Trie use than a hash set in the worst case? · How would you return the top-k autocomplete suggestions?
trie-structure.what:
Type ind into a search bar and suggestions like “india” and “indian railways” appear instantly, without anyone scanning an entire dictionary.

With an array of words, you would have to rescan the whole array for every new character. A Trie turns the words into a tree: each edge from the root represents one character, and reaching a node means “the text so far is a valid prefix”.

Each node also carries a small flag, isEnd, which says whether a complete word ends there. That flag is how “app” and “apple” can live on the same path.

The payoff: lookup time depends only on the length of the word, O(m). It makes no difference whether the dictionary holds 10 words or 1,000,000.
trie-structure.analogy:
Think of searching your phone contacts. Type R and only names starting with R remain; type a and only names starting with “Ra” remain. Each character is a filter that narrows the path.
Reaching “Ra” does not mean a contact named “Ra” exists; the isEnd flag tells you that.
trie-structure.why:
A hash map gives you exact matches only. For “all words that start with app”, it has no answer short of scanning every key.

Interviewers want to see that you understand the space-for-time trade-off: spend a bit more memory and lookups cost O(m), independent of the dictionary size n.

How to think:

1. The root is an empty node. It does not represent any character.
2. Each node has children: either an array of size 26 or a Map.
3. Insert: start at the root and look for a child for each character. If it is missing, create it; otherwise move into it.
4. On the node of the last character, set isEnd = true. Forgetting this step is the most common bug.
5. Common prefixes are shared automatically: the c-a part of “cat” and “car” is a single path.
6. Memory: in the worst case every word has its own separate path, which is O(total characters × 26). The more prefixes overlap, the more you save.

qa.q: Why is a Trie faster than a Set for prefix queries?
qa.a: A Set answers “is this exact word present?” in O(1), but “which words start with this prefix?” forces a scan of every entry. A Trie answers startsWith in O(m) by walking the prefix, because the shared structure is itself the index.

qa.q: Trie vs hash map for a dictionary of words?
qa.a: A Trie gives O(m) prefix search, shares memory across words with common prefixes, and works naturally with DFS for wildcards and prefix counts. A HashMap is simpler and also does exact lookups in O(m) (hashing reads the whole key), but it has no notion of prefixes and spends more memory per word. For pure existence checks the map wins; for prefix work the Trie wins.

trie-ops.name: Trie Insert / Search / Prefix
trie-ops.desc: The three core Trie operations (insert, search, and prefix search) plus the DFS extension for wildcards and collecting words. Once you have a walk helper, everything else is thin.
trie-ops.qsub: How do you count the words that start with a given prefix? · What does the DFS base case return for wildcard matching? · How would you find the longest word whose every prefix is also a word?
trie-ops.what:
The Trie is built. Now we need three operations, and they all follow exactly the same path: descend one character at a time from the root. They differ only at the end.

Insert: create any missing node on the way, then set isEnd = true at the end.
Search: the path must exist and isEnd must be true.
startsWith: the path only needs to exist. isEnd does not matter.

So write a walk helper that follows the path and returns the final node, or null. After that, search and startsWith are one-liners.

On top of this sits a DFS extension: a wildcard . (matches any character) and “collect every word below this node”, which is what powers autocomplete.
trie-ops.analogy: Picture a building where each floor stands for one character. Insert: as you climb, you build any floor that does not exist yet. Search: the whole climb works and someone lives on the top floor. startsWith: you only check that you can climb that far, whether or not anyone lives on the top floor.
trie-ops.why:
People often treat search and startsWith as the same thing, or put the isEnd check in the wrong place. That one-line difference is the real test.

The wildcard DFS shows you can combine recursion and backtracking on top of a Trie. That is exactly the skill needed for hard problems like Word Search II, where the Trie prunes the board search.

How to think:

1. Walk helper: start at the root and look for a child for each character. If one is missing, return null. If you reach the end, return that node.
2. search(word): get the node from walk(word). If it is not null and isEnd is true, return true.
3. startsWith(p): walk(p) !== null. That's it.
4. Wildcard .: for a normal character, go straight down. For ., DFS into every child; if any branch returns true, the result is true.
5. Collect all: DFS from the node downwards, building the string along the path. Whenever you hit isEnd, add the word to the list, but keep going, because longer words may follow.
6. The worst case for wildcards is O(26^dots), and you should mention that caveat.
where: O(m) avg, O(26^w) worst · space: O(depth)
Collect all words from a node

qa.q: How does the wildcard '.' work?
qa.a: At a wildcard position, branch into EVERY child; if any branch completes the word, it matches. This is a DFS over the fan-out. With k wildcards the worst case is O(26^k), but in practice it is fine because the Trie only contains branches that actually exist, so each level is bounded by the stored words.

qa.q: Why is a Trie ideal for Word Search II?
qa.a: Backtracking over the board separately for each word rescans shared prefixes again and again. With a Trie, a single DFS pass checks all words at once: the current Trie node tells you which words are still possible, so you prune any board path that is not a live prefix.

xor.name: XOR Tricks
xor.desc: XOR undoes itself: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. That makes it perfect for cancelling duplicates: every element that appears twice vanishes, leaving only the single one. O(n) time, O(1) space.
xor.q: Why does XORing all elements find the singleton?
xor.qsub: What if TWO elements appear once (find both)? · Can XOR solve the variant where the others appear 3 times? · Why does XOR need O(1) space when a hash set needs O(n)?
xor.what:
Every number in the array appears twice except one. Find it in O(n) time and O(1) space, so no hash map.

Two XOR rules do all the work: x ^ x = 0 (a value XORed with itself disappears) and x ^ 0 = x (XOR with 0 changes nothing).

So XOR the entire array together. Equal pairs cancel each other and the lone element remains. Order doesn't matter: wherever a pair sits, it still cancels.

Condition: every other element must appear an even number of times. Elements that appear three times won't cancel, so that variant needs a different trick.
xor.analogy:
Imagine a building's entry log where every person who walks in is later logged walking out. Each in/out pair cancels. Whoever is still inside at the end is the only person with an unmatched entry.
The order of the log doesn't matter; a pair is a pair.
xor.why:
This turns an O(n)-space hash map solution into an O(1)-space one, and interviewers love that jump.

A follow-up almost always comes: “what if two numbers appear once?” XOR everything, and the result is the XOR of those two numbers. Pick any set bit of that result: at that bit, the two numbers differ. Use that bit to split the array into two groups, then XOR each group separately. Explaining this earns big points.

How to think:

1. Start with result = 0.
2. XOR each element into result.
3. A value that appears an even number of times cancels itself: x ^ x = 0.
4. A value that appears an odd number of times survives: 0 ^ x = x.
5. Missing number: XOR all indices 0..n together with all values. Each present number cancels against its index, leaving the missing one.
6. Two singletons: XOR everything to get a ^ b. Then diff = xor & -xor extracts one differing bit. Use it to form two groups and XOR each group to get a and b.

qa.q: Why does XORing all elements find the singleton?
qa.a: XOR is commutative and associative, and x ^ x = 0. So every duplicate pair cancels to 0, and 0 ^ singleton = singleton. After full cancellation, what remains is the number that appears once.

qa.q: How does XOR find a missing number?
qa.a: XOR the array's values with every index 0..n. Each number that is present appears twice (once as a value, once as an index) and cancels. Only the missing number appears once, as an index, so it is the result.

bit-shifts.name: Bit Shifts & Masks
bit-shifts.desc: Left shift << multiplies by 2 and right shift >> divides by 2. Combined with bitwise AND/OR and masks like (1 << k), you can read, set, clear, and toggle individual bits. This is the basis of bitmask DP and packed-state problems.
bit-shifts.q: How do you check if a number is a power of two in one expression?
bit-shifts.qsub: How do you iterate over every subset of n elements? · How do >>> and >> differ on negative numbers? · How do you reverse the bits of a 32-bit integer?
bit-shifts.what:
Say you need to store 5 permissions for a user: read, write, execute, share, delete. Five separate booleans feel wasteful, yet all five states fit into a single number using 5 bits.

Left shift x << k moves bits k places to the left, which means × 2^k. Right shift x >> k does the opposite, ÷ 2^k.

A mask is (1 << k): a number whose only 1 is at bit k. With it you can read, set, clear or toggle any bit without touching the others.

This is the foundation of bitmask DP and subset enumeration, where an entire state is packed into one integer.
bit-shifts.analogy: Imagine a switchboard with 8 switches, each controlling a different appliance. To flip one switch you don't move the whole board; you touch just that one. A mask is how you say “only this switch”.
bit-shifts.why:
Subset enumeration and bitmask DP depend on this, and you will need it repeatedly in Phases 7 and 8.

Two JavaScript-specific traps are worth knowing. First, operator precedence: x & 1 << k !== 0 does not do what it looks like, so parentheses are required. Second, >> preserves the sign bit while >>> does not, and the difference matters for negative numbers.

How to think:

1. Read: (x >> k) & 1 shifts the bit down and ANDs with 1. Or use (x & (1 << k)) !== 0.
2. Set: x | (1 << k). OR forces that bit to 1 and leaves the others alone.
3. Clear: x & ~(1 << k). The inverted mask has a 0 only at that bit, so AND clears it.
4. Toggle: x ^ (1 << k). XOR flips the bit.
5. Subsets: all subsets of n items correspond to the numbers 0 to 2^n - 1. Each number is one subset, and a bit set to 1 means that item is included.
6. In JavaScript, bitwise operators work on 32-bit integers. 1 << 31 becomes negative, and 1 << 32 wraps back to 1.

qa.q: How do you check if a number is a power of two in one expression?
qa.a: n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) === 0. Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and all the zeros below it. If n is a pure power of two, n & (n - 1) clears its only set bit and gives 0. Any other n keeps at least one bit, so the result is nonzero.

qa.q: What is a bitmask and when is it worth it?
qa.a: A bitmask is a single integer whose bits encode a set of choices, for example bit k = 1 means element k is used. It turns subset and state operations into O(1) integer operations and is the backbone of bitmask DP (e.g. Traveling Salesman). It pays off when n is small (roughly n ≤ 20) and the states are combinations of elements.

n-minus-1.name: n & (n-1) Trick
n-minus-1.desc: The expression n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit of n. Repeating it counts set bits in O(number of set bits), faster than scanning every bit, and it also powers the 'is this a power of two?' check.
n-minus-1.q: Why is this faster than shifting every bit?
n-minus-1.qsub: How many iterations does the loop run for a number with k set bits? · How does this relate to the power-of-two check? · What happens when n = 0 in the counting loop?
n-minus-1.what:
We want to count how many 1s are in a number's binary form. The naive way checks each of the 32 bits one by one, so even a number with only 2 bits set runs the loop 32 times.

n & (n - 1) is a shortcut: it always clears the lowest set bit and leaves every other bit unchanged.

Why it works: subtracting 1 turns the lowest 1 into 0 and flips all the 0s to its right into 1s (a borrow). ANDing with the original n turns those flipped bits back to 0 (they were 0 in n), while the higher bits stay the same.

So the loop runs only as many times as there are set bits, not 32. As a free bonus, n & (n-1) === 0 means there was only one set bit, i.e. a power of two.
n-minus-1.analogy:
Imagine a building where some lights are on and you want to count them. You have a magic switch that, each press, turns off only the lowest light that is still on and leaves the rest alone.
The number of presses until everything is dark equals the number of lights that were on.
n-minus-1.why:
This takes the Hamming weight from O(32) down to O(set bits). But the real interview question is “why does it work?”, so explain the borrow rather than just quoting the formula.

Don't confuse it with its sibling n & -n. That one does the opposite: it keeps only the lowest set bit and clears everything else. They are two different operations.

How to think:

1. Take n - 1: the lowest 1 becomes 0, and all the trailing 0s to its right become 1.
2. In n & (n - 1), those flipped bits become 0 again after the AND (they were 0 in the original).
3. The higher bits are identical in both numbers, so they don't change.
4. Result: exactly one set bit is removed and the rest are untouched.
5. Count: while (n) { n &= n - 1; count++ }. Each iteration consumes one set bit.
6. Power of two: n > 0 && (n & (n-1)) === 0. With a single set bit, one step brings the value to zero. The 0 check is required, since 0 would otherwise pass.

qa.q: Why is this faster than shifting every bit?
qa.a: Shifting always checks all 32 bits. n & (n - 1) skips every 0 bit, so the loop runs once per SET bit. For a sparse number like 8 (1000), that is 1 iteration instead of 32.

qa.q: What does n & -n compute?
qa.a: It isolates the lowest set bit, returning its value as a power of two. In two's complement, -n is ~n + 1, which keeps the lowest 1 bit and inverts every bit above it, so ANDing with n leaves exactly that one bit. It is used in Fenwick trees and other lowest-bit tricks.

memo-vs-tab.name: Memoization vs Tabulation
memo-vs-tab.desc: Two ways to fill the same DP table. Memoization (top-down) uses recursion with a cache and computes only the states it needs. Tabulation (bottom-up) uses iteration and fills a table in dependency order. Same result, different trade-offs.
memo-vs-tab.q: When should you prefer memoization over tabulation?
memo-vs-tab.qsub: Why does naive Fibonacci blow up to O(2^n)? · What is a 'state' in DP terms? · When can you shrink the table down to a few variables?
memo-vs-tab.what:
Run a naive recursive fib(40) and it already takes seconds; a slightly larger input takes minutes. The reason is that subproblems like fib(35) get recomputed millions of times.

There are two fixes, and both eliminate that waste. They differ only in direction.

Memoization (top-down): keep the recursion you already wrote and add a cache. Compute each answer the first time, store it, and return the stored value on every later call.

Tabulation (bottom-up): drop the recursion. Start from the base cases and fill a table forward until you reach the final answer.

Both approaches fill the same table. In interviews, start with memoization, because it is a small change to the recursive solution you already have.
memo-vs-tab.analogy:
Think of exam practice. Memoization: whenever you solve a new problem, write the answer in a notebook. If the same problem shows up again, just look it up.
Tabulation: first write down the answers to all the easy problems, then use them to build up the harder ones, so you never have to look back.
memo-vs-tab.why:
Interviewers ask about the trade-off. Memoization is easy to write because it comes straight from the recursive solution, but deep recursion can overflow the call stack, and it only computes the states that are actually reached.

Tabulation needs a little planning (the fill order must respect the dependencies), but it is usually faster and safer, and it enables space optimization: if you only need the previous two values, don't keep the whole array.

A follow-up that almost always comes: “Can you convert this to bottom-up?”

How to think:

1. Write a brute-force recursion first. Get it correct; optimize later.
2. Identify the state: the parameters that change between calls.
3. Add a memo (array or Map) keyed by the state. Check the cache at the start of the function and store the result in it before returning.
4. To go bottom-up, size the table to the number of states and loop in dependency order, so whatever a state needs is filled before it.
5. Seed the base cases in the table.
6. Finally, check whether each dp[i] depends only on the previous 1-2 entries. If so, replace the array with a few variables for O(1) space.
where: O(#states × cost per state) · space: O(#states) + O(depth)
O(#states × cost per state) · space: O(table) or optimized O(1)-O(n)

qa.q: When should you prefer memoization over tabulation?
qa.a: Memoization is easier to get right (add a cache to a working recursion), computes only reachable states, and reads naturally. Prefer it unless recursion depth is a risk or the interviewer asks for the iterative version, in which case write tabulation.

qa.q: What's the key to a space-optimized DP?
qa.a: Find the dependency window. If dp[i] only needs dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], keep two variables instead of the full table. 2D problems often reduce to two rolling rows (or even one) when each cell reads only from the row above.

identify-dp.name: Identifying DP
identify-dp.desc: The pattern-recognition step. A problem is DP when it has overlapping subproblems (the same sub-solve is computed many times) and optimal substructure (the best answer is built from best sub-answers). Phrases like 'count ways', 'min/max cost', and 'is it possible' are strong signals.
identify-dp.q: How do you recognize DP vs a greedy solution?
identify-dp.qsub: What is the difference between 'count ways' and 'min cost' recurrences? · Why does a single counterexample kill a greedy approach? · How do you define a state for a two-string problem like Edit Distance?
identify-dp.what:
A new problem arrives. The first decision: greedy, plain recursion, or DP? Picking the wrong one is the most common mistake.

Check two things. Overlapping subproblems: draw the brute-force recursion tree and see whether the exact same subproblem (same parameters) shows up repeatedly.

Optimal substructure: does the best answer for the whole come directly from the best answers to its parts, without having to revisit earlier decisions?

If both hold, use DP. If only one holds, plain recursion or greedy is usually the better fit. A shortcut helps too: the problem's wording often gives it away, such as “how many ways”, “minimum/maximum cost”, or “is it possible”.
identify-dp.analogy:
Imagine planning routes through a city by subway. Whichever way you start, you keep asking the same question: “what is the fastest way from Central Station to the airport?”
When the same question gets asked again and again from different paths, you have overlapping subproblems, and that is your cue to cache the answer.
identify-dp.why:
Interviewers won't ask this step directly, but they know whether you did it. If you start coding without defining a state, they see right away that you don't really understand DP.

Also remember the greedy trap: a single counterexample kills greedy. In Coin Change with coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6, greedy picks 4+1+1 = 3 coins, but the correct answer is 3+3 = 2 coins. If you can't prove greedy works, switch to DP.

How to think:

1. Imagine the brute-force recursion and draw its call tree on a small input.
2. Does the same subproblem appear again? That means overlapping subproblems, so caching will help.
3. Define the state: “what changes from one call to the next?” One index → dp[i]. Two indices → dp[i][j]. Index plus remaining budget → dp[i][w].
4. Write the recurrence in words first, not code: “the best for this position is this choice or that choice, whichever is better”.
5. Pick the operator from the wording: “how many ways” → +. “minimum/maximum” → min/max. “is it possible” → ||.
6. Write the base case: the smallest input whose answer is known directly.

qa.q: How do you recognize DP vs a greedy solution?
qa.a: Try greedy: does the locally best choice always lead to the global best? If you can't prove it and counterexamples exist, use DP. A telltale sign is when the best answer depends on ALL earlier choices (for example, picking subsets under a constraint), not just the last one.

qa.q: What's the first question to ask when designing any DP?
qa.a: “What is the state?” It is the tuple of everything that changes between recursive calls. For Climbing Stairs it is i (the current step). For Knapsack it is (index, remaining capacity). Get the state right and the recurrence usually follows.

dp-1d.name: 1D DP
dp-1d.desc: dp[i] depends only on earlier indices (usually i-1 and i-2). This covers the Fibonacci, House Robber, and Decode Ways family. It is the simplest DP class, so master it before anything 2D.
dp-1d.q: How do you choose the recurrence for a 1D DP?
dp-1d.qsub: When does dp[i] depend on i-2 versus all previous indices? · How do you optimize LIS from O(n²) to O(n log n)? · What is the base-case trap in Decode Ways (handling '0')?
dp-1d.what:
You are climbing a staircase, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many ways can you reach step n? The answer depends only on the previous one or two steps; no older history is needed.

This pattern is called 1D DP: an array dp where dp[i] stores the answer up to position i, built from dp[i-1] or dp[i-2].

Fibonacci, House Robber, and Decode Ways all belong to this family. Only the transition rule differs: sometimes you add, sometimes you take the max.

There is also a free benefit: if you only need the previous two values, you don't need the whole array. Two variables are enough, which cuts space from O(n) to O(1).
dp-1d.analogy:
Suppose you pick up work shifts, but you can't work two days in a row. On each day, your decision depends on one thing: “what was my best total up to yesterday, or up to the day before?”
You never need to reconsider the whole schedule from the beginning.
dp-1d.why:
This is the first DP pattern that appears in interviews, and it teaches the cleanest form of state definition: one value per index.

If you are confused here (what dp[i] means, which earlier states it needs), that confusion only grows with 2D and bitmask DP.

The base-case traps are also right here: handling '0' in Decode Ways, and n = 0 and n = 1 in House Robber. This is where most people stumble.

How to think:

1. Write the meaning of dp[i] in one line, e.g. “the best/count using the first i elements”.
2. Base cases: handle i = 0 and i = 1 separately (empty input and a single element). Write these two first.
3. State the recurrence in words: “take this element or skip it, whichever is better”.
4. House Robber: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]). Skip gives dp[i-1]. Take means you must have skipped the previous house, so use dp[i-2].
5. Fill the array; dp[n-1] is the answer.
6. Space: if you only need the previous two values, keep two variables, but update them in the right order or you will overwrite the old value too early.

qa.q: How do you choose the recurrence for a 1D DP?
qa.a: Ask “what can happen at index i?” and list each possible choice. For House Robber you either skip (take dp[i-1]) or rob (take dp[i-2] + nums[i]), and the max is the answer. Every 1D recurrence is the best of the available choices, each expressed through earlier dp values.

qa.q: Why is House Robber II solved by running the linear solution twice?
qa.a: The circle makes house 0 and house n-1 adjacent, so you can't take both. Run the linear solution once excluding house 0 and once excluding house n-1, then take the max. Any valid answer skips at least one of them, and each run is an ordinary linear subproblem.

dp-unbounded.name: Unbounded Knapsack (Coin Change)
dp-unbounded.desc: Items can be reused any number of times. Coin Change (minimum coins) and Coin Change II (number of ways) are the templates. For counting ways, put the coins loop outside to avoid counting the same combination in different orders.
dp-unbounded.q: Why does the loop order differ between min-coins and ways?
dp-unbounded.qsub: When does unbounded DP degenerate into 0/1 (each item used once)? · How do you recover WHICH coins were used? · What do dp[0] = 0 and dp[0] = 1 represent?
dp-unbounded.what:
You have coins of 1, 5, and 10, and you can use each type as many times as you like. This is called unbounded.

Two different questions come up: “what is the minimum number of coins?” (Coin Change) and “how many ways are there?” (Coin Change II).

Here is what makes this topic tricky: the code for both is almost identical, and the only difference is the order of the loops. That order changes the answer completely.

Coins outer, amount inner → each coin is introduced once → combinations (order is not counted). Amount outer, coins inner → every coin is tried again for each amount → permutations (order is counted).
dp-unbounded.analogy:
Say you have an unlimited supply of 1 and 2 coins and want to pay 3.
If you finish one coin type completely before moving to the next (all the 1s first, then the 2s), then {1,2} is counted only once, giving 2 ways in total (1+1+1 and 1+2).
But if you reconsider every coin at each amount, {1,2} and {2,1} become two different answers, giving 3 ways.
dp-unbounded.why:
The effect of loop order is subtle but changes the answer completely, and the bug is hard to spot just by reading the code. That is why interviewers like it.

The test is whether you understand that combinations and permutations are different things, and that the loop order decides which one you get.

Another test is the difference between unbounded and 0/1. In unbounded, the loop runs forward (reuse is allowed). In 0/1, it runs backward (reuse is not allowed). That single line changes the whole topic.

How to think:

1. Min coins: dp[a] is the minimum number of coins for amount a. Fill dp with Infinity and set dp[0] = 0.
2. For each amount, try every coin: dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - coin] + 1). Loop order doesn't matter here.
3. At the end, if dp[amount] is still Infinity, the amount is impossible, so return -1.
4. Ways: dp[0] = 1 (there is one way to make zero: take nothing).
5. Keep the coins loop outer and the amount loop inner. Each coin is then considered once, which prevents duplicate combinations.
6. In unbounded, the amount loop runs forward (from coin to amount), so dp[a - coin] may already include the same coin. That is exactly the reuse.

qa.q: Why does the loop order differ between min-coins and ways?
qa.a: For MIN coins, order doesn't matter (1+2 and 2+1 cost the same), so either loop order works. For WAYS, putting coins on the outside treats each answer as a combination: every coin is introduced once, so [1,2] is not also counted as [2,1]. Putting the amount on the outside counts permutations instead.

qa.q: What's the recurrence for Coin Change?
qa.a: dp[a] = min over coins c of (dp[a - c] + 1). Pick one coin, reduce the amount by c, and use the best answer for the smaller amount. Since reuse is unlimited, the subproblem for a - c already allows using that coin again.

dp-2d-grid.name: 2D Grid DP
dp-2d-grid.desc: dp[i][j] is built from the cell above (i-1, j) and the cell to the left (i, j-1). Unique Paths and Minimum Path Sum are the templates; the grid's structure IS the dependency graph. Watch the boundary rows and columns.
dp-2d-grid.q: How do you derive the recurrence for grid DP?
dp-2d-grid.qsub: How do obstacle cells change the table? · What about diagonal or 8-direction movement? · Why are the edge rows and columns seeded with 1?
dp-2d-grid.what:
You stand at the top-left of a grid and need to reach the bottom-right, moving only right or down. How many unique paths are there? Or which path has the minimum cost?

Think backwards. How can you reach any cell (i, j)? Only from two places: from the cell above by moving down, or from the cell to the left by moving right. There is no third way.

So dp[i][j] is built from those two cells. The shape of the grid is the dependency graph; you only decide whether to add (counting paths) or take min/max (cost).

Seed the first row and first column separately, because they have nothing above or to their left.
dp-2d-grid.analogy:
Picture a city of one-way streets where you can only drive east or south. Every intersection can be reached in just two ways: from the intersection to its north, or from the one to its west.
So the number of routes to any intersection = routes to the north neighbor + routes to the west neighbor. You never retrace the whole city; the two neighbors are enough.
dp-2d-grid.why:
This is the first DP where the state is made of two numbers instead of one. The dp[i][j] way of thinking starts here, and it carries over to LCS, Edit Distance, and knapsack.

It is also the clearest place to learn it, because the state is visible: a grid cell is the state, with no imagination required.

In interviews, Unique Paths and Minimum Path Sum are common warm-ups. A direct follow-up then appears: “can you reduce the space?” The rolling-row answer comes from here.

How to think:

1. Define dp[i][j] in one line: “the answer from (0,0) to (i,j)”.
2. Ask how you could have arrived at this cell. With right/down moves, only from up and left.
3. Choose the operator: + when counting, min for cost, max for profit.
4. Boundary seed: the first row and first column each have only one neighbor. In Unique Paths every boundary cell is 1; in Min Path Sum it is a running sum.
5. Loop top-to-bottom, left-to-right, so both neighbors are already computed.
6. The answer is at dp[m-1][n-1].
7. Space: you only need the previous row, so keep a single row and overwrite it left to right as you go.

qa.q: How do you derive the recurrence for grid DP?
qa.a: Ask how you can ARRIVE at cell (i,j). With right/down moves, only from above (i-1,j) or from the left (i,j-1). Counting problems SUM the two ways; min/max problems take the MIN (or MAX) of the two incoming values, plus the cell's own value.

qa.q: How do you reduce 2D DP to O(cols) space?
qa.a: Each cell reads only its left neighbor (in the current row) and its upper neighbor (in the previous row). So keep just one row and update it left to right; the cell you overwrite is exactly the one you no longer need. You never touch rows older than the previous one.

dp-2d-seq.name: 2D Sequence DP (LCS / Edit Distance)
dp-2d-seq.desc: Two strings or arrays compared cell by cell. dp[i][j] is the answer for the first i characters of A and the first j characters of B. When the characters match you step diagonally; when they don't you take the best of the insert, delete, or skip options.
dp-2d-seq.q: Why the +1 sentinel row and column?
dp-2d-seq.qsub: How do you recover the actual LCS, not just its length? · Why is Longest Palindromic Subsequence just LCS(s, reverse(s))? · When can space be reduced to O(min(m,n))?
dp-2d-seq.what:
We have two strings and want to compare them: how much do they have in common (LCS), or how many operations turn one into the other (Edit Distance)?

dp[i][j] means “the answer for the first i characters of A and the first j characters of B”. Not the whole strings, only their beginnings.

Each cell asks one question: do the current two characters match?

Match: advance in both strings and add +1 to the score. This is the diagonal cell.
Mismatch: you must skip a character on one side, either from A or from B. These are the up and left cells, and you take the best of them.

This gives a table of size (m+1) × (n+1). The extra row and column represent the empty string. They provide the base cases and spare you special if checks.
dp-2d-seq.analogy:
Two friends are comparing their playlists.
When the next song is the same in both, they both move on and the match count goes +1.
When it differs, one of them has to skip a song. There are two choices, and the one that leads to more matches later is the right one.
The table remembers all these decisions so you never have to work them out again.
dp-2d-seq.why:
LCS and Edit Distance are two versions of the same table, and once you learn them a whole family opens up: Longest Palindromic Subsequence, Distinct Subsequences, Interleaving String, Regex Matching. They all follow the same pattern.

Edit Distance is used in the real world: spell-check, git diff, DNA alignment, and the “did you mean” suggestion in a search bar all rely on this algorithm.

In interviews, it checks whether you can define the state. If you can explain in words what dp[i][j] represents, the recurrence follows naturally.

How to think:

1. Build a table of size (m+1) × (n+1), with an extra row and column for the empty string.
2. Fill base cases: in LCS everything is 0. In Edit Distance the first row is = j and the first column is = i (turning an empty string into j characters needs j insertions).
3. For each cell compare a[i-1] and b[j-1]. Use minus one because the table is 1-indexed while the strings are 0-indexed.
4. Match: LCS → 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]. Edit Distance → just dp[i-1][j-1] (no cost).
5. Mismatch: LCS → max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Edit Distance → 1 + min(the three neighbors).
6. The answer is at dp[m][n], not m-1, because the table is 1-indexed.
7. Space: you only need the previous row, so keep two rows, giving O(min(m, n)).
where: O(m × n) · space: O(m × n) or O(min(m,n))
O(m × n) · space: O(m × n) or O(n)

qa.q: Why the +1 sentinel row and column?
qa.a: dp[i][j] means “first i characters of a vs first j characters of b”. When i = 0 or j = 0 one side is empty, and the answer is simple: for LCS it is 0, and for Edit Distance it is the length of the other string (all inserts or all deletes). Padding the table with an empty-string row and column gives clean base cases, so the main loop needs no special handling.

qa.q: What's the Edit Distance recurrence in words?
qa.a: If the current characters match, carry over the diagonal value. If not, it is 1 plus the cheapest of: delete a character (dp[i-1][j]), insert a character (dp[i][j-1]), or replace (dp[i-1][j-1]). The three operations ARE the three neighbor cells.

knapsack.name: 0-1 Knapsack
knapsack.desc: Each item is taken at most once: choose it or skip it. The capacity dimension makes it 2D: dp[i][w] is the best value using the first i items within weight w. Partition Equal Subset Sum and Target Sum are its classic LeetCode disguises.
knapsack.q: Why must the capacity loop run backward in 0/1 knapsack?
knapsack.qsub: How does Target Sum map to knapsack (transforming the equation)? · What's the difference between subset-sum and partition? · How do you recover WHICH items were chosen?
knapsack.what:
You have a bag with a fixed weight limit and several items, each with its own weight and value. Each item can be taken only once. What is the maximum total value you can fit?

For each item you have exactly two choices: take it or skip it. That's why it is called 0/1.

dp[i][w] means “the best value using the first i items within weight w”. Two dimensions are needed because two things change: which item you are considering and how much capacity remains.

The key point, the heart of the topic: when you compress dp into a single 1D array, the capacity loop must run backward (from high to low). If you iterate forward, dp[w - wt] may already include the current item, so the item gets used twice. That one detail separates 0/1 from unbounded knapsack.
knapsack.analogy:
Imagine a sheet listing the best haul for each bag size, and a single laptop is added to the market.
If you update the sheet from small bags upward, a big bag will read a smaller entry that already contains the laptop and add it again.
So go backward, starting with the largest bag. That way every entry you read still reflects the sheet before the laptop.
knapsack.why:
This pattern rarely shows up on LeetCode under its own name. It appears as Partition Equal Subset Sum, Target Sum, Last Stone Weight II, and Ones and Zeroes. Once you recognize knapsack, they all become the same problem.

The backward-loop trick is the most important “why” in DP. Once you understand it, you don't need to memorize the recurrence; you can work out for yourself which direction a loop should go.

Interviewers often ask exactly this: “why does the loop run backward?” It is a single question, but it reveals whether you truly understand DP or are just reciting a template.

How to think:

1. Spot it: you must choose a subset, there is a capacity or target, and items cannot be reused, so it is 0/1 knapsack.
2. State: dp[w] is “the best value achievable with weight ≤ w” (or a boolean: “can we reach weight w”).
3. Seed: dp[0] = 0 (or true). An empty bag is always valid, and forgetting this seed is a very common bug.
4. The outer loop iterates over items.
5. The inner loop iterates over capacity, backward: for (w = cap; w ≥ wt; w--).
6. dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt] + val): skip or take.
7. Subset Sum: replace the value with a boolean: dp[w] = dp[w] || dp[w - num].
8. Partition: if the total is odd, return false immediately. Otherwise set the target = total / 2 and run subset-sum.

qa.q: Why must the capacity loop run backward in 0/1 knapsack?
qa.a: Each item may be used once. Going forward, dp[w - x] might already include the current item (it was updated earlier in the same pass), which amounts to unlimited reuse. Going backward, dp[w - x] still holds the value from before this item, so the item is used at most once.

qa.q: How do you recognize a knapsack problem?
qa.a: Look for a subset-selection problem with a capacity-like bound, such as “does a subset sum to the target?” or “what is the max value that fits under weight W?”. If each item can be used once, it is 0/1; if items are reusable, it is unbounded; if the order of selection matters, the state needs a different dimension.

dp-state-machine.name: State Machine DP
dp-state-machine.desc: Track several STATES per day (for Buy/Sell Stock, whether you currently hold a share). dp[i][state] where state is either not holding or holding. The transitions model the buy, sell, and hold decisions.
dp-state-machine.q: What does 'state' mean in state-machine DP?
dp-state-machine.qsub: What does the cooldown state add? · Why start hold at -Infinity? · When is the single-pass min-so-far solution enough?
dp-state-machine.what:
You are given a stock's price for each day. You can buy, sell, or do nothing. What is the maximum profit?

If you define only dp[i] = “max profit up to day i”, you'll get stuck. The next decision depends on something that number doesn't capture: do you hold a stock right now?

If you hold a stock, you can sell today. If you don't, you can buy. The available moves are different in each case.

So put that fact into the state. dp[i][0] is the best profit when you don't hold a stock, and dp[i][1] is the best when you do. Each day, each state has just two roads: stay where you are, or switch to the other state (by buying or selling).

That's the whole pattern, and it scales: add a third state for a cooldown, or another dimension for k transactions.
dp-state-machine.analogy:
Think of a street vendor. Every morning he is in one of two situations: he has produce in stock, or he has only cash in his pocket.
His options differ completely: with produce he can sell, with cash he can buy.
So his books can't be a single number. They need two: “best result so far if I'm holding produce” and “best result so far if I'm not”.
dp-state-machine.why:
The entire Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock family (I, II, III, IV, with cooldown, with fee), six different LeetCode problems, can be built from the same template. Only the number of states changes; the thinking stays the same.

Even more important, it teaches you how to expand a state. When your DP doesn't work, the usual reason is that a necessary piece of information is missing from the state. This topic builds that reflex.

In interviews this is a very common follow-up chain: first the simple version, then “add a cooldown”, then “allow at most k transactions”. With the state-machine approach, all three are the same idea.

How to think:

1. Write the states. What changes your future options? Whether you hold the stock or not. If there is a cooldown, add a third state: sold today.
2. Write the transitions for each state: where you can go from it and what each move costs or earns.
3. Initialize: cash = 0 (nothing done yet) and hold = -Infinity (holding without having bought is impossible). Setting it to 0 is the most common bug.
4. Update both states every day. Both updates must read the old values, so save the old cash first (or compute both from temporaries).
5. The answer at the end is cash, not hold, because profit locked in a held stock isn't realized.
6. Fee? Subtract it when selling. Cooldown? Add a third state. k transactions? Add a dimension for k.

qa.q: What does 'state' mean in state-machine DP?
qa.a: The condition that determines your available moves, such as holding a share or not. dp[holding] and dp[cash] evolve day by day, and each can either “stay” or “transition”. Any other flag that gates decisions (a cooldown, a transaction limit) becomes another state dimension.

qa.q: How does the k-transaction version change?
qa.a: Add k as a dimension: dp[k][holding] and dp[k][cash]. Buying (or selling, depending on how you count) moves you to the next transaction count. The transition logic is the same, just indexed by how many trades you have used.

dp-interval.name: Interval DP
dp-interval.desc: dp[i][j] describes the segment from i to j. The answer for a segment combines the answers of smaller segments, split at some k. Canonical examples are longest palindromic substring/subsequence and burst-balloons-style problems where you 'choose the last action'.
dp-interval.q: How do you know interval DP applies?
dp-interval.qsub: How does palindromic subsequence use LCS? · What makes burst-balloon O(n³)? · When is expand-around-center better than table DP?
dp-interval.what:
So far dp[i] has meant “the answer up to a point”. In interval DP, dp[i][j] means “the answer for the entire segment [i..j]”: a range, not a single point.

Here is the twist. A larger segment can't be built directly from smaller ones. You have to choose a split point k inside the range and combine dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j], plus whatever cost or value the split itself creates.

Which k is right? You can't know in advance, so try all of them and keep the best. That is why the complexity is O(n³).

One more important point: dp[i][j] needs the smaller segments inside it, so the table must be filled in order of increasing length: first length 1, then 2, then 3. If you simply loop over i and j, you will read cells that aren't filled yet.
dp-interval.analogy:
Imagine cutting a long wooden stick where each cut costs the length of the piece you are cutting.
The question is where to make the first cut, because after that the two shorter pieces are handled independently.
You can't know the best cut in advance, so try every position and keep the one with the lowest total cost.
dp-interval.why:
This is the last classic DP shape. In 1D, 2D grid, 2D sequence, and knapsack, the state was built from one or two points. Here the state is a range and the transition is a split. It is a different way of thinking, and it takes practice.

Burst Balloons is the most famous interview question in this category, and it is hard because people think about which balloon to pop first. The right way is the opposite: ask which balloon to pop last. Then the segments on both sides become independent.

Matrix Chain Multiplication, Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick, and Palindrome Partitioning are all variations of this same idea.

How to think:

1. Write what dp[i][j] means: “the best answer for segment [i..j]”.
2. Base case: fill len = 1 by hand (and len = 2 too for palindromes).
3. Outer loop over LENGTH: for (len = 2; len ≤ n; len++). This is the most important line.
4. Inside it, iterate i and compute j = i + len - 1.
5. The innermost k runs from i to j-1: try every split.
6. dp[i][j] = best(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost).
7. The Burst Balloons twist: treat k not as the “first” balloon but as the “last one to pop”. Then both sides are independent, and the balloons bordering the range stay fixed.
8. The answer is at dp[0][n-1], the whole segment.

qa.q: How do you know interval DP applies?
qa.a: The answer is defined over a contiguous range [i, j] and decomposes into smaller ranges. For example, [i,j] is a palindrome iff s[i] === s[j] AND [i+1, j-1] is a palindrome. That “segment built from sub-segments” structure is the signature.

qa.q: Why expand around the center for palindromic substring?
qa.a: There are 2n-1 centers (each character and each gap between characters). Expanding from each takes O(n), so the total is O(n²) time and only O(1) space, beating the O(n²)-space DP table for SUBSTRINGS (contiguous). The table only wins when you need the palindromic SUBSEQUENCE, which isn't contiguous.

dp-bitmask.name: DP with Bitmasks
dp-bitmask.desc: When the state includes which elements have been used, encode it as an integer bitmask: bit i set means item i is taken. With memoization this handles subset partition, TSP, and assignment problems in O(2^n * n). That is exponential, but often the intended answer for n <= 20.
dp-bitmask.q: How do you recognize that bitmask DP is the right tool?
dp-bitmask.qsub: How do you check if bit i is set in a mask? · How do you add item i to a mask? · Why does n have to be small? · How do you prune a partition DP for speed?
dp-bitmask.what:
Sometimes the state must record which items have been used so far: not just how many, but which ones.

Storing a set in an array or a Set to use as a memo key is awkward. But if the number of items is small (n ≤ 20), the whole set fits into a single integer.

Each bit stands for one item. If bit i is 1, item i has been used. For example, 1011 means items 0, 1, and 3 have been taken and item 2 remains. As a number this is 11, and that becomes your array index.

The real benefit: the same set reached in different orders becomes one state. So n! permutations shrink to 2ⁿ subsets. That is still exponential, but 2²⁰ is about a million, which is fine, whereas 20! is about 2.4 quintillion, which is not.
dp-bitmask.analogy:
Imagine a bus seating chart where each seat is a box, filled or empty.
To describe the whole bus you don't need a list of seat numbers. A single line is enough: 1011.
If two groups of passengers book the same seats in different orders, their charts look exactly the same. That is what does half the work for you.
dp-bitmask.why:
This topic gives you a new tool: when the state is a set, turn it into an integer. The trick works well beyond DP, in graphs, backtracking, and state-space search.

There is also a very practical signal: if the constraints say n ≤ 20 or n ≤ 15, that almost always hints at a bitmask solution. A polynomial-time solution wouldn't need such a small limit; it is given because the intended solution is exponential.

Travelling Salesman, Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets, and Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes all appear in interviews and all follow this pattern.

How to think:

1. Look at n. Continue only if n ≤ 20.
2. Give each item a bit: item i gets bit i.
3. Write the state: dp[mask], or dp[mask][last] if it also matters which item was taken last (as in TSP).
4. Base case: mask = 0 (nothing taken) or mask = (1 << n) - 1 (everything taken).
5. Transition: try each unused item. If if (!(mask & (1 << i))) holds, the new mask is mask | (1 << i).
6. Memoize with an array of size 1 << n. It is faster than a map because the key is already an integer.
7. Prune: in partition problems, sort the items in descending order (big first), skip duplicates, and return as soon as the target is exceeded. This improves practical speed many times over.

qa.q: How do you recognize that bitmask DP is the right tool?
qa.a: The state is “which items are used” and n is small (about 20 or less). If the same used-set can be reached through different orders, memoizing on the mask collapses all of those orders into one state.

qa.q: Why is it O(2^n * n) rather than O(n!)?
qa.a: Bitmask DP merges all permutations that share the same used-set into one state. The n! orderings collapse into 2^n subsets, and each state considers at most n next choices. That is the whole win.

dp-digit.name: Digit DP
dp-digit.desc: Counts the integers in a range [0, N] that satisfy digit constraints (e.g. no consecutive 1s, only digits from a given set, not exceeding N). The state is (position, tight, extra flags). Tight means the prefix built so far equals N's prefix, so the current digit is capped.
dp-digit.q: What does the "tight" flag actually do?
dp-digit.qsub: How do you compute f(L, R) from f(N)? · Why is tight only a boolean, not a range? · What changes for properties like digit sums? · When would you need a "started" flag?
dp-digit.what:
The question: “How many numbers from 0 to N have no repeated digit?” and N can be as large as 10¹⁸. Checking each number individually is impossible.

The core idea of Digit DP is to stop seeing a number as a single value and see it as a line of digits that you build from left to right. There may be a huge number of values, but there are at most 19 digits.

At each position there is only one question: which digit can I place here? The answer comes from a flag, tight.

tight being ON means the digits placed so far are exactly equal to N's leading digits. In that case the current digit cannot exceed N's digit, or the number would become larger than N. But as soon as you place a smaller digit, the number is guaranteed to be less than N, and from then on every position can use any digit from 0 to 9. tight never turns ON again.
dp-digit.analogy:
Imagine setting a number on an odometer, turning one dial at a time, with N as the upper limit.
As long as every dial sits exactly on N's digit, you are on the edge: the next dial can't go past N's digit.
But once any dial is set a little lower, you have stepped off the edge. Now you can turn the remaining dials however you like, and the number stays below N.
dp-digit.why:
This is the most specialized topic in Phase 7, and it is worth being clear that it appears very rarely in typical product-company interviews. It does show up in competitive programming and in some hard LeetCode problems.

But it teaches a big idea that works everywhere: adding a flag to the state lets you handle a whole range constraint. tight is a boolean that encodes “am I still pressed against the upper limit?”.

It also gives you a reusable trick: reduce a range to a prefix, since answer(L..R) = f(R) - f(L-1). The same idea works from prefix sums all the way to digit DP.

How to think:

1. Convert N to a string, since you will work position by position.
2. Write the state: (pos, tight, started, problem-specific flag).
3. At each position compute the limit: if tight, it is N[pos]; otherwise it is 9.
4. Recurse on each allowed digit d. The new tight = tight && (d === limit).
5. Base case: pos === N.length. Decide whether this number counts.
6. Memo: cache only when tight is off (and include started in the key). Paths with tight on are visited only once, so caching them gains nothing.
7. Range: f(R) - f(L-1).
8. Leading zeros: keep a started flag, since zeros before the first non-zero digit are not counted as digits.

qa.q: What does the "tight" flag actually do?
qa.a: It records whether the digits chosen so far exactly match N's prefix. If so, the current digit must not exceed N's digit, and if it equals it, tight stays on. Once any digit is smaller, all later positions are free.

qa.q: How do you handle leading zeros?
qa.a: Add a "started" flag: zeros before the first nonzero digit don't count as digits. Turn it on once a nonzero digit is placed, and from then on treat zeros as normal digits.

heap.name: Heap / Priority Queue
heap.desc: A binary tree stored in an array that keeps the minimum (or maximum) at the root. Insert and extract are O(log n), peek is O(1). It is the go-to tool for "top k" and "smallest/largest/closest" problems. JS has no built-in heap, so you write your own small one.
heap.q: Why is a heap better than sorting for top-k?
heap.qsub: What's the difference between a min-heap and a priority queue? · How do you implement a max-heap in JS? · Why is heapify O(n) and not O(n log n)?
heap.what:
Say you have a large list and you repeatedly need just the smallest (or largest) item, while new items keep arriving. Sorting the whole list every time is wasteful, because you never need the full order.

A heap makes exactly one promise: the root is always the smallest (or largest) item. The other elements have no particular order. Promising so little is what makes it so cheap.

It looks like a binary tree, but it lives in a plain array: the children of index i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2. No pointers, no node objects.

peek is O(1). push and pop are O(log n), because the tree is only log n levels tall and an element moves along a single path up or down.
heap.analogy:
Picture the queue in an emergency room. The whole queue is not sorted by severity. The only guarantee is that the most critical patient is at the front.
When a new critical case walks in, they jump to the front and a few others shift back. Nobody re-sorts the entire waiting room.
heap.why:
"Top k" questions come up constantly: Kth Largest Element, Top K Frequent Elements, K Closest Points, Merge k Sorted Lists. The naive answer is to sort, which costs O(n log n). The heap answer is O(n log k).

A heap also works on a stream. Data keeps arriving and you can answer at any moment, whereas sorting would have to start over each time.

Since JS has no built-in heap, interviewers often want to see you write a small one. Knowing the name is not enough; you need to be able to implement it.

How to think:

1. Store the tree in an array. parent(i) = (i-1) >> 1, children(i) = 2i+1, 2i+2.
2. push: add at the end, then swap upward while the parent is larger (siftUp).
3. pop: remove the root, move the last element to the root, then swap it with its smaller child until it settles (siftDown).
4. Need a max-heap? Either reverse the comparator or store negated values.
5. The counter-intuitive top-k rule: to get the k largest, keep a min-heap of size k. A new element enters only if it beats the root, and then the root is evicted.
6. Never let the size exceed k. That is what gives you O(n log k).
7. Ties: if priorities can be equal, add a counter or secondary key so the order is predictable.

qa.q: Why is a heap better than sorting for top-k?
qa.a: A heap of size k costs O(n log k). When k is much smaller than n, that beats the O(n log n) of sorting. A heap also handles a live stream, while sorting has to start over for every new item. When k is close to n, sorting can win on constant factors.

qa.q: How do you find the median of a data stream with heaps?
qa.a: Keep the lower half in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap, with sizes differing by at most one. The median is the root of the larger heap, or the average of both roots when the sizes are equal. Each insert rebalances in O(log n). See the Two Heaps lesson.

heap-variations.name: Heap Variations
heap-variations.desc: Three variations that extend the basic heap: two heaps (median of a stream), k-way merge, and lazy deletion (mark stale entries and skip them later). They cover 'Find Median from Data Stream', 'Merge k Sorted Lists' and scheduling problems.
heap-variations.q: How does the two-heap median pattern work?
heap-variations.qsub: When does the two-heap trick fail? · What is the running time of k-way merge vs merging lists one by one? · Why does Task Scheduler need a cooldown-aware reinsert?
heap-variations.what:
A basic heap supports one question: "what is the smallest?" Real problems often need a little more, and three variations cover most of them.

1. K-way merge. You have k sorted lists to merge into one. Keep only the current front element of each list in the heap. Pop the smallest, append it to the output, then push the next element from the same list. The heap never holds more than k items, so the total cost is O(n log k).

2. Lazy deletion. Removing an arbitrary element from a heap costs O(n). Instead of deleting right away, mark the element stale and quietly discard it when it reaches the root.

3. Count, then heapify. In problems like Task Scheduler, count frequencies first, build a max-heap, run one task at a time, and push each task back once its cooldown is over.
heap-variations.analogy:
Imagine a station with 10 platforms and you need to build a single arrivals board.
You don't read every train's schedule. You look only at the next train on each platform, write the earliest one on the board, then look at the following train on that same platform.
The board never has more than 10 candidates at a time, no matter how many trains run in total.
heap-variations.why:
These patterns show up directly in well-known LeetCode problems: Merge k Sorted Lists (hard), Task Scheduler, Sliding Window Median and Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists.

They also teach a useful mindset. When a data structure lacks the operation you need, don't fight it. Reshape the problem to fit the structure. Lazy deletion is the clearest case: can't delete? Then don't delete, just ignore.

External sorting, used when data doesn't fit in RAM, is essentially a k-way merge, so this idea also appears in system design.

How to think:

K-way merge:
1. Push the first element of each list into the heap as [value, listIndex, pos].
2. Pop the smallest and add it to the output.
3. Push the next element from that list, if there is one. Repeat until the heap is empty.

Lazy deletion:
4. Keep a Set or counter of items that have been removed.
5. Before every pop, run a while loop that discards the root as long as it is stale.
6. The real size is the heap size minus the stale count.

Task Scheduler:
7. Count frequencies and build a max-heap.
8. In each round, pop up to n+1 distinct tasks, then push back those that still have remaining count.
where: O(log n) per insert · space: O(n)

qa.q: How does the two-heap median pattern work?
qa.a: The lower half sits in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap, with sizes differing by at most one. To insert, push into the lower heap, move its max to the upper heap, then move the upper heap's min back if the upper heap became larger. The median is the lower heap's root when sizes are unequal, otherwise the average of both roots.

qa.q: What is lazy deletion and when do you need it?
qa.a: A heap only lets you remove the root efficiently. To "remove" an arbitrary element, mark it as stale (a tombstone) and discard it when it surfaces at the root. Use it when real deletion would cost O(n), for example in Sliding Window Median or a priority queue with updates.

backtracking.name: Backtracking
backtracking.desc: A systematic exhaustive search: make a choice, recurse, then undo it. One template covers subsets, permutations, combinations and board search. Prune early so you don't explore dead branches.
backtracking.q: What is the one template behind all backtracking?
backtracking.qsub: When is backtracking the right tool and when is DP? · How do you prune a board search like Word Search early? · Why must you copy the path before adding it to the results?
backtracking.what:
Some questions don't ask for the best answer. They ask you to list every possibility: all subsets, all permutations, all valid boards. There is no shortcut, so you have to look at everything. The goal is to do it methodically and abandon bad paths early.

Backtracking has exactly three steps:

1. Choose: pick an option and add it to path.
2. Explore: recurse on the remaining decisions.
3. Unchoose: remove the option again (path.pop()).

The third step is the one people forget. Without it, the next branch starts with leftovers from the previous one and the answers come out wrong. It is the most common backtracking bug.

One more thing separates a decent solution from a good one: pruning. As soon as a branch cannot succeed, return right there and skip its entire sub-tree.
backtracking.analogy:
Walking through a maze, you chalk a mark at every turn.
When you hit a dead end, you go back and erase your marks. Otherwise, the next time you walk that corridor you'd think you had already been there.
Erasing the mark is exactly what path.pop() does.
backtracking.why:
This single template unlocks a whole family of problems: Subsets, Subsets II, Permutations, Permutations II, Combination Sum I/II/III, Palindrome Partitioning, Letter Combinations, N-Queens, Sudoku Solver, Word Search. They all share the same three lines. Only the pruning and the base case differ.

That makes it a great investment. Learn one template and a dozen interview questions open up.

Interviewers also want an honest complexity. Saying O(n × 2ⁿ) and knowing that the n factor comes from copying each answer is the kind of detail that stands out.

How to think:

1. Ask what the choices are at each step and when to stop.
2. Keep a path array holding the choices made so far.
3. Base case: if the path is complete, do res.push([...path]). Copy it. Otherwise every entry in the results list points to the same array, which ends up empty.
