4. For each choice, write three lines: push, recurse, pop.
5. Avoid repeats: for combinations, advance a start index; for permutations, use a used[] array.
6. Duplicates in the input: sort first, then if (i > start && a[i] === a[i-1]) continue.
7. Prune: if the sum exceeds the target or the board is already invalid, return immediately and skip the rest of that sub-tree.

qa.q: What is the one template behind all backtracking?
qa.a: Choose, explore, unchoose. Build the answer step by step, recurse on the remaining decisions, then undo the last choice so sibling branches start from the same state. Subsets, permutations, combinations and board search all fit this shape. Only the pruning rules change.

qa.q: How do you avoid duplicates (Subsets II, Permutations II)?
qa.a: Sort the input, then skip a value when it equals the previous one and the previous one was not used at this level: if (i > start && nums[i] === nums[i-1]) continue. This prunes sibling branches that would produce identical results.

greedy.name: Greedy
greedy.desc: Make the locally best choice at each step and trust that it leads to the global optimum. That only works when a proof (or strong intuition) shows local choices can't block a better overall result. Interval scheduling and Jump Game are the classics.
greedy.q: How do you know a greedy solution is correct?
greedy.qsub: Why does sorting by end time maximize non-overlapping intervals? · When does a two-pointer greedy fail? · How do you disprove a greedy with a counterexample?
greedy.what:
Greedy means taking the choice that looks best right now at each step and never looking back. No table, no recursion, just one pass.

When it works, it is the cleanest and fastest solution. The catch is that it often doesn't work, and when it fails you get no error, only a wrong answer.

So the real work in a greedy problem is not writing code. It is deciding whether greedy is valid at all.

There are two ways to decide. Exchange argument: assume the optimal solution does something different at the first step, then swap in the greedy choice. If the result never gets worse, greedy is correct. Counterexample: find one small input where greedy fails. Found one? Then greedy won't work, so reach for DP.
greedy.analogy:
You have one meeting room and want to fit in as many meetings as possible today.
Instinct says pick the one that starts first. That's wrong: a meeting from 9 am to 6 pm would eat the whole day.
The right rule is to pick the one that ends earliest. The sooner the room frees up, the more meetings fit.
greedy.why:
Interviewers like greedy problems because misusing greedy is such a common mistake. Candidates apply a greedy rule to a DP problem, pass a few sample cases, then fail the hidden ones. The interviewer wants to see whether you think first or start coding straight away.

When greedy is correct, it gives O(n log n) or O(n) where DP would take O(n²). That is a big difference.

Interval problems (Merge Intervals, Non-overlapping Intervals, Meeting Rooms) and reachability problems (Jump Game, Gas Station) are very common, and greedy is the intended solution for them.

A line that works well in an interview: "First I check whether greedy is safe. If an exchange argument works, I use greedy; otherwise DP."

How to think:

1. Write down the greedy rule: "at each step I will choose this."
2. Test it: run it by hand on 3-4 small inputs. If it fails, you need DP, and you found out in two minutes instead of twenty.
3. Prove it: use an exchange argument. Replace the optimal solution's first choice with yours and check that the result doesn't get worse.
4. The sort key matters most. Non-overlapping intervals: sort by end. Merging intervals: sort by start. Swapping them breaks the solution.
5. Keep a "best so far" variable: farthest reach (Jump Game), current end (scheduling), running sum (Gas Station).
6. Aim for a single pass. If you need to go back, greedy probably doesn't apply.
7. The complexity is often O(n log n) because of the sort.
where: O(n log n) or O(n) · space: O(n)

qa.q: How do you know a greedy solution is correct?
qa.a: Give an exchange argument: if an optimal solution differs from greedy at this step, swapping in the greedy choice never makes the result worse. The classic example is interval scheduling: replacing the first chosen interval with the one that ends earliest always works.

qa.q: Greedy vs DP: how do you decide quickly?
qa.a: If the locally best choice stays optimal no matter what comes later, use greedy. If later decisions can undo earlier ones, or the future depends on the choices accumulated so far (subsets, paths), use DP. When unsure, look for a counterexample; if you find one, DP is the safe fallback.

monotonic-stack-2.name: Monotonic Stack
monotonic-stack-2.desc: A stack that stays strictly increasing or decreasing: pop elements that break the order, then push. Each element is pushed and popped at most once, so it runs in O(n). It answers the 'next greater/smaller' and 'largest rectangle' families of problems.
monotonic-stack-2.q: When is the answer computed: on push or on pop?
monotonic-stack-2.qsub: How do you handle circular arrays (Next Greater Element II)? · What invariant keeps it O(n)? · Why store indices instead of values?
monotonic-stack-2.what:
In Phase 1 we used a monotonic stack to find the next greater element. Here the same idea goes one step further: we need both boundaries of each element, and from them we compute an area or a contribution.

Take Largest Rectangle in a Histogram. For each bar the question is: how far can this bar stretch at its full height? The answer depends on two things: the first smaller bar to the left and the first smaller bar to the right.

A monotonic stack finds both in a single pass. When an element is popped, two facts become known at once: the current element is its right boundary, and the new top of the stack is its left boundary.

So the key rule is: compute the answer on pop, not on push. Pushing is just bookkeeping.
monotonic-stack-2.analogy:
Stand in front of a building and ask how far your view extends on each side.
You can't know until you meet a taller building on each side.
The left side is already known. The moment the right side shows up, everything about that building can be computed at once, and you can cross it off your list.
monotonic-stack-2.why:
This whole family carries a "hard" label yet relies on one trick: Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Maximal Rectangle, Sum of Subarray Minimums, Trapping Rain Water, Next Greater Element II.

The naive solution is O(n²) and will time out on large inputs. A monotonic stack gives O(n), and explaining that difference clearly earns real credit in interviews.

It also teaches a useful mindset: count each element's contribution separately. In Sum of Subarray Minimums you don't loop over every subarray. You ask each element, "in how many subarrays are you the minimum?" and that count comes from its boundaries.

How to think:

1. Decide whether the stack should be increasing or decreasing. For Largest Rectangle it is increasing (heights rise from bottom to top).
2. Push indices, not values. You need positions to compute widths.
3. For each new element, while the top of the stack breaks the order, pop, and compute that element's answer at each pop.
4. Width formula: i - stack[top] - 1. Here stack[top] is the top after the pop, which is the left boundary.
5. Put a -1 sentinel on the stack at the start, so the index-0 case needs no special if.
6. At the end, pop whatever remains. Their right boundary is the end of the array. (Or append a 0 to the heights.)
7. Circular array? Loop up to 2n using index i % n, but push only during the first pass.

qa.q: When is the answer computed: on push or on pop?
qa.a: On pop. When the current element pops the stack top, the current element is that top's "next greater" (or its right boundary, in the histogram problem). Pushing is just bookkeeping; the pop is where the information is revealed.

qa.q: Why does the histogram solution use a -1 sentinel?
qa.a: The width is i - leftBound - 1, where leftBound is the new stack top after popping. A -1 sentinel makes that formula work even when the popped bar extends to the very start of the array, so index 0 needs no special case.

two-heaps.name: Two Heaps
two-heaps.desc: A max-heap holds the smaller half and a min-heap holds the larger half, balanced so their sizes differ by at most one. Insert is O(log n) and the median is an O(1) peek. This is the standard answer to 'Find Median from Data Stream'.
two-heaps.qsub: How does sliding-window median use lazy deletion? · What breaks if the two heaps use the wrong comparators? · Why may low be one element bigger but not high?
two-heaps.what:
Numbers arrive one at a time, and after each one you must report the median immediately. Sorting every time costs O(n log n) per query, which is wasteful. A sorted array with insertion still costs O(n) per insert because elements must shift.

The trick is to stop searching for the median and keep it always within reach.

Split the data into two halves. The smaller half goes into a max-heap (largest element on top) and the larger half goes into a min-heap (smallest element on top). Keep the sizes equal, or let low hold one extra element.

Now the median is always at the tops of the two heaps. No searching, just O(1).

To insert, use a round trip: always push the new number into low, move low's max to high, then if high is now larger, move its min back to low. These three lines maintain both invariants together: correct halves and balanced sizes.
two-heaps.analogy:
At a school assembly, split the children into two lines by height. In the short line, the tallest child stands at the front. In the tall line, the shortest child stands at the front.
To find the middle height, you don't need to scan the whole assembly. Just look at the first child in each line.
When a new child arrives, put them in one line and rebalance the lines. That's all.
two-heaps.why:
Find Median from Data Stream is a classic hard problem that shows up at Amazon, Google and Microsoft. Sliding Window Median is its harder sibling.

The bigger lesson is this: if you need something repeatedly, don't search for it each time. Maintain it as an invariant of your data structure. The same idea appears in LRU cache, sliding window maximum and many design questions.

It also shows you can reason about streaming data. Real systems receive a constant flow of stock prices, latency metrics and sensor readings, so re-sorting everything each time is not an option.

How to think:

1. Create two heaps: low is a max-heap (smaller half) and high is a min-heap (larger half).
2. Insert (three lines, always in this order):
  low.push(num)
  high.push(low.pop())
  if (high.size > low.size) low.push(high.pop())
3. This round trip guarantees both properties at once: the halves are correct and the sizes are balanced. No separate if checks are needed.
4. Median: if the sizes are equal, use (low.top + high.top) / 2. Otherwise use low.top.
5. Decide once that low gets the extra element, not high, and follow that rule everywhere.
6. Sliding window median: removing the element that leaves the window directly is expensive, so use lazy deletion and keep separate size counters.

qa.q: Why does this stay balanced?
qa.a: On every insert, push into low, move low's maximum to high, then if high is larger, move high's minimum back. This round trip guarantees that low always holds the smaller half and that the sizes differ by at most one, so the median is always at the two roots.

qa.q: What is the alternative to two heaps?
qa.a: A balanced BST with subtree sizes (an order-statistic tree) can find the median in O(log n), but it is much more work to implement. A plain sorted array makes inserts O(n). Two heaps give O(log n) inserts and an O(1) median, which is why they are the accepted solution for streaming medians.

heapify.name: Heapify / Build Heap in O(n)
heapify.desc: Turning an arbitrary array into a valid heap. Sift down every node, starting from the last internal node and moving back to the root. This is O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes are near the leaves and only sift down a short distance.
heapify.q: Why is heapify O(n) and not O(n log n)?
heapify.qsub: What is the index of the last internal node? · Why is building by sift-down faster than inserting n times? · How do you do heapsort with this? · Where does the O(n) come from mathematically?
heapify.what:
Say you have a random array and need to turn it into a heap. The obvious way is to call push() on each element. Each push is O(log n), so the total is O(n log n).

There is a better method that takes only O(n), and it surprises many people.

Heapify works in reverse. Start at the array's last internal node (i = n/2 - 1) and move backward to the root, running siftDown on each node.

Why is it cheaper? Because most nodes sit near the bottom, where there is little work to do. The leaves (about half of all nodes) are already valid heaps, so their cost is zero. The next n/4 nodes above them move down at most one level. Only the root can travel the full height.

Add it all up and the series sums to less than 2n, hence O(n).

Repeated pushing is expensive for the opposite reason: half the nodes are leaves, and with siftUp those same nodes may have to climb the full height.
heapify.analogy:
Imagine reorganizing a whole company by seniority.
If you start with the CEO, every change ripples all the way down.
If you start with the smallest teams, sorting out a few people among themselves, and work upward, there is very little left to fix by the time you reach the top, because each higher level has fewer people to sort out.
heapify.why:
"How long does it take to build a heap?" is a very common interview question, and O(n log n) is a very common wrong answer.

Giving the right answer and the reason in one line ("half the nodes are leaves, so their work is zero") shows that you understand the complexity rather than having memorized it.

It matters in practice too. For top-k style problems where the whole array is already available, heapify plus k pops costs O(n + k log n). Heapsort relies on it as well: O(n log n) time and O(1) space, guaranteed, since unlike quicksort it has no bad worst case.

How to think:

1. Find the last internal node: i = (n >> 1) - 1. Everything after it is a leaf.
2. Loop backwards, from i down to 0.
3. Run siftDown on each node, not siftUp. This is what makes the difference.
4. Why the reverse order works: by the time you reach a node, both its children are already valid heaps, so each siftDown only has to fix one node against its children.
5. Everything happens in place, with O(1) extra space.
6. Heapsort: build a max-heap, then repeat n times: swap the root with the last element, shrink the heap by one and run siftDown.
7. In an interview, say one line: "heapify is O(n) because half the nodes are leaves and need no sifting."

qa.q: Why is heapify O(n) and not O(n log n)?
qa.a: Most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a few levels. Summing each node's height over the whole tree gives a geometric-style series that converges to less than 2n. Building by repeated insertion is O(n log n) in the worst case, because about n/2 nodes may sift up the full height.

qa.q: Why start at the last internal node and sift down?
qa.a: A leaf is already a valid heap of size 1. Working bottom-up guarantees that both children of a node are heaps before the node itself is processed, so a single sift-down per node fixes the whole array. Going top-down or using sift-up instead is the insert-based approach, which is O(n log n) in the worst case.

timed-mocks.name: Timed Mock Sessions
timed-mocks.desc: 45-minute, no-hints, think-aloud problem solving under a timer, the closest rehearsal for the real thing. You have been doing one per week since Phase 3. Here the pace rises to one every other day for 30 days (10+ more mocks). The goal is performance, not learning new algorithms.
timed-mocks.q: How do you choose mock problems?
timed-mocks.qsub: How do you handle a problem you have never seen? · When should you stop coding and talk? · How do you simulate the phone-screen format?
timed-mocks.what:
You have solved 200 problems in your own room, with no timer, in your own editor. Then in an interview you get 45 minutes, a person watching you think, and your mind goes blank.

That is not a knowledge gap. It is a performance gap, and it needs its own practice.

A timed mock recreates that exact situation: a 45-minute timer, no hints and no Google, and you speak your thought process out loud the whole time, even if nobody else is in the room.

The real benefit isn't the mock itself but the review afterward. Watch the recording. Where did you go silent for 40 seconds? Where did you need a hint? Did you state the complexity correctly? After each mock, fix one habit.

Stop learning new patterns now. Learn to deliver what you already know under pressure.
timed-mocks.analogy:
Full-length timed papers before board exams aren't meant to make you revise the syllabus.
They teach you how to split three hours across the paper, and how to keep panic over one hard question from costing you the rest.
That skill never comes from reading chapters. It only comes from sitting down with a clock ticking.
timed-mocks.why:
The interviewer is not just looking for the right answer. They score four separate things: problem solving (what you do when you're stuck), coding (clean code), communication (can they follow your thinking?) and testing (do you catch your own mistakes?).

Three of those have little to do with the LeetCode grind. They only improve with mock practice.

There is also a practical point: onsite interviews are 4-5 rounds back to back, so mocks build stamina too. If you have never done two 45-minute sessions in one day, your mind will tire by the third round, and that round can decide the outcome.

How to think:

1. Choose a new problem, one you haven't seen, from your weaker patterns.
2. Set a 45-minute timer and start a screen recording with audio.
3. Keep talking the whole time. Silence is the biggest mistake, because the interviewer needs to see your thinking.
4. State the brute-force approach first, however naive it looks. The optimization grows from there.
5. Get your approach confirmed before you start coding. Jumping straight into code can waste 20 minutes on the wrong path.
6. At the end, test your own solution with one normal case and one edge case. Don't wait to be asked.
7. Review (15-20 min): watch the recording and write down three things: where you were silent, where you needed a hint, and whether your complexity analysis was right.
8. Log every mock. After a week, redo the same problem. That shows retention, not just a lucky first try.
where: 15-20 min after · space: write down gaps

qa.q: How do you choose mock problems?
qa.a: Draw from your weakest patterns, the ones you rate lowest in your confidence scores. Alternate: one mock from a weak area, one from a strong area. Repeat the same problem a week later to measure retention, not just first-try success.

qa.q: What should the review focus on?
qa.a: Three things: (1) silence, meaning where you stopped talking; (2) the moment you reached for a hint, and whether you could have pushed through; (3) whether your complexity analysis was correct. Each mock should fix one concrete habit, not just "do better".

system-design.name: System Design Basics
system-design.desc: Design a large system in 45 minutes: requirements, estimation, data model, API, components, deep dive. A simple framework beats memorized designs. Know the URL shortener, rate limiter and chat app cold.
system-design.q: What is the difference between a senior and a mid-level design interview?
system-design.qsub: When do you choose a queue over synchronous calls? · What does 'eventually consistent' mean for a feed? · How do you estimate storage for 100M users?
system-design.what:
Imagine the interviewer says "design a URL shortener" and you immediately start writing the database schema. Five minutes later they ask "what's the scale?" and you have no answer.

The biggest risk in a system design round is improvising. You always miss something important, and it is a different something each time.

The cure is a framework that you apply to every question, whatever the topic:

Requirements → Estimations → Data model → API → Components → Deep dive.

It doesn't make you smarter. It stops you from forgetting things, and it shows the interviewer that you break a vague problem down methodically.

Also, there is no single correct answer here. You earn points not for the answer but for discussing trade-offs: "I chose this, its downside is X, and in this case that downside is acceptable."
system-design.analogy:
A wedding planner doesn't start with decorations.
First comes how many guests and what budget (requirements), then how big the venue must be (estimation), then who sits where (data model), and only after that the stage and catering details (deep dive).
Following that order keeps a huge event under control, while skipping it can derail even a small one.
system-design.why:
In senior and staff loops, system design takes up a large share of the onsite, and mid-level candidates now commonly get a round too.

It is a completely different skill from DSA. In DSA there is one correct answer; here there isn't. In DSA you solve a problem; here you drive the conversation.

The mid vs senior gap shows up here as well. A mid-level candidate needs prompts ("what about caching?", "what if it fails?"), while a senior candidate raises those points unprompted and discusses the trade-offs.

A practical tip: learn three reference systems cold: URL shortener, rate limiter and chat app. Most questions are built from the same building blocks (hashing, sharding, queues, fan-out, websockets, caches).

How to think:

1. Requirements (5 min). Cover both functional and non-functional needs, and trim the scope: "I'll leave analytics out for now and add it later if time permits."
2. Estimations (5 min). DAU × requests per user ÷ 86,400 = QPS. Peak is 2-3× that. Storage = item size × item count. Say the numbers out loud; this is where most people stumble.
3. Data model (5 min). Which entities, which indexes, SQL or NoSQL, and why.
4. API (5 min). Two or three endpoints are enough. What goes in, what comes out.
5. Components (10 min). Boxes and arrows: client, load balancer, service, cache, DB. Add a queue when work can be asynchronous.
6. Deep dive (15 min). Pick one hard part: hot keys, ID generation, consistency, fan-out. Choosing a trivial part is the biggest mistake.
7. For every major choice, also state its downside. This habit can change the whole round.
where: Req → Est → Data → API → Comp → Dive · space: ~10 min each

qa.q: What is the difference between a senior and a mid-level design interview?
qa.a: Seniors are expected to drive the conversation and handle trade-offs (consistency vs availability, caching strategy, failure modes) without being prompted. A clear framework plus explicit trade-off reasoning is what separates the two.

qa.q: How deep should estimations go?
qa.a: One or two levels: daily active users × requests per user gives QPS, and storage per item × number of items gives total storage. Exact numbers matter less than a clear chain of reasoning and a sanity check on the order of magnitude (thousands vs billions).

spaced-repetition.name: Spaced Repetition & Review
spaced-repetition.desc: Revisit every problem you got wrong in phases 0-8 at growing intervals: next day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks. Re-solve without looking at old notes. This turns "I've seen this" into "I can solve this cold".
spaced-repetition.q: Why use spaced repetition instead of mass review?
spaced-repetition.qsub: How do you decide a problem has 'graduated'? · What do you do with a problem you keep failing? · How many problems should be in the active review queue?
spaced-repetition.what:
You solved a hard DP problem. You understood the solution and felt good about it. Three weeks later the same problem appears and you get stuck again.

This is normal. The brain discards what it doesn't use, and the forgetting pattern is predictable.

Spaced repetition exploits that predictability. You re-solve each problem you got wrong at growing intervals: the next day, then after 3 days, then after 1 week, then after 2 weeks. Each review lands just as you are about to forget, so the memory gets stronger.

The most important rule: don't open your old note and read it. Solve from scratch first, and open the note afterward to compare, not to get a prompt.

Reading only trains recognition ("yes, I've seen this"), while solving trains recall. Interviews test recall.
spaced-repetition.analogy:
Think of learning vocabulary with flashcards.
Cram a word once and it is gone in a week. But review it at growing intervals (tomorrow, in three days, in a week) and it sticks for good.
Forgot a card? Move it back to a shorter interval and build up again.
spaced-repetition.why:
An interviewer won't ask about this directly, but the result is obvious. When you read a problem and instantly think "this is a sliding window" without long analysis, that is spaced repetition paying off.

The first and most important step in an interview is recognizing the pattern. If that takes you five minutes, writing a full solution in 45 minutes becomes hard.

It also saves time. Mastering 150 problems you can actually solve is more valuable than skimming 300. People who rush through 300 still go blank in interviews, because they never practiced recall.

How to think:

1. Every day, log any problem you got wrong, needed a hint for, or found very hard, with today's date.
2. Next day: re-solve it without looking at the note. Try from scratch first.
3. If you solve it cleanly (within the time, no hints), lengthen the interval to 3 days.
4. If you get stuck, drop the interval back to 1 day. There is no shame in it; the system is built for exactly this.
5. Ladder: 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks, then graduate.
6. After solving, open your old note and compare. Was the approach the same? Was there a better one?
7. Keep the queue under 10. If it grows, stop adding new problems and clear the backlog first.
8. Failing the same problem three times isn't about that problem. It points to a gap in the pattern. Study the topic again, then put the problem back in the queue.

qa.q: Why use spaced repetition instead of mass review?
qa.a: Forgetting follows a predictable curve, and reviewing just before you would forget strengthens memory most efficiently. Spaced intervals beat re-solving everything in one weekend, both for retention and for time spent.

qa.q: Why re-solve before reading your own notes?
qa.a: Reading your solution first tests recognition, not recall: you nod along without being able to reproduce it. Re-solving cold forces retrieval, which is what an interview measures. The note then becomes a comparison, not a prompt.

behavioral.name: Behavioral Prep (STAR)
behavioral.desc: Five polished STAR stories (Situation, Task, Action, Result): toughest challenge, team conflict, failure and lesson, mentoring or leading, and a data-driven decision. Numbers and ownership language turn a story into a strong signal.
behavioral.q: What makes a STAR story strong rather than generic?
behavioral.qsub: How do you answer 'tell me about a failure' without sounding bad? · What is a good question to ask the interviewer? · How do you handle behavioral questions in a system-design round?
behavioral.what:
Imagine the interviewer asks: “Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate.” You ramble for five minutes with no clear situation and no clear result. All the interviewer learns is that you can't explain your work clearly.

STAR is a framework that turns your real experience into a tight 2-3 minute story:

Situation — where, when and what the context was (20%)
Task — what you were responsible for (10%)
Action — what you did, and why (60%)
Result — what happened, with numbers (10%)

The point isn't to invent anything. It is to frame what you actually did so the interviewer clearly sees what you thought and what you did.

Two things make a big difference: say "I" instead of "we", and put a number in the result.
behavioral.analogy:
Think of telling a friend a good story: you set the scene, explain the problem, describe what you did, and finish with how it ended.
If you jump straight to the ending, the story feels empty. If you wander through details with no point, it gets boring.
STAR simply keeps your story in that tight shape.
behavioral.why:
The behavioral round is often one of the first conversations of an onsite, and it creates the first impression that colors the rest of the day.

Interviewers use it because coding skill and teamwork are different things. They want to see how you actually handle conflict, failure and ambiguity, not how you would hypothetically.

It is also the round candidates prepare for least, so a small amount of effort here has the biggest payoff. Even strong engineers come across as vague or defensive when a tough question arrives and they have no prepared stories.

At large companies, your level can also depend on this round, because it is where they hear the language of scope, ownership and impact.

How to think:

1. Choose five stories from your career: your toughest project, a team conflict, a mistake and its lesson, a time you taught or led someone, and a data-driven decision.
2. Write each one in STAR format. Action should be the longest part, because that is where your decisions show.
3. Include a number. Not "it got faster" but "p95 latency dropped from 800 ms to 120 ms". If there is no number, describe the before and after.
4. Say "I". Credit the team in a separate sentence, but keep your own contribution clear.
5. Rehearse out loud and record yourself. Reading in your head isn't enough; speaking reveals where you wander.
6. Keep it to 2-3 minutes. If it runs long, trim it. The interviewer will ask for more if they want it.
7. "Why this company" in three lines: what they do (specifically), why you like it, and what you'll bring.
8. Prepare two questions for them. Having "no questions" is a bad signal.
where: S → T → A → R · space: Action ~60%, Situation ~20%
out loud, 3+ times · space: record yourself

qa.q: What makes a STAR story strong rather than generic?
qa.a: Specificity and ownership. Use real numbers, name the tools, and make your own contribution clear instead of saying "we". The Action part should be the longest and should show your decision-making, and the Result should be measurable.

qa.q: How do you prepare for "why this company"?
qa.a: Use three sentences: what they do (specifically, not a tagline), why that excites you (tied to your experience), and what you would bring (one concrete skill). Rehearse it, and be ready to adapt it to the interviewer's team.

platforms.name: Practice Platforms
platforms.desc: Where to practice: neetcode.io for pattern-based roadmaps, LeetCode weekly contests for speed under pressure, and Pramp or interviewing.io for free peer mocks. Use each one for its strength.
platforms.q: NeetCode vs LeetCode Top 150 vs Grind 75: how do you choose?
platforms.qsub: How many problems a day is sustainable? · When do you use company-tagged problem sets? · What role do editorial videos play, and when do they hurt?
platforms.what:
Say you start doing random LeetCode problems, easy arrays one day and hard graphs the next. After two months your solved count has gone up, but nothing feels solid.

The problem isn't the platform. An interview demands three different skills, and no single place trains all three:

1. Pattern recognition. The moment you read a problem you should think "this is a sliding window". neetcode.io builds this, because its problems are grouped by pattern rather than by topic.

2. Speed. Solving while the clock runs. LeetCode contests build this. One per week, 90 minutes, and the real benefit is the post-contest review.

3. Coding in front of a person. This only comes from peer mocks on Pramp or interviewing.io. Test cases don't judge you; a human does.

One tip saves a lot of time: which list you pick matters least. NeetCode 150, Grind 75 and Top Interview 150 overlap by about 80%. The real decision is to pick one list and finish it.
platforms.analogy:
In the gym, each machine trains something different: the treadmill builds stamina, weights build strength, and a sparring partner gives you the feel of a real fight.
Three months on the treadmill won't teach you to throw a punch.
And switching gyms every week stops you from progressing on any machine.
platforms.why:
Most people waste time here. They keep switching roadmaps, pad their count with easy problems, and believe they've learned something by watching solution videos.

None of that resembles a real interview.

People especially avoid contests because they're uncomfortable, and that is their real value. In a contest you face a new problem with the clock ticking, exactly like an interview. Your rank is meaningless; the review of the problems you failed is everything.

As for peer mocks, coding aloud in front of a stranger feels very odd the first time. By the fourth or fifth mock it feels normal, and you'll notice that difference in a real interview.

How to think:

1. Pick one list. NeetCode 150 is a good choice because it's organized by pattern. Work through it in order rather than jumping around.
2. Solve 2-3 problems a day. More isn't sustainable, and you need time for review.
3. Spend 20-30 minutes on each problem on your own first. Only then look at the solution.
4. One contest per week. Take the full 90 minutes. Ignore the rank and review which problems you missed and why.
5. One peer mock per week (Pramp is free). Playing the interviewer teaches you as much as playing the candidate.
6. When should you start contests? When you can solve medium problems comfortably without a timer. Before that, contests only demotivate.
7. Do company-tagged problems in the 2 weeks before the onsite. Doing them earlier has no benefit.
8. Don't watch an editorial video before you've attempted the problem. Watch it after you've written your own solution.

qa.q: NeetCode vs LeetCode Top 150 vs Grind 75: how do you choose?
qa.a: They overlap heavily. Pick one structured list (NeetCode 150 is well organized by pattern) and work through it in order. Which list you choose matters less than consistently mapping problems to patterns and reviewing at spaced intervals. Contests add the pressure.

qa.q: When should you start contests?
qa.a: When you can consistently solve mediums without a timer. Contests measure speed, and speed without correctness is just noise. One contest a week is enough; the real value is reviewing the problems you failed afterward.
